assumptions.title: Product managers and business owners will participate in scope validation and use-case review
assumptions.description: The program assumes that product managers and business owners will actively participate in validating HIPAA scope and reviewing use cases where PHI may be processed.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Accurate identification of in-scope products and PHI use cases requires detailed knowledge held by product managers and business owners, and the program is designed around their engagement.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The corporate culture and governance model generally require product and business owner involvement in compliance projects; however, competing priorities could limit their availability, so this assumption is reasonable but not guaranteed.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If engagement is lower than expected, escalate to segment and functional leadership, leverage SteerCo authority to mandate participation, and consider dedicating central resources or business analysts to perform additional discovery in under-engaged areas.
assumptions.validation_method: Track participation of product managers and business owners in scope workshops, assessments, and reviews; confirm that each product with potential PHI use cases has documented input from its owner.

validation_owner.name: Program Manager for HIPAA Compliance Program

assumptions.title: Privacy Office and Risk & Compliance will continue to provide centralized guidance
assumptions.description: The project assumes that existing support functions, specifically the Privacy Office and Risk & Compliance, will continue to provide centralized guidance for HIPAA compliance activities.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The future-state HIPAA compliance framework and oversight model rely on these functions to define controls, policies, and monitoring, and they are already acting as central guidance providers.
assumptions.validity_explanation: These functions are integral to enterprise risk and privacy governance and are already leading aspects of the HIPAA program, making it highly likely they will continue to provide guidance throughout the project.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If centralized guidance capacity is reduced, appoint interim leaders or expand responsibilities of existing officers (e.g., interim HIPAA Compliance Officer) and consider external advisory support to maintain momentum.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm that Privacy Office and Risk & Compliance maintain dedicated roles for HIPAA and continue participating in SteerCo, program design, and assessments.

assumptions.title: Leadership sponsorship from the Chief Operating & Technology Officer and Chief Legal Officer will remain in place
assumptions.description: The project assumes that the Chief Operating & Technology Officer and Chief Legal Officer will continue to sponsor the HIPAA Controls Enhancement Program.

owner.name: Chief Operating & Technology Officer and Chief Legal Officer

assumptions.rationale_basis: Executive sponsorship is critical to secure funding, resources, and cross-functional participation for a multi-year HIPAA program.
assumptions.validity_explanation: While executive sponsorship is currently strong, leadership priorities can shift over a multi-year period, so continued sponsorship is likely but not guaranteed.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If sponsorship weakens, seek formal endorsement from broader executive leadership (e.g., RC, O&T, Legal leadership), present risk and compliance implications, and adjust program scope to focus on highest-risk areas while attempting to regain executive support.
assumptions.validation_method: Review SteerCo membership and confirm ongoing participation and approvals from the sponsoring executives; monitor whether their directives continue to support the program.

assumptions.title: Contractual obligations imposing HIPAA-like requirements can be identified and included in scope
assumptions.description: The project assumes that contractual obligations (BAAs/BASAs or BAA-like clauses) that impose HIPAA or HIPAA-like requirements on products not directly regulated will be identifiable and can be incorporated into scope assessments.
assumptions.rationale_basis: To ensure comprehensive coverage, the program must account for contractual obligations beyond strictly regulated HIPAA products, and this requires being able to identify such obligations in contracts.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Initial contract searches have begun and data dumps are being produced, indicating feasibility; however, contract complexity and legacy agreements may make it difficult to ensure 100% coverage.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If comprehensive identification proves difficult, prioritize high-risk segments (e.g., healthcare, insurance, GLLF) and implement forward-looking controls such as standardized BAA templates and contract intake processes to better capture future obligations.
assumptions.validation_method: Complete contract searches for BAAs/BASAs and BAA-like clauses, validate findings against proposed in-scope products, and confirm with legal and commercial teams that the coverage is comprehensive.

assumptions.title: Funding and staffing will be sufficient to execute assessments and initial control enhancements
assumptions.description: The program assumes that funding and staffing levels will be adequate to complete HIPAA assessments, gap analyses, and initial control enhancement roadmaps across in-scope products and services.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The scope of assessments and remediation (including external advisory support) requires material investment and dedicated resources over multiple years.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Some funding and staffing have already been secured, but future phases and remediation costs may require additional approvals, creating some uncertainty.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If funding or staffing constraints arise, re-prioritize assessments and remediation to focus on highest-risk products and obligations, leverage external advisors selectively, and seek incremental funding with clear justification based on risk reduction and contractual requirements.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor budget approvals, actual spend, and staffing assignments against the planned assessment and remediation roadmap.

assumptions.title: Steering Committee (SteerCo) and program governance will be established and effective
assumptions.description: The program assumes that a SteerCo with representation from key functions (Commercial Excellence, GCO, O&T, Product, Finance, etc.) will be formed and will effectively drive accountability and decision-making.

owner.name: HIPAA Program Sponsor and Program Manager

assumptions.rationale_basis: The complexity and cross-functional nature of HIPAA compliance requires a governance body to prioritize work, resolve trade-offs, and oversee risk decisions.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Initial steps toward governance (identifying membership and scheduling kickoff) are underway, but effectiveness will depend on ongoing engagement and clarity of mandate.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If SteerCo participation or effectiveness is weak, refine the charter, seek stronger executive sponsorship, adjust membership, or institute smaller working groups with delegated authority for operational decisions.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm SteerCo formation, membership, charter, and regular meeting cadence; evaluate whether key decisions and escalations are being handled through this forum.

assumptions.title: Scope of in-scope products can be accurately determined based on upload capability and known PHI use cases
assumptions.description: The program assumes that focusing on products with upload capabilities and known PHI-related patterns will allow accurate determination of which products and services are in-scope for HIPAA.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Upload capability is a primary driver of whether customers can input PHI, and initial surveys have identified specific patterns (interaction with clients of customers, matter/document management, billing products).
assumptions.validity_explanation: The approach is aligned with how customers typically supply PHI (through file uploads and similar mechanisms), but edge cases or indirect data flows may still exist.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If gaps emerge during audits or data handling reviews, expand the scoping methodology to include additional criteria (e.g., integrations, logs, support channels) and revisit products initially deemed out of scope.
assumptions.validation_method: Compare scope results against contract data (BAAs/BASAs), customer use cases, and findings from data handling reviews to confirm that no significant PHI-processing products are overlooked.

validation_owner.name: R&C and Privacy in partnership with Product

assumptions.title: Planned HIPAA assessments (HighQ, SIU, Legal Tracker, Contract Express, CLEAR, CoCounsel, etc.) will be completed on current timelines

assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If assessment timelines slip, adjust remediation priorities, communicate revised timelines to stakeholders, and consider allocating additional resources or simplifying scope for initial phases.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

LHR3 DC Exit is delivering the migration of all business applications out of the LHR3 colo data center, followed by dilapidation and site closure to unlock infrastructure cost savings. The program matters because it retires end‑of‑life data center assets, reduces licensing and facility spend, and consolidates workloads onto modern cloud platforms in AWS and Azure.

To date, 0 of 3 major delivery milestones are complete, with Abacus/Barossa and OTP migrations in progress and showing no schedule variance against their planned dates of 31 Dec 2026 and 30 Jun 2027 respectively. Dilapidation and final colo closure activities remain scheduled to run in Jul 2027, aligned to the overall program end date of 20 Sep 2027, and key risks such as TAXONE SFTP geo‑restriction are under mitigation with dated action plans.

Overall status is Green, driven by all active migration and closure milestones currently tracking to plan without schedule variance.

## Path to Green

Top risk is the TAXONE geo‑restricted SFTP dependency on Globalscape in LHR3, which is being mitigated by delivering an AWS Transfer Family solution by 31 Jul 2026 and targeting risk closure by 01 Sep 2026.

## Milestones

- Deliver AWS Transfer Family replacement for TAXONE SFTP and remove dependency on Globalscape in LHR3 by 31 Jul 2026.  
- Complete Abacus / Barossa migration to Azure/AVD with 50% of planned application migrations delivered by 31 Dec 2026.  
- Complete OTP (Tax Provisioning) client migration to the NextGen AWS offering and submit LHR3 infrastructure decommission requests, achieving 100% of planned migrations by 30 Jun 2027.  
- Complete all dilapidation and colo closure activities for LHR3 by 31 Jul 2027.  
- Achieve full LHR3 DC exit and transition to steady‑state operations by 20 Sep 2027.

At the time of LHR3 closure, the only alternate GlobalScape location available will be MSP, USA. One of the TaxOne customers has a contractual georestriction requirement; must be hosted in EU / UK. An alternate solution is available, migrating to AWS Transfer Family, but timeline is not committed.

## Executive Summary

Disaster Recovery Optimization will deliver reusable cross‑region infrastructure templates and failover automation modules via a centralized Platform Engineering team. This matters because current single-region dependencies for shared back-end services and the Auth0/CIAM login layer expose Westlaw and CoCounsel to simultaneous outages in a single AWS region.

Of six defined milestones, one is in progress and five are planned, with all tracking to baseline dates and zero schedule variance recorded so far. The first target-state design milestone is on track for completion by 29 May 2026, which will unlock downstream remediation planning in June.

Overall status is Green, driven by all current milestones tracking to their planned dates with no schedule variance to date.

## Path to Green

The primary mitigation is to clean and reconcile disaster recovery application data in Fusion, Asset Insights and Service Health dashboards ahead of further design and remediation work, to ensure decisions are based on accurate Tier 1 inventories.

## Milestones

- Complete target state disaster recovery architecture designs for prioritized Tier 1 applications by 29 May 2026.
- Jointly approve remediation plans for identified Tier 1 disaster recovery compliance gaps with Risk and Product teams by 30 Jun 2026.
- Initiate AI-assisted disaster recovery assessments for remaining Tier 1 applications by 31 Jul 2026.
- Define and publish standard enterprise resilience patterns and ensure at least five patterns are adopted by multiple Tier 1 applications by 30 Sep 2026.
- Complete implementation of approved remediation plans for Q1 and Q2 identified Tier 1 applications and close the program by 31 Dec 2026.

## Executive Summary

FindLaw Divestiture – Office Hours is providing extended post-migration support to the buyer through a weekly, informal forum to resolve data and operational questions and reduce friction following separation from Thomson Reuters. The objective is a smooth transition to business-as-usual support with clear ownership and minimal residual issues.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

The NYNJ Port Authority Compliance Program is delivering Port Authority-ready government environments for HighQ, Contract Express, and CoCounsel, aligned to TR’s Government Compliance Baseline (NIST 800-53 Rev 5, HIPAA, and privacy). This enables contractual and regulatory compliance for government customers while consolidating security and privacy controls.

Overall status is AMBER. HighQ and Contract Express have a June delivery date and continue to remain Amber due to very tight timelines with no room for additional scope, errors or variance from planned timeline. The team is confident in the June delivery. The Outlook Add-In is amber trending green with a dependency on the Azure Gov environment ready in June. CoCounsel US moved from Red to Green this week with resource gaps filled and the work back on track for delivery in Q3. The green RAG status is dependent on the out of sync EPC ask for funding to complete the HIPAA and Privacy and Security Control remediations.

## Path to Green

The path to Green focuses HighQ and Contract Express environment build and control implementation complete next week and EPC funding approval for CoCounsel US HIPAA and Privacy Control implementation.

## Milestones

-   Complete CIAM integration and customer onboarding readiness for Port Authority products by 30 May 2026.
    
-   Make Contract Express available in production for NYNJ Port Authority onboarding by 05 Jun 2026.
    
-   Make HighQ available in production for NYNJ Port Authority onboarding and achieve the associated 30 Jun 2026 HIPAA and NIST 800-53 Rev 5 control implementations for HighQ and Contract Express by 30 Jun 2026.
    
-   Deliver CoCounsel FedRAMP available in production, CoCounsel production readiness for NYNJ Port Authority onboarding, and the CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add-In (HighQ integration only) available in production by 30 Sep 2026.
    
-   Complete the overall NYNJ Port Authority Compliance Program and transition to steady-state operations by 01 Apr 2027.

assumptions.rationale_basis: The path-to-green narrative and weekly status reports state that teams expect to move to Green in early June once Azure Gov is available, so they can surface infrastructure issues and resolve compatibility gaps before HighQ integration in Q3 2026.
assumptions.validity_explanation: As of late May 2026, sprint plans for CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add-In and CoCounsel US HIPAA/privacy work continue to assume Azure Gov availability by early June. The May 21, 2026 Weekly Status explicitly states that teams "hope to be Green in early June once Azure Gov is available" for both privacy/security controls and HIPAA documentation/testing, indicating ongoing confidence while acknowledging some uncertainty.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If Azure Gov is not available in early June, adjust sprint timelines by extending or intensifying E2E testing once the environment becomes ready, consider using interim non-Gov environments for limited functional validation where compliant, and re-sequence lower-priority tasks so that critical compliance and integration testing still completes ahead of the Q3 2026 HighQ integration milestone.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm Azure Gov environment readiness via environment build status from infrastructure teams and successful execution of initial pre-production compliance tests using the HighQ-managed environment in Azure Gov.

validation_owner.name: CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add-in team

dependencies.title: Assign owners for all privacy controls
dependencies.description: Each PRIVACY control must have a direct owner to provide implementation direction. Without assigned ownership, guidance on implementation will be delayed and the program timeline is at risk.
dependencies.dependent_on: Privacy control owners (mirroring FedRAMP ownership where possible)
dependencies.consumer: All Port Authority product workstreams
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Lack of clear ownership for privacy controls would delay implementation guidance and jeopardize the Port Authority compliance timeline.
dependencies.mitigation: Direction from Maria, Jenna, and Jim to copy ownership from the FedRAMP program where possible and otherwise select one of the responsible parties listed in the control spreadsheet.

dependencies.title: Assign owners for all security controls
dependencies.description: Each SECURITY control must have a direct owner to provide implementation direction. Without assigned ownership, guidance on implementation will be delayed and the program timeline is at risk.
dependencies.dependent_on: Security control owners (mirroring FedRAMP ownership where possible)
dependencies.consumer: All Port Authority product workstreams
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Delays in assigning security control ownership will slow implementation planning and could cause the Port Authority compliance timeline to slip.
dependencies.mitigation: Maria, Jenna, and Jim instructed the team to copy ownership from the FedRAMP program where possible and otherwise select one of the responsible parties in the spreadsheet.

dependencies.title: Complete HighQ NIST 800-53 Rev 5 security gap analysis
dependencies.description: HighQ must complete a NIST 800-53 Rev 5 security gap analysis via Fortreum to identify gaps against FedRAMP/Port Authority requirements.
dependencies.dependent_on: Fortreum (third‑party vendor) interviews and analysis
dependencies.consumer: HighQ Port Authority compliance workstream
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without the completed gap analysis, HighQ cannot fully understand or estimate the work required to meet Port Authority security requirements, risking delivery timelines.
dependencies.mitigation: Schedule and conduct interviews and gap analysis with Fortreum; interviews were scheduled for February 2–5, 2026.

dependencies.title: Complete Contract Express NIST 800-53 Rev 5 security gap analysis
dependencies.description: Contract Express must complete a NIST 800-53 Rev 5 security gap analysis via Fortreum to identify gaps against FedRAMP/Port Authority requirements.
dependencies.dependent_on: Fortreum (third‑party vendor) interviews and analysis
dependencies.consumer: Contract Express Port Authority compliance workstream
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without the completed gap analysis, Contract Express cannot fully understand or estimate the work required to meet Port Authority security requirements, risking delivery timelines.
dependencies.mitigation: Schedule and conduct interviews and gap analysis with Fortreum; interviews were scheduled for February 2–5, 2026.

dependencies.title: Define and communicate Thomson Reuters definition of PII for Port Authority scope
dependencies.description: A clear Thomson Reuters definition of personally identifiable information (PII) is needed across CoCounsel, HighQ, and Contract Express to correctly scope privacy controls and data handling.
dependencies.dependent_on: TR Data Classification Standard and related PII documentation
dependencies.consumer: CoCounsel, HighQ, and Contract Express privacy and security workstreams
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without a consistent PII definition, teams may mis‑scope or inconsistently implement privacy controls, risking non‑compliance with Port Authority and internal standards.
dependencies.mitigation: Use the TR Data Classification Standard as the basis; treat all 'Strictly Confidential' data and specified 'Confidential' items as PII, as documented in the referenced PII definition document.

dependencies.title: Obtain government authorization of CoCounsel FedRAMP legal research packet
dependencies.description: CoCounsel FedRAMP onboarding is dependent on government authorization of the legal research packet.
dependencies.dependent_on: Government authorization of CoCounsel legal research packet
dependencies.consumer: CoCounsel FedRAMP authorization and Port Authority onboarding
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If authorization is delayed, CoCounsel FedRAMP and subsequent Port Authority onboarding could be pushed back, impacting the program’s overall timeline.
dependencies.mitigation: Actively monitor for approval and raise awareness and planning activities early if delays appear likely.

dependencies.title: Review Contract Express HIPAA gap analysis and share identified gaps
dependencies.description: The Contract Express HIPAA gap analysis must be reviewed and any identified gaps communicated to the team so that estimation and remediation work can be completed.
dependencies.dependent_on: Maria & Jenna (Privacy workstream leads) completing HIPAA assessment for Contract Express
dependencies.consumer: Contract Express Port Authority HIPAA compliance workstream
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without clarity on HIPAA gaps, Contract Express cannot be accurately estimated or remediated, putting HIPAA compliance for the Port Authority at risk.
dependencies.mitigation: Maria and Jenna, as privacy workstream leads, will complete the assessment and share detailed findings with the team.

dependencies.title: Review HighQ HIPAA gap analysis and share identified gaps
dependencies.description: The HighQ HIPAA gap analysis must be reviewed and any identified gaps communicated to the team so that estimation and remediation work can be completed.
dependencies.dependent_on: Maria & Jenna (Privacy workstream leads) completing HIPAA assessment for HighQ
dependencies.consumer: HighQ Port Authority HIPAA compliance workstream
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without clarity on HIPAA gaps, HighQ cannot be accurately estimated or remediated, putting HIPAA compliance for the Port Authority at risk.
dependencies.mitigation: Maria and Jenna, as privacy workstream leads, will complete the assessment and share detailed findings with the team.

dependencies.title: Review CoCounsel HIPAA gap analysis and share identified gaps
dependencies.description: The CoCounsel HIPAA gap analysis (covering FedRAMP and commercial environments) must be reviewed and any identified gaps communicated to the team for estimation and remediation. It appears commercial CoCounsel is already suitable for HIPAA; the FedRAMP environment must adhere to the same HIPAA control implementations.
dependencies.dependent_on: Maria & Jenna (Privacy workstream leads) completing HIPAA assessment for CoCounsel
dependencies.consumer: CoCounsel Port Authority HIPAA compliance workstream
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without clarity on HIPAA gaps, CoCounsel cannot be accurately estimated or remediated, risking HIPAA compliance for Port Authority.
dependencies.mitigation: Maria and Jenna will complete the HIPAA assessment and share detailed findings with the team.

dependencies.title: Collect Port Authority CIAM requirements for potential separate workstream
dependencies.description: Government will collect any Port Authority CIAM requirements and relay them to Harvarinder Batth. Any resulting work from this effort will be treated as its own workstream and not handled under security or privacy.
dependencies.dependent_on: Government (Port Authority) customer requirement gathering
dependencies.consumer: Potential future CIAM workstream for Port Authority
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Delay in collecting customer requirements could postpone planning and initiation of any necessary CIAM work but does not directly block the core security/privacy workstreams.
dependencies.mitigation: Paul McClaughry to proactively collect requirements from the customer and provide them to the relevant CIAM owner.

dependencies.title: Ensure FedRAMP is fully operational before CoCounsel Port Authority onboarding
dependencies.description: CoCounsel Port Authority onboarding cannot begin until the FedRAMP environment is fully operational.
dependencies.dependent_on: Completion and operational readiness of CoCounsel FedRAMP environment
dependencies.consumer: CoCounsel Port Authority onboarding
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If FedRAMP is not operational, CoCounsel cannot be onboarded for Port Authority, pushing back delivery for CoCounsel in the program timeline.
dependencies.mitigation: Plan CoCounsel Port Authority onboarding only after FedRAMP is live; sequence Port Authority work post‑FedRAMP go‑live.

dependencies.title: Resolve cryptography/encryption-decryption approach with FARB and ISRM
dependencies.description: HighQ, Contract Express, and the CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in require clarity and approval on the cryptography/encryption‑decryption approach, requiring a FARB outcome and ISRM input.
dependencies.dependent_on: FARB decision and ISRM guidance on cryptography/encryption
dependencies.consumer: HighQ, Contract Express, and CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in security implementations
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without agreed cryptography and encryption‑decryption guidance, implementation and compliance with FedRAMP and HIPAA could be delayed, impacting timelines.
dependencies.mitigation: Engage FARB and ISRM to obtain an outcome and formal input for cryptographic standards and ensure implementation across products.

dependencies.title: Review HighQ integrations for HIPAA compliance
dependencies.description: HighQ’s integrations with third‑party and Thomson Reuters products (e.g., Microsoft Teams, Contract Express, Microsoft Office, DocuSign, Office 365 Gov/WOPI, and others) must be reviewed to confirm HIPAA compliance under the revised scope.
dependencies.dependent_on: Assessment of over 20 integration components including Mail Server, DocuSign, Office 365 Gov (WOPI), Teams, and others
dependencies.consumer: HighQ Port Authority HIPAA compliance workstream
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If integration components are not reviewed and remediated as needed, HighQ may fail to meet HIPAA expectations for Port Authority, risking compliance and go‑live timelines.
dependencies.mitigation: Review each integration component against HIPAA requirements under the new scope and track high‑risk items such as mail server, DocuSign, and Office 365 Gov (WOPI).

dependencies.title: Build HighQ FedRAMP/HIPAA environment within buffer to protect dependent activities
dependencies.description: The HighQ environment build has exhausted its schedule buffer; any delays will impact a range of dependent activities.
dependencies.dependent_on: HighQ engineering and infrastructure teams completing environment build
dependencies.consumer: All downstream HighQ Port Authority workstreams and integrations
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Delays in environment build will directly push out all dependent testing, integration, and compliance activities, jeopardizing delivery timelines.
dependencies.mitigation: Actively track and manage this as a risk even though it is currently on track, ensuring rapid response to emerging delays.

dependencies.title: Select compliant antivirus scanning tool for HighQ (Sophos/SentinelOne/Defender)
dependencies.description: HighQ must identify an antivirus/malware scanning tool that meets FedRAMP FIPS 140-2/3 cryptographic requirements, evaluating options such as Sophos, SentinelOne, and Microsoft Defender. License procurement has been completed and verification of the selected option is in progress.
dependencies.dependent_on: Tool evaluation and compliance verification for Sophos, SentinelOne, and Defender
dependencies.consumer: HighQ FedRAMP/HIPAA environment security posture
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If a compliant antivirus solution is not selected and verified in time, HighQ may need to make late changes to security tooling, impacting the engineering timeline and potentially delaying FedRAMP/HIPAA readiness and Port Authority commitments.
dependencies.mitigation: Continue evaluation and compliance verification of Sophos, SentinelOne, and Defender; license procurement has been completed and verification is in progress for the selected option(s). If no single tool meets requirements, explore alternate strategies based on Fortreum and security team guidance.

decisions.title: Host HighQ and Contract Express in Azure GovCloud
decisions.description: The HighQ and Contract Express environments for the Port Authority program will be hosted in Azure GovCloud rather than commercial Azure.
decisions.rationale: Using Azure GovCloud aligns with FedRAMP requirements and government customer expectations for data residency and security.
decisions.options_considered: Commercial Azure versus Azure GovCloud for HighQ and Contract Express environments.

decisions.title: Use CoCounsel FedRAMP Moderate for Port Authority security requirements
decisions.description: To meet Port Authority contractual security requirements, CoCounsel will satisfy all security obligations by achieving FedRAMP Moderate authorization (anticipated completion in Q3 2026), without separate additional security work specifically for Port Authority.
decisions.rationale: Leveraging the existing FedRAMP Moderate program avoids duplicative work and ensures a standardized security posture that meets Port Authority expectations.
decisions.options_considered: Performing separate Port Authority‑specific security enhancements for CoCounsel versus relying on the broader FedRAMP Moderate authorization.

decisions.title: Layer privacy and HIPAA controls onto CoCounsel FedRAMP environment
decisions.description: CoCounsel will implement required privacy and HIPAA controls on top of its FedRAMP version to meet full Port Authority requirements, rather than maintaining separate implementations.
decisions.rationale: Extending the FedRAMP environment with privacy and HIPAA controls consolidates compliance into a single hardened environment and simplifies operations.
decisions.options_considered: Implementing privacy and HIPAA controls separately outside the FedRAMP environment versus layering them onto the FedRAMP CoCounsel platform.

decisions.title: Use product-level templates for privacy controls
decisions.description: For each privacy control, control templates will be maintained at the product level (one template per control per product) rather than a single shared template across products.
decisions.rationale: A single shared template approach, as used for FedRAMP, would be too time‑consuming for the Port Authority program timeline; product‑level templates provide flexibility while allowing reuse where possible.
decisions.options_considered: A single control template per control shared across products (FedRAMP-style) versus separate control templates per product for each privacy control.

decisions.title: Rely on CIAM FedRAMP for authentication
decisions.description: CIAM FedRAMP will be used as the authentication system. HighQ and Contract Express will reuse all FedRAMP systems, including the CIAM FedRAMP solution.
decisions.rationale: Reusing the existing CIAM FedRAMP solution leverages an already FedRAMP-audited component, reduces additional security work, and maintains consistency across products.
decisions.options_considered: Using CIAM FedRAMP for authentication versus deploying a separate or local account authentication solution for Port Authority.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Decision 0018 regarding local account support; dependency 0024 regarding CIAM requirements gathering.

decisions.title: Exclude CoCounsel integration from June Port Authority deliverable
decisions.description: CoCounsel integration is not required for the June Port Authority deliverable. CoCounsel will instead deliver with FedRAMP in Q3 2026.
decisions.rationale: Deferring CoCounsel integration to Q3 aligns its delivery with FedRAMP and reduces scope and risk for the June Port Authority milestone.
decisions.options_considered: Including CoCounsel integration in the June Port Authority deliverable versus deferring it to align with FedRAMP in Q3 2026.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel FedRAMP authorization dependency (0014) and broader CoCounsel HIPAA/privacy schedule decisions (0038, 0062).

decisions.title: Define critical HighQ features for June 30 Port Authority deliverable
decisions.description: For the June 30 Port Authority deliverable, the critical HighQ features are iSheets, Rule Builder, and Contract Express (document automation).
decisions.rationale: Focusing on iSheets, Rule Builder, and Contract Express ensures the HighQ government environment meets the core contractual requirements by the June 30 deadline.
decisions.options_considered: Various possible HighQ feature sets, including broader or narrower subsets, for the government version.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Dependencies on HighQ environment build and Contract Express integration; estimation exercises referenced in decisions 0027 and 0028.

decisions.title: Schedule HighQ Office Plug‑In for Q3 2026, not June deadline
decisions.description: The HighQ Office Plug‑In will be delivered as part of the Q3 2026 version and does not have an end‑of‑June deadline for the Port Authority project.
decisions.rationale: The Office Plug‑In is not critical to the June 30 Port Authority deliverable and can be deferred to reduce near‑term scope and risk.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering the HighQ Office Plug‑In by June 30 versus deferring it to Q3 2026.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ Q3 2026 release planning and engineering capacity.

decisions.title: Do not support local accounts; rely on CIAM FedRAMP federated SSO
decisions.description: The Port Authority will use CIAM FedRAMP, which supports only federated SSO. Local username/password authentication will not be supported. No additional security work is required for the CIAM team for Port Authority because the CIAM solution has already passed FedRAMP audit. Some privacy controls may be implemented in CIAM FedRAMP in the second half of 2026 after FedRAMP ATO, subject to scope definition.
decisions.rationale: The CIAM FedRAMP solution was consciously designed for federated SSO only and has already passed FedRAMP audit; maintaining this model avoids additional work and preserves the FedRAMP boundary integrity.
decisions.options_considered: Supporting local account authentication for Port Authority versus requiring onboarding via federated SSO through CIAM FedRAMP.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CIAM FedRAMP solution and FedRAMP privacy controls scoping with James Pena and Jenna Perrin.

decisions.title: Move HighQ to Azure GovCloud
decisions.description: HighQ will be moved to Azure GovCloud for the government version.
decisions.rationale: Hosting HighQ in Azure GovCloud aligns the product with FedRAMP and government customer requirements and is consistent with decisions made for other products in the program.
decisions.options_considered: Retaining HighQ in commercial Azure versus moving to Azure GovCloud.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ environment build dependency (0060) and FedRAMP/HIPAA-related decisions such as 0040 and 0052.

decisions.title: Keep separate commercial and government systems for HighQ and Contract Express
decisions.description: There will be two systems for each application: one commercial system, which remains as it is today, and a separate government system maintained independently from the commercial version.
decisions.rationale: Separating commercial and government systems simplifies compliance and operational boundaries for FedRAMP/HIPAA and Port Authority requirements.
decisions.options_considered: Maintaining a single unified system for both commercial and government use versus running separate commercial and government systems.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Azure GovCloud hosting decisions (0008, 0011) for HighQ and Contract Express and FedRAMP Moderate planning (0026).

decisions.title: Defer FedRAMP Moderate independent assessment for HighQ and Contract Express
decisions.description: HighQ and Contract Express will implement the technical work needed to achieve FedRAMP Moderate level security by June 30, 2026, to meet Port Authority requirements, but an independent third‑party FedRAMP Moderate assessment will only be performed later when they formally pursue FedRAMP Moderate authorization.
decisions.rationale: Port Authority requires a FedRAMP‑equivalent security posture but does not require an immediate formal FedRAMP Moderate assessment; deferring the assessment reduces near‑term cost and schedule pressure while still delivering the necessary technical controls.
decisions.options_considered: Completing a full independent FedRAMP Moderate assessment by June 30 versus implementing the technical controls by June 30 and deferring the formal assessment.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Security control implementation for HighQ and Contract Express and future FedRAMP PMO involvement for templates (0029).

decisions.title: Decide on subset of features for government HighQ
decisions.description: It was agreed that, following estimation exercises targeted for February 6, 2026, a decision would be made regarding whether the government version of HighQ will deliver a subset of features and, if so, which features will be included or excluded.
decisions.rationale: Understanding the effort and constraints first via estimation allows an informed decision on which HighQ features can be delivered in the government environment by the required timelines.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering the full HighQ feature set for government versus delivering a subset of features tailored to Port Authority needs and resource constraints.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Estimation exercises for HighQ; follow‑on action to share list with April Jones.

decisions.title: Decide on subset of features for government Contract Express
decisions.description: It was agreed that, following estimation exercises targeted for February 6, 2026, a decision would be made regarding whether the government version of Contract Express will deliver a subset of features and, if so, which features will be included or excluded.
decisions.rationale: Estimation results are needed before committing to a specific subset of Contract Express features for the government environment.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering the full Contract Express feature set for government versus delivering a subset of features tailored to Port Authority requirements and capacity.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Estimation exercises for Contract Express; follow‑on action to share list with April Jones.

decisions.title: Do not complete control templates for each security control prior to FedRAMP certification
decisions.description: The team will not complete a control template for each security control as part of the Port Authority program. When HighQ and Contract Express pursue FedRAMP certification, the FedRAMP PMO will own the control templates.
decisions.rationale: Deferring control template creation reduces workload and focuses the program on implementing necessary controls rather than duplicating FedRAMP PMO responsibilities.
decisions.options_considered: Creating control templates for each security control during the Port Authority program versus relying on the FedRAMP PMO to own templates during formal certification.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Security control implementation for HighQ and Contract Express; future FedRAMP PMO engagement.

decisions.title: Run Contract Express as a separate service, not hosted inside HighQ
decisions.description: Contract Express will not be hosted or run inside HighQ; it will operate as an independent system even in the government environment.
decisions.rationale: Separating Contract Express reduces architectural coupling and simplifies security and operational boundaries, especially under FedRAMP and Port Authority constraints.
decisions.options_considered: Hosting/embedding Contract Express inside HighQ versus running Contract Express as a standalone service.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ–Contract Express integration patterns and environment design.

decisions.title: Exclude HIPAA compliance for WL and PL at launch
decisions.description: HIPAA compliance is not in scope for Port Authority for Westlaw (WL) and Practical Law (PL) at launch because customers cannot upload information into these products unless additional upload capabilities are added later.
decisions.rationale: Since no PHI will be uploaded, WL and PL do not need HIPAA compliance for the initial Port Authority scope, reducing unnecessary work.
decisions.options_considered: Including WL and PL in scope for HIPAA compliance versus excluding them due to lack of PHI upload capabilities.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Product feature set for WL/PL; any future features enabling data upload could change scope.

decisions.title: Remove CoCounsel data migration tool from Port Authority scope
decisions.description: The CoCounsel data migration tool is removed from the Port Authority scope. Port Authority users will not require migration of previously uploaded documents; they can re‑import items as needed since they will retain access to the commercial instance.
decisions.rationale: Accounts have confirmed that migration of uploaded data from the commercial to the FedRAMP environment is not required, so removing this work reduces scope and complexity without impacting user outcomes.
decisions.options_considered: Including a CoCounsel document upload migration tool in scope versus relying on users to re‑import documents from the existing commercial instance.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel FedRAMP deployment and user access to the commercial CoCounsel environment.

decisions.title: Scope product integrations for CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in (HighQ focus only)
decisions.description: For the CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in, HighQ is the only required product integration for the Port Authority deliverable. CoCounsel and Legal Tracker integrations will be disabled and should not be available.
decisions.rationale: Limiting integrations to HighQ minimizes scope, reduces security and compliance complexity, and focuses on the required integration for Port Authority.
decisions.options_considered: Enabling multiple product integrations (HighQ, CoCounsel, Legal Tracker) in the Outlook Add‑in versus restricting the integration to HighQ only for the Port Authority deployment.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in architecture and HighQ FedRAMP/HIPAA environment.

decisions.title: Set delivery date for Outlook CoCounsel Web Add‑in (HighQ integration) to Q3 2026
decisions.description: The Outlook CoCounsel Web Add‑in, with HighQ integration only, is required by the Q3 go‑live and is not required for June 30, 2026, as it does not impact data ingestion.
decisions.rationale: Deferring the Outlook Add‑in to Q3 avoids overloading the June 30 milestone with non‑critical functionality that does not affect data ingestion or compliance.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering the Outlook CoCounsel Web Add‑in by June 30 versus delivering it for the Q3 go‑live.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ Q3 go‑live timeline and CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in development.

decisions.title: Defer CoCounsel privacy control delivery for Port Authority to 2027 (superseded by later decision)
decisions.description: The CoCounsel privacy control delivery for Port Authority will be delayed until 2027, alleviating 2026 funding constraints while still meeting customer contractual needs. FedRAMP and HIPAA work will continue as originally planned. CoCounsel estimates for this deferred work will be included in the 2027 EPC funding asks.
decisions.rationale: Deferring privacy controls to 2027 reduces 2026 funding pressure while preserving the ability to meet overall contractual obligations by extending the delivery timeline.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering CoCounsel privacy controls in 2026 versus deferring their delivery to 2027 while continuing FedRAMP and HIPAA work.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Later decision 0062, which updates the CoCounsel HIPAA and privacy control delivery timeline; CoCounsel FedRAMP and HIPAA remediation schedules.

decisions.title: Set CoCounsel HIPAA remediation and privacy control implementation timeline to Q1/Q2 2027 (later updated)
decisions.description: With the delay in CoCounsel privacy control delivery, it was decided that CoCounsel would have until Q1/Q2 2027 to deliver, with the expectation that HighQ is FedRAMP certified for integration by then and CoCounsel privacy controls are in place at integration time.
decisions.rationale: Aligning CoCounsel privacy control implementation with HighQ’s FedRAMP certification and integration schedule provides a realistic timeframe and consistent security posture.
decisions.options_considered: Completing CoCounsel work in 2026 versus extending delivery into Q1/Q2 2027.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ FedRAMP certification schedule; CoCounsel HIPAA and privacy control implementation; later updated by decision 0062.

decisions.title: Clarify that TDE/TFE is not a Port Authority contractual requirement for HighQ
decisions.description: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) and Transparent File Encryption (TFE) are not Port Authority contractual requirements for HighQ. They are being pursued to meet HIPAA expectations and Thomson Reuters’ internal “reasonable and appropriate” risk posture. Port Authority requirements are satisfied as long as encryption is FIPS 140‑2 validated and data at rest and in transit are protected.
decisions.rationale: Separating contractual requirements from internal and HIPAA expectations clarifies priorities and ensures Port Authority obligations are met without mandating TDE/TFE for contract compliance.
decisions.options_considered: Treating TDE/TFE as mandatory for Port Authority contractual compliance versus treating them as internal/HIPAA‑driven enhancements while still meeting Port Authority encryption requirements via FIPS‑validated encryption.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ encryption implementation decisions and HIPAA compliance planning; cryptography dependency 0051.

decisions.title: WL FedRAMP does not require HIPAA compliance at launch
decisions.description: For the WL FedRAMP environment, no PHI will be uploaded by the client; therefore, HIPAA compliance is not required at launch.
decisions.rationale: Since WL FedRAMP will not process PHI at launch, pursuing HIPAA compliance would be unnecessary for the initial release, conserving resources.
decisions.options_considered: Making WL FedRAMP HIPAA compliant for launch versus omitting HIPAA compliance due to absence of PHI uploads.
decisions.dependencies_linked: WL FedRAMP feature set and data ingestion capabilities.

decisions.title: Use Privacy SharePoint as system of record for privacy control documentation
decisions.description: The authoritative copy of privacy control documentation will be stored on the Privacy SharePoint page. While this is the system of record, teams may continue to store architecture documents, ADO artifacts, and other related documentation in their usual internal repositories.
decisions.rationale: Centralizing privacy control documentation in a dedicated SharePoint repository improves governance and traceability while allowing teams to maintain supporting artifacts where they normally work.
decisions.options_considered: Using multiple distributed repositories with no single system of record versus designating the Privacy SharePoint page as the authoritative source for privacy control documentation.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Privacy workstreams across CoCounsel, HighQ, Contract Express, and Outlook Add‑in.

decisions.title: Reuse HighQ hosting model for IAM/CoCounsel in Azure Gov for Outlook Add‑in
decisions.description: For the CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in on HighQ, the group agreed to reuse the HighQ hosting model for IAM/CoCounsel in Azure Gov to maintain consistency, minimize scope changes, and meet project timelines. Improvements may be considered after the Port Authority project.
decisions.rationale: Reusing the existing HighQ hosting model reduces complexity, avoids new architectural risk, and supports meeting aggressive timelines.
decisions.options_considered: Designing a new hosting model for IAM/CoCounsel in Azure Gov versus reusing the established HighQ hosting model.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in architecture and HighQ Azure Gov environment.

decisions.title: Leverage existing HighQ standards and controls for IAM/CoCounsel deployment
decisions.description: The group agreed to leverage existing HighQ standards and controls for deployment, logging, and compliance for IAM/CoCounsel in order to align with FedRAMP/HIPAA requirements and reduce additional engineering effort.
decisions.rationale: Using proven HighQ standards reduces engineering workload and ensures consistency with FedRAMP/HIPAA practices already in place.
decisions.options_considered: Creating new deployment and logging standards for IAM/CoCounsel versus reusing HighQ’s existing standards and controls.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in deployment pipeline and compliance controls.

decisions.title: Exclude OpenAI/AI components from government Outlook Add‑in architecture
decisions.description: OpenAI/AI components will be excluded from the current CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in architecture for government compliance; only HighQ and IAM microservices will be deployed.
decisions.rationale: Excluding AI components reduces compliance and security complexity and ensures a cleaner FedRAMP/HIPAA boundary for the initial government deployment.
decisions.options_considered: Including OpenAI/AI components in the government Outlook Add‑in architecture versus limiting the deployment to HighQ and IAM microservices.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in architecture and FedRAMP/HIPAA scope.

decisions.title: Confirm thomsonreuters.com as the valid domain for public-facing URLs
decisions.description: The group confirmed that thomsonreuters.com will be used as the valid domain for public‑facing URLs, as required for DNSSEC and FedRAMP compliance.
decisions.rationale: Using thomsonreuters.com ensures alignment with DNSSEC and FedRAMP requirements and avoids complications with alternative domains.
decisions.options_considered: Using alternative domains versus standardizing on thomsonreuters.com for public‑facing URLs.
decisions.dependencies_linked: DNS configuration, FedRAMP compliance, and Outlook Add‑in public endpoint design.

decisions.title: Defer some HighQ application-level encryption work to post-June 30 and log risk in Protecht
decisions.description: The tech team proposed a layered encryption solution with proper access controls for HighQ, which the Privacy team accepted as sufficient for now. A formal risk entry will be logged in Protecht after April 7. Additional application-level work to further protect index and temporary files is acknowledged but intentionally deferred until after June 30, 2026, and will be tracked as a separate item.
decisions.rationale: The accepted layered encryption solution meets near‑term needs, allowing the June 30 milestone to be met while deferring more complex application-level work to a later phase.
decisions.options_considered: Implementing full application‑level protections for index and temp files before June 30 versus adopting a layered encryption approach now and deferring additional protections.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Cryptography dependency 0051; HighQ HIPAA and FedRAMP compliance work; Protecht risk tracking.

decisions.title: Do not adopt Plexus for HighQ and related projects at this time
decisions.description: The group decided not to adopt Plexus for HighQ at this time due to its lack of mature Azure cloud offerings and an associated budget ask that HighQ could not commit to. If the scanning problems persist, the project teams may be unable to complete required security checks in time to meet non-production and production cloud integration timelines.
risks.impact_description: If the Snyk scanning issue is not resolved promptly, security scans for three critical projects (SafeSend One, Signature Standalone, and TTC Standalone) may not be completed on time. This would delay sign-offs and cloud integration activities for SIGSA 3x environments, push back the start of production cloud integration planning, and jeopardize the overall delivery timelines for these products.
risks.mitigation: ISRM-Platforms-Security-Dev (Efstathios) and Sachin are working together to resolve the Snyk scanning issue. If the issue is still not resolved into early the following week (after Feb 25), the project team and management will consider approving and proceeding with a manual intervention process to complete the required checks for SIGSA 3x environments cloud integration. This manual process is expected to take 1–2 days and would allow production cloud integration planning to begin on time.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

Datadog Hygiene is delivering enterprise-wide monitoring hygiene improvements across 110+ Datadog organizations, with Tier 1 products prioritized, so alerts carry accurate asset and service context into ServiceNow and support scalable, AI-ready incident management. The program progresses through baseline hygiene, enforcement and automation, outcome-driven maturity, and long-term sustainability to reduce noise, improve detection, and tie infrastructure signals to customer journeys.

The incident correlation MVP between ServiceNow and Datadog is in development with the latest target for first production deployment on 29 May 2026, 29 days later than the original 30 April 2026 plan. Foundational data work is advancing, with a full metadata extraction script across approximately 113 Datadog accounts delivered by 22 May 2026 as planned, and the Phase 1 Legal and Corporate monitoring review pilot running from 01 April to 30 June 2026 against its baseline.

Overall status is Green, driven by successful delivery of enriched inventory and monitoring review pilots.

## Path to Green

With overall status Green, the focus is on containing top risks by completing enriched metadata and synthetic-filtering fixes by 29 May 2026 and locking in Phase 1 timelines, minimum alert standards, and governance decisions by 30 June 2026 so later enforcement and AI Ops onboarding can proceed on a stable foundation.

## Milestones

-   Deploy the ServiceNow–Datadog incident correlation MVP to production by 2026-05-29.
    
-   Deliver enriched Datadog inventory metadata in Power BI to support asset ID remediation and synthetic-monitor filtering by 2026-05-29.
    
-   Complete the Phase 1 Datadog alert and monitoring review pilot for Legal and Corporate incidents and assess outcomes by 30 Jun 2026.
    
-   Define and baseline Phase 1 timelines, monitoring hygiene metrics, and minimum alert standards, including backlog grooming and governance cadence, by 30 Jun 2026.
    
-   Complete the Datadog Hygiene program and transition to steady-state Sustainability and Governance operations by 29 Jun 2027.

risks.title: Low attendance at wider project team meetings impedes progress
risks.description: Action A22 notes that attendance at wider project team meetings has been poorly represented, leading to a shift toward smaller group sessions per segment to drive forward progress on critical deliverables and timelines.
risks.impact_description: If attendance at broader project meetings remains low, key stakeholders may not be aligned on priorities, standards, and timelines. This could slow decision‑making, create miscommunication, and delay completion of critical Phase 1 deliverables, particularly where cross‑segment coordination is needed.
risks.mitigation: Shift to small group breakout sessions per segment (e.g., TRTA, PLE) to review and set expectations on critical deliverables and timelines. Use these focused sessions to secure commitments and follow up on progress, while keeping a lighter‑weight broader forum for high‑level updates.

risks.title: Unvalidated overall project status pending backlog review
risks.description: April 14 meeting notes indicate that the team agreed to reassess overall project status (e.g., On Track/Green) after the backlog review and progress validation. Until this reassessment occurs, the current status may not reflect actual risk and progress.
risks.impact_description: If project status remains marked as On Track/Green without validation against a cleaned and prioritized backlog, stakeholders may underestimate risks, misjudge progress, and delay corrective actions. This could result in late discovery of schedule or scope issues and reduced trust in status reporting.
risks.mitigation: Complete the Phase 1 backlog grooming and prioritization, review progress against key deliverables, and then formally reassess and update the project RAG status. Communicate any status changes and associated risks to SteerCo and leadership.

risks.title: Infeasibility of effective governance with 110+ Datadog organizations
risks.description: The team questioned whether effective governance is feasible with over 110 Datadog organizations. The group agreed that governance is significantly harder at this scale and that deeper analysis and architectural discussion are required to determine a sustainable governance model.
risks.impact_description: If governance remains fragmented across 110+ Datadog organizations, it will be difficult to enforce standards, perform consistent audits, implement hygiene guardrails, and track compliance. This could lead to persistent noise, inconsistent alert quality, uneven incident detection, and slower progress toward enterprise‑wide observability maturity.
risks.mitigation: Schedule a dedicated governance and architecture session to assess options for managing or consolidating Datadog organizations, define a governance operating model that can scale (including standards, audit mechanisms, and ownership), and incorporate the chosen approach into the Datadog Hygiene roadmap.

risks.title: Program timelines and Phase 1 schedule not yet defined
risks.description: The team acknowledged that target timelines for Phase 1 deliverables and overall Datadog Hygiene program reporting are not yet defined. Timelines are required for reporting, and work needs to be time‑boxed via a backlog, but specific dates have not been set.
risks.impact_description: Without defined timelines, the program may experience unmanaged scope creep, delays in delivering Phase 1 outcomes, difficulty reporting status to leadership, and challenges coordinating dependent work across teams. This could undermine confidence in the program and delay benefits such as improved alert hygiene and incident response.
risks.mitigation: Create and groom a Phase 1 backlog in Azure DevOps, define target dates for key deliverables, and agree a reporting cadence. Use the backlog to time‑box work and establish clear milestones that can be tracked and reported in SteerCo and leadership forums.

risks.title: Insufficient Datadog monitor metadata blocks scalable cleanup
risks.description: Tax, Corporate, and Legal teams have indicated that current Datadog inventory exports do not include critical metadata such as "who created the monitor", "who the monitor is assigned to", and "when the monitor last fired". Dominique reported that Tax explicitly called this a "showstopper" for performing ongoing cleanup of monitors without Asset IDs. Without this metadata, teams cannot efficiently group, prioritize, or assign remediation work across hundreds or thousands of monitors.
risks.impact_description: If richer Datadog monitor metadata is not made available in inventory and analytics (e.g., Power BI) in the near term, product and engineering teams (starting with TRTA Tax, Corporate, Legal/HighQ) will be unable to run scalable, targeted monitor cleanup campaigns. Cleanup will either stall or require labor-intensive manual investigation of each monitor, delaying remediation of Asset ID coverage gaps and alert hygiene issues. This will slow Phase 1 outcomes, extend periods of noisy or low-quality monitoring, and reduce stakeholder confidence in the Datadog Hygiene program’s ability to support teams with actionable data.
risks.mitigation: Eric Sand will extend the Datadog inventory refresh script to pull full monitor metadata from the Datadog API, including creator, assigned/owned-by details, last-fired timestamps, environment tags, and other grouping attributes, and surface these fields in the Datadog inventory Power BI report. Eric is already in touch with LJ, who has built a "Datadog Jacker" tool that pulls alert metadata, evaluates tagging compliance, and supports bulk tag updates for two Datadog accounts; Eric will reuse or integrate LJ’s approach where possible to accelerate delivery. Once enhanced metadata is available in reports, the core team will share updated views with Tax, Corporate, Legal/HighQ so they can group monitors by owner and last-fired date and resume continuous cleanup of monitors lacking Asset IDs or required tags.
risks.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

risks.title: Alert-threshold hygiene may be misreported if synthetic monitors are not excluded
risks.description: Nick and Dominique discussed that a "large chunk" of monitors show no alert threshold configured. Dominique clarified that, based on review with Tax, many of these are synthetic monitors, for which a traditional threshold is not expected. Current counting and reporting of "monitors without thresholds" does not filter out synthetics, which can overstate the problem and distort hygiene metrics.
risks.impact_description: If synthetic monitors continue to be included in counts of "monitors without alert thresholds", the program’s analytics and dashboards will overstate threshold hygiene issues (e.g., reporting 20–30% of monitors as missing thresholds). This will mislead stakeholders about the true severity of the problem, cause remediation backlogs to prioritize the wrong monitors, and waste engineering time chasing expected configurations instead of genuine gaps. It may also undermine trust in Datadog Hygiene metrics and delay focused work on real threshold defects.
risks.mitigation: Update the Datadog inventory refresh logic, Eric’s Power BI reporting, and any related analytics to explicitly identify monitor type and filter out synthetic monitors when calculating metrics and backlogs for "missing alert thresholds". Confirm with Tax, Corporate, and Legal/HighQ that the refined views correctly separate synthetic monitors from other monitor types, and adjust the monitoring hygiene metrics dictionary so threshold-related KPIs explicitly exclude synthetics unless a specific exception is defined.
risks.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

risks.title: Potential negative impacts of reducing the number of Datadog organizations
risks.description: The program is considering whether to reduce the current number of Datadog organizations (110+). High complexity and several risks have been acknowledged, including possible loss of historical data, anomaly detection model resets, and AI/MCP rate‑limit or capacity impacts if organizations are consolidated without a carefully designed approach.
risks.impact_description: If Datadog organizations are consolidated without proper design and mitigation, historical monitoring data may be lost, anomaly detection models may reset and lose learned behavior, and AI/MCP features may hit rate or capacity limits. This could degrade incident detection, reduce confidence in alerts, cause gaps in trend analysis, and prolong time to restore service in major incidents.
risks.mitigation: Conduct a structured impact analysis of potential Datadog org consolidation options, including data retention, anomaly model behavior, and AI/MCP rate limits. Present options with clear risks and trade‑offs to stakeholders and only proceed with consolidation under a controlled migration plan that preserves critical data and service continuity.

risks.title: Misalignment of Datadog default maturity scorecards with Thomson Reuters standards
risks.description: The team is exploring whether existing Datadog maturity scorecards can be used to measure observability maturity. Datadog’s default scorecards are generic and likely not aligned to Thomson Reuters’ internal observability and monitoring standards. If they are adopted without proper alignment or customization, measurements of maturity may be misleading or inconsistent across teams.
risks.impact_description: If generic Datadog scorecards are used without alignment, the program may report inaccurate or non‑actionable maturity levels. This could lead to false confidence, misdirected remediation efforts, difficulty comparing maturity across business units, and reduced credibility of the Datadog Hygiene Program’s reporting with executives.
risks.mitigation: Review Datadog’s default maturity scorecard capabilities with Platform Engineering, assess alignment effort vs. value, and either customize the scorecards to match Thomson Reuters standards or define a TR‑specific maturity model. Do not adopt the default scorecards for official reporting until alignment is validated.

risks.title: Insufficient engineering and architecture participation in the core working group
risks.description: The program raised the question of which engineering and architecture resources should be formally aligned to the core working group. Current attendees form the core team, but additional engineering participation is needed to provide sufficient implementation depth and coverage across domains.
risks.impact_description: If adequate engineering and architecture representation is not secured, the core team may lack the domain expertise and capacity to design and implement standards, integrations, and remediation at scale. This could delay Phase 1 deliverables, result in poorly designed solutions, and reduce adoption across engineering teams.
risks.mitigation: Follow up with Engineering leadership to identify and formally align additional engineering and architecture representatives to the core working group, ensuring coverage for key domains (e.g., Platform Engineering, Legal, Research, Content). Define roles, expectations, and engagement cadence for these resources.

risks.title: Phase 1 backlog remains ungroomed and unprioritized
risks.description: April 14 notes and tracker actions indicate that the Phase 1 backlog (epics, features, and stories in Azure DevOps) requires cleanup and prioritization. Backlog grooming has been deferred to an offline working session.
risks.impact_description: If the Phase 1 backlog remains unstructured and unprioritized, teams may lack clarity on sequencing and dependencies, leading to inefficiencies, delays, and uneven focus. Status reporting may not accurately reflect progress, and high‑impact hygiene work may be delayed in favor of lower‑value items.
risks.mitigation: Schedule and complete an offline working session to groom and prioritize the Phase 1 backlog in Azure DevOps, ensuring each item has a clear owner, definition of done, and target timeframe. Use this prioritized backlog as the basis for status reporting and risk assessment.

risks.title: Missing or blank Datadog Monitor IDs in ServiceNow payloads
risks.description: During progress on ServiceNow–Datadog incident correlation reporting, the team identified that some ServiceNow payloads contain missing or blank Datadog Monitor IDs. This gap affects the ability to correlate incidents to specific monitors and impacts the accuracy of the correlation MVP.
risks.impact_description: If missing or blank Monitor IDs are not resolved, ServiceNow incidents cannot be reliably linked to Datadog monitors. This breaks correlation dashboards, limits the ability to analyze alert effectiveness during incidents, and weakens the hygiene backlog derived from these insights. It may also erode stakeholder trust in reporting and slow down adoption of correlation tooling.
risks.mitigation: Investigate the sources of missing or blank Monitor IDs in ServiceNow payloads, identify whether issues arise in the Datadog–ServiceNow integration or upstream configurations, and remediate mapping or payload generation issues. Add validation checks to ensure Monitor IDs are present and correct before incidents are created or processed.

risks.title: Significant Asset ID coverage gaps in Datadog monitors
risks.description: Based on a February snapshot, about 25% of Datadog monitors lack an associated Asset ID. The team highlighted this as a critical data quality gap and a priority risk, and noted the need for a repeatable approach and ongoing inventory refresh to improve Asset ID coverage.
risks.impact_description: If Asset ID coverage remains low, it will be difficult to tie alerts to specific assets, services, and configuration items. This undermines ownership clarity, incident routing, impact analysis, and automation opportunities. It also weakens correlation between Datadog alerts and ServiceNow incidents, reducing the effectiveness of dashboards and remediation prioritization.
risks.mitigation: Establish a recurring Datadog inventory refresh that includes Asset ID fields, validate the accuracy of inventory exports, define minimum data completeness and validity requirements for Asset ID and service associations, and create a prioritized remediation backlog for monitors without Asset IDs. Track remediation outcomes for prioritized services and implement a data quality operating rhythm to prevent regression.

risks.title: Data quality issues in correlation IDs and Datadog–ServiceNow mappings prevent reliable analytics
risks.description: Phase 1 discussions highlighted current data quality issues such as missing or inconsistent correlation IDs and gaps between Datadog alerts and ServiceNow incidents. These issues currently prevent reliable analysis and prioritization, and undermine the foundational analytics and dashboards needed for the program.
risks.impact_description: If correlation IDs, asset/service associations, and Datadog–ServiceNow mappings remain inconsistent or incomplete, analytics and dashboards used to drive remediation will be inaccurate or misleading. This will impede the ability to prioritize high‑impact hygiene work, reduce confidence in metrics, and may lead to misallocation of remediation effort and slower reduction in alert noise.
risks.mitigation: Develop a standard metrics dictionary and data quality standards for correlation IDs, asset IDs, and service associations. Implement validation rules and checks to detect missing or invalid IDs, create a prioritized remediation backlog for data quality issues, and standardize the Datadog–ServiceNow integration to preserve context. Use ongoing reporting to track improvements and prevent regression.

risks.title: Absence of minimum alert standards constrains remediation
risks.description: The March 17 meeting recap explicitly noted that minimum alert standards do not yet exist. Without defined standards (e.g., required fields, service/asset associations, runbooks, thresholds), remediation work in Phase 1 is constrained and may be inconsistent across teams.
risks.impact_description: If minimum alert standards are not defined, teams may remediate alerts in inconsistent ways, leaving critical gaps such as missing thresholds, incomplete associations, and absent runbooks. This will reduce the effectiveness of baseline hygiene efforts, prolong noisy or low‑value alerts, and make it harder to enforce consistent practices in later phases.
risks.mitigation: Define and document minimum alert standards covering thresholds, asset and service associations, correlation IDs, runbook linkage, and tagging. Socialize these standards with teams, integrate them into the Datadog–ServiceNow integration guidelines, and use the standards as a basis for Phase 1 remediation and Phase 2 enforcement and automation.

risks.title: Limited communication of the new monitoring review process beyond Problem Management
risks.description: April 14 meeting notes state that current communications about the new Datadog alert/monitoring review process have been internal to Problem Management. The need for broader communication to Service Management leadership, with cascade to their teams, was acknowledged.
risks.impact_description: If the new monitoring review process is not communicated beyond Problem Management, other stakeholders (e.g., Service Management leadership, Platform Engineering, GCC, product teams) may not follow the process, leading to inconsistent adoption, missed reviews, and incomplete feedback into the Datadog Hygiene backlog. This will limit the effectiveness of the review framework and slow improvement of alert quality.
risks.mitigation: Communicate the new monitoring review process to Service Management leadership, provide clear guidance and expectations, and ask leaders to cascade to their teams. Use pilot sessions with Legal and Corporate incidents to refine messaging and incorporate feedback before broader rollout.

risks.title: Monitoring effectiveness review process not yet fully operationalized
risks.description: The Datadog Alert & Monitor Effectiveness Review framework was introduced on April 7, with agreement to anchor it in Problem Tasks (P‑tasks). However, the review cadence is still being refined, and operationalization (including P‑task structure and review cadence) is pending alignment between Robin and Dominique.
risks.impact_description: If the monitoring effectiveness review process is not fully operationalized, the program may miss opportunities to learn from major incidents, improve alerts, and feed actionable items into the Datadog Hygiene backlog. Reviews may be ad‑hoc or inconsistent, reducing the impact of Phase 1 pilots and delaying broader adoption into BAU problem/post‑incident reviews.
risks.mitigation: Robin to align with Dominique on how to operationalize the review process, including defining the P‑task structure, specifying required inputs, and agreeing on a practical review cadence (e.g., grouped periodic reviews). Pilot the process with Legal and Corporate incidents in April and iterate based on feedback.
