assumptions.title: Hybrid operating model combining central standards with active product and engineering engagement
assumptions.description: The program has decided to adopt a hybrid operating model in which central teams provide standards, governance, and visibility while product and engineering teams actively collaborate on implementation, rather than relying on purely top‑down enforcement or self‑serve models.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Stakeholder discussions revealed broad, non‑conflicting pain points across teams, and leadership agreed that a mix of centralized standards with local ownership is needed to achieve enterprise‑wide hygiene without over‑centralizing control.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The hybrid model balances centralized control of standards and metrics with local accountability for implementation, which aligns with how large enterprises typically manage cross‑cutting programs. The decision is supported by consensus (DL‑04) that the program should not be purely top‑down or purely self‑serve.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If the hybrid model fails (e.g., persistent non‑engagement from product teams), shift toward stronger top‑down enforcement with clearer mandates, or alternatively, invest in more enablement resources and incentives to drive bottom‑up adoption.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor participation and responsiveness of product and engineering teams in Phase 1, review outcomes of pilot efforts, and solicit feedback in SteerCo and core team meetings.

assumptions.title: Existing standards are sufficient; the main gap is enforcement, auditability, and governance
assumptions.description: The group concluded that standards largely exist and that the core problem is enforcement, auditability, and sustained governance, rather than a complete absence of standards.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Discussion in the March 20 kick‑off and decision DL‑05 indicated consensus that standards are already in place but are not consistently enforced or audited across Datadog organizations and teams.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Decision DL‑05 recorded consensus that standards exist, and early Phase 1 work is already leveraging these standards as a basis for enforcement planning.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If significant gaps are identified, add a workstream to define or refresh missing standards and adjust the program plan to include standard creation before or alongside enforcement activities.
assumptions.validation_method: Inventory existing standards from Architecture, Data, and Service Management teams, compare them against current practice and program needs, and identify any true gaps that must be filled.

assumptions.title: Datadog inventory exports, once validated, will be accurate enough to drive remediation outreach and tracking
assumptions.description: The program assumes that the Datadog inventory dataset, once refreshed and validated, will provide sufficiently accurate details (including Asset IDs and other fields) to support outreach to teams and tracking of hygiene remediation work.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Actions have been raised to establish recurring inventory refreshes, grant required permissions to developers, and validate exports before contacting teams, indicating reliance on this data as a core input to analytics and remediation.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Core team updates on 4/28 note that Eric Sand is joining to build the inventory refresh script and that validations will be performed before outreach, indicating a structured approach to ensuring data quality.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If exports cannot be sufficiently validated, limit their use to internal analytics and require teams to confirm details before acting, while in parallel exploring alternative data sources or integration enhancements to improve inventory quality.
assumptions.validation_method: Have the Datadog team and Eric Sand develop and run an inventory refresh script, validate sample exports against live Datadog and ServiceNow data, and obtain sign‑off from data and architecture leads before using the dataset for outreach.

assumptions.title: Synthetic monitors are expected to lack traditional alert thresholds and should be excluded from threshold-gap metrics
assumptions.description: During review of monitors without alert thresholds, Dominique and Nick agreed that many of the monitors counted as "missing thresholds" are actually synthetic monitors, for which the absence of a traditional threshold is expected behavior. The team is assuming that synthetic monitors generally do not require the same threshold configuration as other monitor types and therefore should be excluded from metrics and remediation backlogs that track missing alert thresholds.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Analysis with TRTA Tax showed that a large portion of monitors counted as lacking thresholds were synthetic monitors. Dominique noted that for these, the lack of a threshold is expected, suggesting that current counts are conflating valid synthetic configurations with genuine hygiene issues.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Current empirical review indicates that many no-threshold monitors are synthetic and that teams treat this configuration as normal. However, this behavior must be confirmed against Datadog best practices and internal standards before it is encoded into metrics and remediation logic, hence a medium confidence level.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If validation shows that synthetic monitors should be treated as having required threshold-like conditions, update the metrics and dashboards to include synthetics in threshold-gap counts, define clear minimum configuration standards for synthetics, and create targeted remediation stories for affected product teams, starting with Tax, Corporate, and Legal/HighQ.
assumptions.validation_method: Have Zafar, Dominique, Eric, and LJ review Datadog documentation and a sample of synthetic monitor configurations across Tax, Corporate, and Legal/HighQ to confirm expected behavior and align on whether synthetic monitors should generally be excluded from threshold-gap metrics. Reflect the outcome in the monitoring hygiene metrics dictionary and dashboard logic.
assumptions.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

assumptions.title: Azure DevOps (ADO) will be available and suitable as the system of record for the Datadog Hygiene backlog
assumptions.description: The team identified Azure DevOps as the likely system for tracking Phase 1 deliverables and the broader hygiene backlog, assuming it can support the needed epics, features, stories, and reporting.
assumptions.rationale_basis: ADO is already in use for other initiatives, and leadership directed that deliverables be entered into a formal backlog system for tracking and reporting.
assumptions.validity_explanation: March 17 notes explicitly mention ADO as the likely tracking system, and subsequent actions reference Phase 1 tasks created in Service Management ADO.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If ADO proves unsuitable, select an alternative enterprise‑approved tool (e.g., Jira) and migrate existing backlog items, ensuring minimal disruption by maintaining consistent IDs and references.
assumptions.validation_method: Configure the Datadog Hygiene backlog in ADO, verify that core fields and workflows meet program needs, and test basic reporting before committing to it as the system of record.

assumptions.title: Program can proceed through a four‑phase structure as proposed
assumptions.description: The program plan assumes that work will proceed through four phases: Baseline Hygiene, Enforcement & Automation, Outcome‑Driven Maturity, and Sustainability, with later phases building on the foundations established in earlier ones.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Stakeholder input showed the problem space is broad and best addressed via a phased approach rather than a single remediation effort. Each phase targets distinct but related outcomes that depend on prior work.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The March 17 recap documented group alignment on the four‑phase structure, and the Phase 1 plan is already being operationalized, suggesting organizational buy‑in to this approach.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If all four phases cannot be executed as planned, reprioritize and merge elements of later phases into ongoing operations or other initiatives, focusing on the most critical outcomes (e.g., enforcement and customer journey monitoring).
assumptions.validation_method: Review progress and feasibility at the end of each phase; confirm continued sponsorship, funding, and alignment with strategic priorities before progressing to subsequent phases.

assumptions.title: Anchoring monitoring effectiveness reviews in Problem Tasks (P‑tasks) will provide sufficient evidence without per‑incident meetings
assumptions.description: The process is designed to fold evidence gathering and conclusions into existing Problem Tasks, avoiding a dedicated review meeting for every incident. This assumes P‑tasks can be structured to capture the necessary monitoring evidence and outcomes.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Teams want to avoid creating an additional meeting for every major incident and instead leverage existing problem management workflows for efficiency and scalability.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The April 7 meeting highlighted strong agreement to avoid per‑incident meetings and to rely on P‑tasks, provided input expectations are clearly defined.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If P‑tasks prove insufficient, introduce a lightweight periodic review meeting (e.g., weekly) of completed P‑tasks or define a short template for supplemental documentation to capture missing details.
assumptions.validation_method: Pilot the P‑task‑anchored process with Legal and Corporate incidents, review a sample of completed P‑tasks for completeness, and adjust guidance based on gaps.

assumptions.title: Monitoring review scope limited to forward‑looking, net‑new major incidents
assumptions.description: The team agreed that the Datadog Alert & Monitor Effectiveness Review process will initially apply to new major incidents going forward and will not be retrospective (e.g., March incidents are out of scope for now).
assumptions.rationale_basis: Limiting scope to forward‑looking incidents keeps the process manageable for Phase 1 pilots and avoids overloading teams with retrospective analysis while the framework and tooling are still being established.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Forward‑only scope is a common way to pilot new review processes, and the team explicitly agreed to this in the April 7 meeting. It allows for real‑time learning while minimizing initial overhead.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If forward‑only scope is insufficient, selectively add high‑impact historical incidents (e.g., recent severe outages) into the review pipeline, prioritizing them based on business impact and available capacity.
assumptions.validation_method: Assess the volume and quality of insights produced from forward‑looking reviews during the pilot with Legal and Corporate incidents, and evaluate whether historical incidents need to be brought into scope.

issues.title: Missing or blank Datadog Monitor IDs in ServiceNow payloads
issues.description: Some ServiceNow incidents generated from Datadog alerts are missing or have blank Datadog Monitor IDs in their payloads, causing gaps in incident‑to‑monitor correlation.
issues.impact_assessment: The project is building a ServiceNow–Datadog incident correlation MVP that relies on accurate Datadog Monitor IDs being present in ServiceNow payloads. Missing or blank Monitor IDs prevent reliable linkage between incidents and their originating monitors, which undermines analytics on monitor effectiveness, complicates root‑cause analysis, and reduces the value of the MVP for Phase 1. This issue also impairs the ability to feed monitoring gaps into the Datadog Hygiene backlog.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on completion and deployment of the ServiceNow–Datadog correlation MVP and on remediation of Datadog–ServiceNow integration mappings. Affects the alert and monitor effectiveness review process and reporting.
issues.resolution: Investigate root causes of missing or blank Monitor IDs in ServiceNow payloads, then remediate configuration issues in the Datadog–ServiceNow integration or payload mapping so Monitor IDs are consistently populated. The incident correlation MVP will be updated as needed once causes are addressed.

issues.title: Governance difficulty with 110+ Datadog organizations
issues.description: The current landscape includes more than 110 Datadog organizations, making centralized governance significantly harder and raising questions about whether consolidation is needed.
issues.impact_assessment: During the March 20 discussions, the group acknowledged that operating more than 110 Datadog organizations makes consistent governance, standards enforcement, and reporting far more complex. It increases fragmentation of configuration, complicates access and oversight, and may limit the feasibility of unified maturity measurement. However, consolidation carries risks such as historical data loss and changes to anomaly detection behavior, so analysis is required before proceeding.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Linked to decisions DL‑02 and DL‑03 on Datadog org strategy and governance feasibility, and to the assessment of Datadog maturity scorecard usage (DL‑01).
issues.resolution: Conduct a detailed impact analysis of potential Datadog organization consolidation, including risks such as historical data loss, anomaly resets, and AI/MCP rate‑limit impacts, and define governance options that may include improved standards enforcement without consolidation. The analysis will inform the open decisions on Datadog org strategy and governance feasibility.

issues.title: Synthetic monitors inflate reported count of monitors without alert thresholds
issues.description: Current analytics count monitors without alert thresholds without distinguishing synthetic monitors, leading to a reported figure of 20–30% of monitors lacking thresholds. The majority of these are synthetic monitors, for which the absence of a threshold is expected, causing the analytics to overstate the true threshold gap.
issues.impact_assessment: Analytics and dashboards used in the Datadog Hygiene program currently highlight a large percentage of monitors without alert thresholds (20–30%). However, May 5 discussions confirmed that most of these are synthetic monitors that are not expected to have thresholds. Treating these as defects misrepresents the scale of the problem, can misdirect remediation effort, and may erode stakeholder confidence in the reported metrics.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on availability of enriched Datadog monitor metadata (including monitor type) via scripts developed by Eric Sand and/or LJ's 'Data Doc Jacker' tool.
issues.resolution: Update analytics and reporting logic to filter out synthetic monitors when calculating monitors without alert thresholds so that reported threshold gaps reflect only monitors where thresholds are required. This will likely be implemented in the Datadog inventory Power BI report and underlying queries.
issues.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

issues.title: Lack of Datadog monitor metadata in inventory exports blocks team-level cleanup
issues.description: Current Datadog inventory exports (e.g., those produced by Jacob Kinsa) lack critical metadata such as who created each monitor, who it is assigned to, and when it last fired. Tax and Corporate stakeholders have stated that without this metadata they cannot practically group and address monitors with missing Asset IDs and other hygiene issues, calling it a showstopper for ongoing cleanup.
issues.impact_assessment: Tax and Corporate teams must remediate large numbers of Datadog monitors with missing Asset IDs and other hygiene defects. Without metadata indicating monitor creator, ownership and last-fired time, they cannot efficiently group monitors, prioritize work, or route questions to the correct owners. This significantly slows baseline hygiene remediation, risks leaving noisy or orphaned monitors in place, and undermines the usefulness of the Datadog inventory Power BI report as a driver for action.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on Eric Sand obtaining necessary Datadog permissions, developing or integrating scripts to pull complete monitor metadata, and coordination with LJ's 'Data Doc Jacker' tool where applicable.
issues.resolution: Enhance the Datadog inventory extraction process (via scripts developed by Eric Sand and/or LJ's tooling) so that exports include key metadata fields (monitor creator, owner/assignee, last-fired timestamp, and relevant tags). Update the Power BI inventory report to surface this metadata for filtering and grouping, enabling teams such as Tax and Corporate to run targeted cleanup campaigns.
issues.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

issues.title: Asset ID data quality gap in Datadog monitors
issues.description: A significant portion of Datadog monitors lack associated Asset IDs, creating a critical data quality gap that undermines monitor-to-asset correlation and limits the effectiveness of Datadog hygiene analytics and remediation.
issues.impact_assessment: During the April 14 meeting, the team noted that approximately 25% of Datadog monitors did not have an associated Asset ID based on a February snapshot. This lack of asset associations prevents reliable correlation between monitors and configuration items, impairs the ability to prioritize remediation by asset criticality, and undermines reporting on coverage. It also increases the risk that noisy or broken monitors will not be tied back to the correct services or infrastructure, delaying remediation and reducing confidence in monitoring data.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on granting Eric Sand the required Datadog system permissions, development of the inventory refresh script, and regular inventory refreshes owned by Mike Krause and the Datadog team. Affects the Phase 1 analytics and data quality workstreams and the ability to build accurate dashboards.
issues.resolution: Establish a recurring Datadog inventory refresh to track Asset ID coverage, improve the inventory with additional data points via a scripted refresh, validate inventory exports before outreach to teams, and drive remediation of monitors without valid Asset IDs.

dependencies.title: ServiceNow–Datadog incident correlation MVP for monitor effectiveness reviews
dependencies.description: The Datadog Alert & Monitor Effectiveness Review process depends on the ServiceNow–Datadog incident correlation MVP to reliably link incidents to Datadog monitors via monitor IDs.
dependencies.dependent_on: Development and deployment of the ServiceNow–Datadog incident correlation MVP and correct population of Datadog Monitor IDs in ServiceNow payloads
dependencies.consumer: Problem Management and the Datadog Hygiene Program (monitoring review process)
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If the incident correlation MVP is delayed or inaccurate, the monitoring effectiveness review process will lack reliable linkage between incidents and monitors, reducing its ability to identify misconfigured or noisy monitors and slowing Phase 1 remediation.
dependencies.mitigation: Proceed with manual or partial correlation using available data while the MVP is finalized, and prioritize fixing missing Monitor ID issues to improve correlation accuracy.

dependencies.title: Datadog inventory refresh permissions for Eric Sand
dependencies.description: Development of a scripted Datadog inventory refresh depends on granting Eric Sand the necessary system permissions to access Datadog data and generate enriched inventory extracts.
dependencies.dependent_on: Datadog platform permissions and access controls managed by the Datadog team
dependencies.consumer: Eric Sand and the Datadog Hygiene core team (including TRTA Professional)
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If permissions are delayed, Eric Sand cannot build the inventory refresh script, which will postpone availability of refreshed Datadog inventory data, slow remediation of Asset ID coverage gaps, and delay analytics and reporting improvements required for Phase 1.
dependencies.mitigation: Use existing manual exports as a temporary measure while permissions are being granted and coordinate with the Datadog team to prioritize access approvals.

dependencies.title: Enriched Datadog inventory metadata for monitor cleanup
dependencies.description: Teams such as Tax, Corporate, and Legal require enriched Datadog inventory exports that include monitor creator, assigned owner, last-fired timestamp, and key tags to effectively group and remediate monitors with missing Asset IDs and other hygiene issues.
dependencies.dependent_on: Scripts and tools developed by Eric Sand and LJ (Legal Tracker AI Ops pilot) to pull complete Datadog monitor metadata and support bulk tagging.
dependencies.consumer: Tax, Corporate, Legal, and other product/engineering teams participating in Datadog Hygiene monitor cleanup
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If enriched metadata is not available, teams cannot efficiently identify monitor owners, group similar monitors, or prioritize remediation, making large-scale cleanup of monitors without Asset IDs or required tags impractical and slowing Phase 1 baseline hygiene progress.
dependencies.mitigation: Continue to iterate on the Datadog inventory Power BI report and underlying scripts, leveraging LJ's 'Data Doc Jacker' tool where possible, and provide interim manual extracts for critical teams until a fully automated enriched export is available.

decisions.title: Reduce number of Datadog organizations to improve governance
decisions.description: The program is considering whether to reduce the current number of Datadog organizations (approximately 110+) as a strategy to improve governance and consistency.
decisions.rationale: Operating with 110+ Datadog organizations creates high complexity for governance, makes it difficult to enforce standards, and complicates reporting. However, consolidation carries risks such as historical data loss, anomaly detection resets, and AI/MCP rate‑limit impacts, which must be weighed before deciding.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain current number of organizations with improved governance vs. consolidate organizations to reduce complexity, accepting potential data and anomaly impacts.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to issues around governance feasibility, historical data retention, anomaly detection behavior, and AI/MCP rate limits.

decisions.title: Feasibility of governance with current number of Datadog organizations
decisions.description: The team is assessing whether effective governance is feasible with the current number of Datadog organizations or if structural changes such as consolidation are necessary.
decisions.rationale: During discussions on 2026-03-20, the group agreed that governance is significantly harder at the current scale. A more detailed architectural and governance analysis is required to understand whether process and tooling changes can address the issue without consolidation.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain current multi‑org structure with improved governance processes vs. consolidate or restructure organizations to simplify governance.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Related to DL‑02 (Datadog Org Strategy) and impacts ongoing governance of standards enforcement and reporting.

decisions.title: Program operating model: enforcement vs. adoption approach
decisions.description: The Datadog Hygiene program will operate using a hybrid model: central standards and governance with active engagement of product and engineering teams, rather than purely top‑down enforcement or purely bottom‑up self‑service adoption.
decisions.rationale: Stakeholders agreed that standards already exist and need enforcement, but also that success requires engagement and ownership by product and engineering teams. A hybrid model balances the need for central governance with distributed implementation and avoids a purely self‑serve model that lacks accountability.
decisions.options_considered: Top‑down enforcement model vs. bottom‑up self‑serve adoption vs. hybrid model combining central governance with collaborative engagement.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Influences governance structures, stakeholder engagement plans, and how enforcement mechanisms are designed in later phases.

decisions.title: Standards vs. enforcement and governance gap
decisions.description: The team concluded that standards for Datadog monitoring largely exist, and that the primary gap is in enforcement, auditability, and sustained governance rather than in the absence of standards.
decisions.rationale: Stakeholder input and core team discussions indicated that many standards are already documented, but they are not consistently enforced or auditable. Focusing on enforcement and governance is therefore more impactful than creating entirely new standards.
decisions.options_considered: Create new standards vs. improve enforcement and governance of existing standards.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Shapes Phase 2 (Enforcement & Automation) and informs how metrics and controls are designed.

decisions.title: Balance of customer journey monitoring vs. infrastructure alerting
decisions.description: Customer journey monitoring and infrastructure alerting will both be treated as required and must be explicitly connected so that infrastructure signals map to customer experience outcomes.
decisions.rationale: The group recognized that focusing solely on infrastructure health without connecting to customer experience would be insufficient, and that customer journeys must be first‑class monitoring priorities. At the same time, infrastructure signals are necessary inputs to understanding service health.
decisions.options_considered: Prioritize customer journey monitoring over infrastructure alerting vs. prioritize infrastructure alerting vs. treat both as required with explicit linkage.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Influences Phase 3 (Outcome‑Driven Maturity) and how monitors and alerts are designed across infrastructure and customer journeys.

decisions.title: Exclude synthetic monitors when measuring alert-threshold gaps
decisions.description: Analytics and reporting for monitors without alert thresholds will exclude synthetic monitors from the calculation so that metrics reflect only monitors where thresholds are expected.
decisions.rationale: May 5 discussions confirmed that the majority of monitors reported as lacking thresholds are synthetic monitors, for which missing thresholds are expected. Including them inflates the reported threshold gap (20–30%) and misrepresents the actual issue. Filtering synthetic monitors provides a more accurate picture of threshold hygiene.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Continue counting all monitors without thresholds, including synthetic monitors; 2) Exclude synthetic monitors from the threshold-gap metric; 3) Report both figures separately. The team opted to at least exclude synthetic monitors from the primary threshold-gap metric.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Depends on enriched Datadog inventory metadata (including monitor type) supplied by scripts and tools under development by Eric Sand and LJ.
decisions.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

decisions.title: Use or customize existing Datadog maturity scorecards for observability measurement
decisions.description: The team is evaluating whether existing Datadog maturity scorecards can be used to measure observability maturity at Thomson Reuters. Initial assessment indicates that Datadog’s default scorecards are generic and likely not aligned to internal standards, so customization or redefinition may be required.
decisions.rationale: Datadog provides built‑in maturity scorecards, but they may not reflect Thomson Reuters’ governance standards and operational practices. Using them as‑is might misrepresent true maturity and misalign with internal expectations.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to the need for consistent program measurement and potentially to standards enforcement decisions.

decisions.title: Engineering and architecture resources aligned to core working group
decisions.description: Current attendees will form the core Datadog Hygiene program team, but additional engineering participation is needed to provide implementation depth, and specific resources must be identified and aligned.
decisions.rationale: The initial core team covers key roles, but additional engineering and architecture expertise is required to implement standards and remediation at scale. Aligning named individuals will improve execution capability.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain current core team membership vs. expand to include additional engineering and architecture resources.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Depends on action A4 and Masthanaiah’s follow‑up with Engineering leadership; impacts the delivery capacity for Phase 1 and beyond.

decisions.title: Define target timelines for Phase 1 and overall program delivery
decisions.description: The program acknowledged the need to define target timelines for Phase 1 and overall Datadog Hygiene delivery, time‑boxed via a backlog, but no dates were set during the initial discussions.
decisions.rationale: Timelines are required for reporting and to provide accountability for deliverables. However, the group wanted to better understand scope and scale before committing to dates.
decisions.options_considered: Set immediate timelines vs. defer timeline definition until after backlog creation and scope refinement.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to backlog creation and grooming actions (e.g., A15) and to program reporting requirements.

risks.title: Snyk scanning process and challenges may delay SafeSend One, Signature Standalone, and TTC standalone timelines
risks.description: Unresolved Snyk scanning issues in the TTC/SafeSend codebase may prevent completion of required security scans in time, creating delays for three critical projects: SafeSend One, Signature Standalone (SIGSA), and TTC Standalone cloud integrations.
risks.impact_description: If Snyk scanning issues are not resolved, required security scanning may remain incomplete, delaying sign‑off and promotion of builds for SafeSend One, SIGSA, and TTC Standalone. This would push back completion of SIGSA and TTC non‑production cloud integrations in Q1 2026 and delay subsequent production cloud integration planning, potentially impacting SafeSend One production in Q2 and SIGSA/TTC production environments in Q3.
risks.mitigation: ISRM-Platforms-Security-Dev (Efstathios) and Sachin are actively investigating and addressing the Snyk scanning issues. If the problem persists into early the following week, the project team and management will consider approving a manual intervention process (estimated 1–2 days of effort) to bypass the automated Snyk pipeline blockers so that SIGSA 3x environments cloud integration can proceed and production cloud integration planning can start on time.

assumptions.title: Snyk scanning issues will be resolved or manually bypassed in time to avoid delays to SIGSA and TTC non‑prod and production cloud integrations
assumptions.description: Project planning assumes that the current Snyk scanning issues in the SafeSend/TTC codebase will either be fully resolved by the ISRM-Platforms-Security-Dev team or, if not, that a manual intervention process will be approved and executed (within 1–2 days) so that SIGSA and TTC non‑production cloud integrations can complete in Q1 2026 and production cloud integration planning can start on schedule.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Non‑production cloud integration for SIGSA and TTC must complete in Q1 2026 to keep SafeSend One production in Q2 and SIGSA/TTC production in Q3 on track. Automated Snyk scanning is a prerequisite for promotion, so the team planned on either timely resolution of the Snyk issue or an approved manual workaround.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The risk log shows that the Snyk scanning risk was managed with direct involvement from the ISRM security team and a clearly defined contingency of manual intervention. The risk entry is marked as resolved by 2026-02-26, indicating that either the automated scanning was restored or an acceptable workaround was implemented in time, confirming the assumption held true for planning purposes.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If automated Snyk scanning cannot be restored promptly, proceed with the agreed manual intervention process (1–2 days) to perform required security checks and unblock deployments, while coordinating with ISRM and project leadership to document approvals and ensure compliance.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor progress of ISRM-Platforms-Security-Dev work on the Snyk issue and confirm either successful restoration of automated scans or completion of the manual intervention process; verify that SIGSA and TTC non‑production integrations complete by Q1 2026 and that production planning starts as scheduled.

issues.title: Priority issues during Azure Databricks migration
issues.description: SafeSend encountered two priority issues during Azure Databricks migration: the need to create a Private DNS Zone for Azure Databricks (REQ0069376), and a blockage where Azure Databricks with VNet injection requires subnets delegated to Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces but the frontend subnet non-prod-databricks-frontend delegation is blocked (REQ0070250).

## Executive Summary

**A. Scope: To integrate Development, QA, Staging and Production environments into the TR Azure Cloud platform.**

**B. RAG Status: GREEN – Key Success: In alignment with the agreed timeline set by our Project Stakeholders, all non-prod env’s (Dev, QA, UAT/Staging) have been successfully cloud integrations were completed by Q4, 2025**

**C. Metric: Azure Cloud integration is currently at 50% completion. The project team is confident that the remaining critical production integration will be completed by June 30, 2026.**

**E. IMPORTANT UPDATE: Recently, the SafeSend Leadership team has officially finalized and confirmed that the SafeSend production cutover date that will take place on June 20th, 2026. This cutover will involve a planned downtime window of 6 to 12 hours and has been strategically scheduled to align with a low-usage period during the Juneteenth long weekend to minimize operational impact.**

**D. NEXT STEPS: SafeSend One Production Cutover Planning**

1.  **\[Completed\] Microsoft Support Coordination: Prasanna/PM has scheduled a call with Corey and Bill Plankers to ensure proactive Microsoft support and secure a dedicated resource for the SafeSend production cutover weekend (June 20th).**
    
2.  **\[IN-PROGRESS\] Production Cutover Planning Calls: Beginning the week of May 25th, Prasanna will organize twice-weekly planning meetings to monitor/track pre-migration progress, address task completions, and identify early-stage blockers. A formal GO/NO-GO decision call with the project team and key stakeholders is scheduled for the week of June 8th, 2026, to finalize the migration plan.**
    
3.  **\[YET TO INITIATE\] Network Team Standby Coordination: Prasanna/PM will work with ISRM to identify required FLS network sub-departments for standby coverage during the cutover. A support ticket will be raised with FLS to confirm resource availability.**
    
4.  **\[YET TO SUBMIT\] SNOW Change Request Submission: Prasanna/PM will prepare and submit a SNOW change request for the SafeSend production cutover, including all schedule details, planning information, approval groups, CTasks, and rollback steps. The request will be ready for review at the CAB meeting by June 17th.**
    
5.  **\[COMPLETED\] Runbook Integration and Tracking: Team will integrate the runbook into the SafeSend main master tracker to enhance visibility and tracking of pre-migration and actual tasks and to identify potential blockers early.**
    
6.  **\[YET TO START\] Executive Summary Updates During Cutover: Prasanna/ PM will develop templates for executive summary updates to be shared with all stakeholders and project teams every 1-2 hours throughout the cutover on June 20th.**

risks.title: Datadog training and integration may not be completed before production migration
risks.description: Datadog training is a prerequisite for setting up monitoring integrations for the new TR Azure subscriptions. Notes indicate that key tasks for Datadog IaC, RUM, and APM monitoring cannot be fully defined or executed until SafeSend and TR staff complete training and understand TR Datadog standards. If training and integration are delayed, monitoring for infrastructure and applications in the new TR Azure tenant may not be ready before or during production migration.
risks.impact_description: If Datadog training and integration are not completed before production migration, the project may go live without fully functional observability. This could lead to limited visibility into application and infrastructure health, slower incident detection, difficulty in troubleshooting migration issues, and increased risk of prolonged outages or performance degradation in production. Lack of compliance with TR monitoring standards could also trigger rework or governance escalations.
risks.mitigation: Arrange and complete Datadog training sessions for SafeSend and TR DevOps staff; use the documented TR Datadog integration procedures to configure log forwarding from Azure Log Analytics to Datadog and to enable RUM, APM, and infrastructure monitoring. Run a proof-of-concept to push application insights and metrics (including event logs) to Datadog in non-production, refine dashboards and alerts, and then apply the same configurations in production before the June 2026 production migration.

risks.title: Cutover and rollback planning for production migration may be incomplete before migration window
risks.description: The RunBook_Prod sheet shows that cutover and rollback planning tasks (including detailed cutover steps and rollback actions for application, database, storage, and domain changes) are marked as 'Not yet Started'. These activities are essential to safely execute the production migration and to revert changes if issues occur.
risks.impact_description: If cutover and rollback plans are not fully defined, reviewed, and tested before the production migration window, the team may be forced to improvise during cutover. This can lead to extended downtime, confusion during incident handling, inability to cleanly revert to the pre-migration state, potential data corruption or data loss, and reputational risk if customer-facing systems remain unavailable or unstable.
risks.mitigation: Finalize a detailed cutover plan covering all steps for storage, SQL, Cosmos DB, APIM, Key Vault, and application deployment, including timings and responsibilities. Define and document a rollback plan covering re-deploying the Q1 release via Azure DevOps, reverting Key Vault secrets, undoing storage and database changes, and reversing domain changes via GoDaddy. Conduct at least one rehearsal of critical steps in a non-production environment to validate feasibility and timing, and ensure all stakeholders understand their roles during cutover.

risks.title: Production storage and table migrations may fail or overrun due to untested migration service setup
risks.description: Production storage blob and table migrations depend on deploying a migration service and VM/AKS-based tooling (AzCopy, scripts, jobs) during April 17–27, 2026. The RunBook_Prod notes that the service for storage migration needs to be deployed and that Ravindra must update the storage migration plan with prerequisites and tasks. If these prerequisites are not ready or adequately tested, the production storage migrations may fail or take longer than the planned window.
risks.impact_description: If the migration service, VM/AKS infrastructure, and scripts for storage and table migration are not properly set up and tested, data transfers may fail, stall, or run longer than expected. This can result in incomplete or inconsistent storage content in TR Azure, requirement for multiple re-runs, extended maintenance windows, potential data loss, and unavailability of application features that rely on blob or table storage during or after migration.
risks.mitigation: Implement and validate the full storage migration toolchain (VM, AKS, AzCopy-based scripts, configuration generation, failed-job handling) in non-production environments (Dev, QA, STG), leveraging the detailed POC steps already executed there. Update the production storage migration plan with all prerequisites and tasks, including change feed configuration, SAS-based transfers, delta container handling, and cleanup procedures. Schedule sufficient buffer in the production window, and pre-run trial migrations on a sample of production containers to validate performance and error handling before the full migration.

risks.title: Key Vault secret migration and validation may delay production deployment readiness
risks.description: In the RunBook_Prod, key vault secret migration tasks (creating target Key Vault, bulk secret migration, ATUM deployment, and secret validation) are all marked as 'Not yet Started'. Dev notes from earlier environments indicate that application deployment depends on Key Vault being updated and operational. If key vault tasks slip, production deployment readiness may be delayed.
risks.impact_description: If Key Vaults are not created and populated with correct secrets before production deployment, applications may fail to start or function correctly due to missing or incorrect configuration secrets (e.g., connection strings, API keys). This could block production cutover, require emergency changes during the migration window, or lead to post-migration incidents and rollbacks.
risks.mitigation: Create the target production Key Vaults and configure access as per TR standards, then use bulk migration tools or scripts (and ATUM) to populate secrets. Validate secret correctness with EMs and application owners before the migration window by running application readiness checks in a pre-production setup. Incorporate Key Vault readiness checks into the production runbook and treat them as mandatory gates before proceeding with application deployment.

risks.title: Incomplete CI/CD migration from Azure DevOps to GitHub Actions could impact non-production DevOps migration timeline
risks.description: The DevOps Migration Phase (Non-Prod) indicates that ADO to GitHub migration is in progress with several outstanding tasks such as bulk creation of CI/CD pipelines as GitHub Actions workflows, validation of builds and artifacts, and full end-to-end dry runs. Notes highlight constraints around JFrog version updates and limitations with variable group mapping, requiring conversion of variable groups into YAML files.
risks.impact_description: If the migration of CI/CD pipelines from Azure DevOps to GitHub Actions is not completed and validated before the non-production DevOps migration deadline (Q4 2025 / availability to developers in early February 2026), developers may be forced to continue using legacy pipelines or experience disruptions in build and deployment workflows. This can slow feature delivery, complicate production migration readiness, and increase operational overhead by maintaining dual tooling.
risks.mitigation: Finalize the design and implementation of GitHub Actions workflows for all CI and CD pipelines, including addressing JFrog version alignment and converting ADO variable groups to YAML-based configuration. Run all CI pipelines to generate artifacts and validate pushes to JFrog, verify test coverage, and perform end-to-end dry runs across CI, CD, CT, and CO stages. Address any issues in mapping test cases and service connections, and ensure developers are onboarded and trained on the new workflows before the planned non-prod DevOps migration date.

risks.title: Wildcard certificate and domain management constraints may impact SSL and customer subdomain strategy
risks.description: The QA and Dev runbooks note ongoing POCs for SSL certificates via Venafi and for adapting existing domains, as well as discussion around wildcard certificates for customer-specific subdomains (thousands of potential subdomains). TR standards typically do not accept wildcard certificates, requiring exceptions or design changes. Although one historical RAID entry indicates the team decided not to proceed with wildcard certificates, the broader production SSL and domain strategy (including potential migration from GoDaddy to AWS Route 53) still requires alignment and impact analysis.
risks.impact_description: If SSL and domain strategies (including handling of customer-specific subdomains) are not fully aligned with TR standards and implemented before production, the team may face blockers in obtaining required certificates, delays in domain configuration, or security policy exceptions. This may delay production cutover, force suboptimal workarounds, or require post-migration rework of customer access patterns and portal design.
risks.mitigation: Complete the Venafi-based certificate POCs, finalize the decision to avoid wildcard certificates for customer portals, and document the new design approach for handling customer access without wildcard certs. Coordinate with TR PKI, security, and domain management teams to confirm migration plans from GoDaddy to AWS Route 53 where applicable, and ensure required certificates and DNS records are provisioned and tested in non-prod before production cutover.

entities.name: Digita Virtual Office AVD/Azure Migration (DVO)
entities.okrs: In Progress

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

Digita Virtual Office AVD/Azure Migration is moving the UK Digita Virtual Office product from Citrix in AWS to Azure Virtual Desktop in Azure UK, including all required infrastructure, testing, and documentation. This enables retirement of Citrix licensing, aligns with the strategic AVD platform, and must fit within UK tax blackout windows while maintaining service for UK customers.

As of 14 May 2026, 2 of 8 defined milestones are in progress and both are tracking with zero start and end variance against plan. The key KPI is to have all UK DVO user access via AVD by May 2027, and the current schedule has Production Migrations completing by 02 May 2027, leaving clear buffer ahead of the November 2027 Citrix license expiry.

Overall status is Green, driven by early-phase milestones progressing to plan and a delivery timeline that currently respects both the UK tax blackout period and the Citrix license end date.

## Path to Green

We are mitigating the Citrix license expiry risk by aligning Non-PROD migration completion by 31 Jul 2026, Non-PROD testing by 31 Aug 2026, PROD infrastructure readiness by 31 Oct 2026, and PROD migration completion by 01 Apr 2027, and by monitoring schedule progress against these dates with early escalation of any slippage.

## Milestones

- Complete Project Discovery and Planning, including identity ownership and domain controller connectivity decisions, by 29 May 2026.
- Complete Non-Prod Planning and Environment Setup for AVD compute, storage, and SQL Managed Instance by 06 Jul 2026.
- Complete Non-PROD Migrations, including associated testing of DVO on AVD, by 09 Aug 2026.
- Complete Production Migrations so that production data and customer access are fully on Azure Virtual Desktop in Azure UK by 02 May 2027.
- Decommission all AWS infrastructure used for Digita Virtual Office by 31 May 2027 and transition the program to closure by 30 Jun 2027.

risks.title: Production blackout windows may constrain migration schedule
risks.description: Production migration activities cannot occur during UK tax blackout windows (no PROD migrations between December 2026 and March 2027 / blackout noted as Nov 2026 to Mar 1 2027 in the charter). This reduces the available windows to complete the Digita Virtual Office (DVO) migration from Citrix in AWS to Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD).
risks.impact_description: If the project schedule is not aligned to the UK tax blackout windows, production migration waves could be delayed or blocked. This may force compressing remaining work into fewer windows, increase the risk of schedule overrun past Q2 2027, require additional coordination with business stakeholders, and potentially drive additional operational cost or extended dual-running of AWS and Azure environments.
risks.mitigation: Plan the overall migration timeline so that Non-PROD infrastructure and migrations are completed by Q3 2026 and PROD infrastructure is ready by October 2026. Schedule dry run migrations and final PROD cutover in allowable windows outside of the blackout period (e.g., PROD dry run by 2026-12-31 and PROD migration by 2027-04-01). Coordinate with business/product stakeholders to confirm exact blackout dates and embed these constraints in the detailed project plan and ADO milestones.

risks.title: Citrix license expiry may be reached before migration completes
risks.description: Thomson Reuters is not renewing the Citrix license for the Digita Virtual Office (DVO) environment, and the existing Citrix license expires in November 2027. The DVO migration from Citrix in AWS to Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD) must therefore be completed before the license expiry.
risks.impact_description: If the DVO migration to Azure Virtual Desktop is not completed before the Citrix license expiry in November 2027, the project could lose the ability to run production workloads on the existing Citrix platform. This could lead to service disruption for UK customers, emergency unplanned spend to extend or re-establish licensing, rushed and higher-risk cutovers, and damage to customer trust and regulatory compliance posture.
risks.mitigation: Align key milestones so that Non-PROD migration completes by July 31, 2026, Non-PROD testing by August 31, 2026, PROD infrastructure is ready by October 2026, and PROD migration completes by April 1, 2027. Monitor schedule progress against these dates, escalate slippage early, and maintain a contingency plan to negotiate a short-term Citrix extension only if absolutely required. Track this as a critical path risk in ADO and regular status reviews.

decisions.title: Potential dependency on CIAM migration for UK customers
decisions.description: There may be an external dependency to migrate UK Digita Virtual Office customers to CIAM, and this CIAM-related work must be completed prior to production migration to Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD). The exact dependency and timing are not yet fully confirmed.
decisions.rationale: Confirm whether CIAM migration for UK customers is a mandatory prerequisite for PROD cutover by engaging CIAM, Identity Management, and Product/Service Management teams. If mandatory, define and agree a CIAM migration plan and timeline that completes before the planned PROD migration (April 1, 2027). Track CIAM activities as a separate workstream with clear milestones and ensure they are included in the overall project critical path. Escalate any CIAM delays early and prepare interim access patterns if needed.

## Executive Summary

VMware to Hyper-V Migration is delivering a full move of VMware workloads into Hyper-V, including handling out-of-scope, suspect, and orphaned VMs so that every workload is either migrated, decommissioned, or has clear ownership. This matters because Thomson Reuters must completely eliminate VMware from all datacenters by 30 Jun 2026 with no exceptions.

As of 14 May 2026, 96% of VMware workloads are migrated to Hyper-V against a 100% migration target by 31 May 2026, leaving only a small tail of edge-case workloads to complete. The remaining work focuses on final batches and validation ahead of ESX host decommissioning on 30 Jun 2026.

Overall status is Green, driven by migration execution tracking close to the 31 May 2026 workload completion milestone with sufficient runway to meet the 30 Jun 2026 full VMware elimination deadline.

## Path to Green

The top risk is the still-open App Migration Tracker completion item, which is being mitigated by finishing the remaining tracker entries in line with the already scheduled production migration batches, using the built-in contingency so that decommissioning plans for 30 Jun 2026 are not affected.

## Milestones

- Project initiation and migration planning were established on 30 Jun 2025.
- Complete all VMware workload migrations to Hyper-V by 31 May 2026.
- Achieve 100% completeness in the App Migration Tracker by 04 May 2026.
- Decommission all ESX hosts and confirm 0 VMware workloads remaining, marking formal program closure, by 30 Jun 2026.

milestones.description: This feature enables sales reps to add one or more eligible products to an already-active GLLF or MLF Enterprise Trial directly from the trial record in Salesforce. When a product is added mid-trial, entitlements must be provisioned seamlessly via TFMS for all users on the trial — both those who have already activated and those who have been invited but not yet activated.

milestones.name: Rep Led Trials | Y26Q3 | GLLF/MLF | Calendar-Based Trial End Date Selection with Segment-Specific Creation Limits
milestones.description: For GLLF and MLF accounts, the calendar picker must enforce a maximum initial trial period of 60 days from the trial start date. Reps may select any end date within the 1–60 day window, but the system must prevent selection or saving of any date that exceeds this limit. latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

Customer Ticket Journey is delivering an end-to-end, standardized customer ticket journey across Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Azure DevOps so every customer issue can be traced with clear ownership and consistent handoffs. The Q2–Q3 MVP focuses on Boomi-based Salesforce ↔ Azure DevOps integration for Pagero, HighQ, Indirect Tax, and GSTOIT to reduce escalation friction and avoid Exalate renewal costs.

Foundational integration work is ahead or on plan, with Salesforce–ADO mapping reviews and Sprint 9 readiness completed on 17 Apr 2026 as scheduled, and Pagero Salesforce–Boomi–ADO development completed on 05 May 2026 against a 20 May 2026 plan. The MVP scope reset and leadership approval on 06 May 2026 confirmed a phased, agent-ready rollout (Pagero by 30 Jun 2026, HighQ/Indirect Tax by 11 Jul 2026, GSTOIT by 19 Oct 2026), with CSS change management and communications now aligned to these dates.

Overall status is Green, driven by the leadership-approved MVP scope reset on 06 May 2026 that prioritizes Pagero agent go-live by 30 Jun 2026 and staggers HighQ/Indirect Tax and GSTOIT go-lives to match capacity and peak-season constraints.

## Milestones

-   Achieve Pagero Salesforce–ADO agent go-live and complete the June 30 MVP scope by 30 Jun 2026.
    
-   Deliver HighQ and Indirect Tax Salesforce–ADO agent go-lives, with support agents using the integration in production, by 11 Jul 2026.
    
-   Deliver the initial Salesforce ↔ ServiceNow integration to the target environment and ready it for downstream validation by 24 Aug 2026.
    
-   Achieve GSTOIT Salesforce–ADO agent go-live in production, avoiding disruption to Fall Peak Tax Season, by 19 Oct 2026.
    
-   Transition Customer Ticket Journey to steady-state operations and close the program by 31 Dec 2026.

risks.title: GSTOIT production cutover colliding with GST tax peak season
risks.description: Business stakeholders highlighted that GSTOIT has a tax peak season beginning around August 15 and intensifying into early September, during which support volumes and ADO ticket creation are very high. If the GST/GSTOIT integration is deployed to production close to or during this window, agents may have to learn and adopt new flows while handling peak volumes, increasing operational risk.
risks.impact_description: If the GSTOIT integration goes live near the Aug 15–mid-September tax peak, support agents will have to adapt to new Salesforce–ADO flows while handling very high ticket volumes. This could lead to confusion, slower handling times, mis‑escalations, and reduced willingness to use the new integration. Customer experience and SLA performance during peak could degrade, and the team might choose to delay or roll back the integration, wasting preparation effort.
risks.mitigation: Plan GST/GSTOIT integration so that the technical build and testing can complete ahead of tax peak, but schedule production cutover either well before Aug 15 or after the peak window. Use the existing Power Automate–based integration during peak if necessary. As part of the upcoming GSTOIT mapping session with ADO and GST teams, explicitly define a production blackout window around Aug 15–mid‑September and incorporate it into the release plan. Per the May 6, 2026 sponsor status report, GSTOIT agent go‑live is now explicitly targeted for October 19 to ensure no disruption to Fall Peak Tax Season, aligning production cutover after the peak window.
risks.source_file_name: Weekly Sponsor Touch Base - Customer Ticket Journey.docx

risks.title: Change-management-driven validation and business go-live may significantly lag technical MVP
risks.description: Technical MVP for Salesforce–ADO (and later ServiceNow) is on track, but validation testing and business go‑live are being planned as part of a separate CSS change‑management process led by Darren Thurin’s team. Current indications are that this process could add roughly two months between technical readiness and agent rollout, with unclear ownership of validation and limited early exposure of flows to stakeholders.
risks.impact_description: If validation and business go‑live remain owned exclusively by the CSS change‑management team with a long lead time, the tool may be technically ready by June 30 but not in use by agents until much later. This would delay realization of MVP value, compress the window before critical business periods (e.g., tax peak season for GSTOIT), and increase the chance of late discovery of usability or process issues because sponsors and agents would see end‑to‑end flows only at the end of the change‑management cycle.
risks.mitigation: Work with CSS change‑management (Darren Thurin) and Salesforce leadership (including Mike Polk) to clarify ownership of validation testing and right‑size the change‑management approach. Introduce early demo days and simple end‑to‑end flows (e.g., a basic Salesforce‑to‑engineering escalation) so sponsors and agent representatives can review UX and process well before formal go‑live. Align on a concrete business go‑live date per product that keeps rollout comfortably ahead of critical periods such as GSTOIT tax peak season, and adjust the plan if the change‑management duration cannot be shortened.

risks.title: Incomplete validation of Area Path routing in non‑production ADO environments
risks.description: ADO does not support full Dev/QA/Prod parity for Area Paths, and the team decided not to duplicate full production Area Path trees into non‑prod. Only a small set of sample Area Paths will be created in the TR Sandbox project for Boomi routing tests, leaving many production combinations untested.
risks.impact_description: If Area Path routing behaves differently in production than in the limited Sandbox tests, some Salesforce cases may be routed to incorrect ADO teams or Area Paths after go‑live. This could cause mis‑assignments, slower triage, and uneven workload distribution, affecting the quality and timeliness of defect handling in the MVP.
risks.mitigation: Create a small, representative set of sample Area Paths in the TR Sandbox project and use them to validate Boomi routing logic. Accept reduced fidelity testing as a calculated risk for the MVP and plan to update production mappings carefully to minimize discrepancies.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Service principal (SPN) strategy across environments may increase cost or operational overhead
risks.description: There was uncertainty about how many ADO service principals Boomi should use for non‑prod and prod. Using too many SPNs can increase connector costs and operational complexity; using too few may complicate security and access management.
risks.impact_description: If the SPN strategy is not optimized, the team may incur unnecessary connector licensing costs or create operational overhead managing multiple service accounts, potentially straining budgets and administration for the MVP.
risks.mitigation: Confirm a strategy that uses two service principals—one for non‑prod/TR Sandbox and one for production—to balance cost and operational complexity while maintaining appropriate separation.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Fallback Area Path behavior defaulting to root when mapping fails
risks.description: If Area Path mapping fails during ADO work item creation, work items will land in the root Area Path. The team has not yet formally confirmed that this fallback behavior is acceptable for MVP operations.
risks.impact_description: If Area Path mapping failures send work items to the root Area Path without clear ownership, items may be misrouted or overlooked. This would impair triage, delay issue resolution, and undermine reporting accuracy for the MVP.
risks.mitigation: Confirm acceptance (or rejection) of the default‑to‑root fallback behavior for MVP operations. If not acceptable, adjust routing or introduce monitoring and reassignment processes for root Area Path items.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Increased scope for GST (GSTOIT and GST must be delivered together)
risks.description: The GST scope must include both GST and GSTOIT together, and the business has confirmed they both need to go together. GST development work is in a different ADO org (tr tax project = TaxTrade).
risks.impact_description: If the combined GST and GSTOIT scope is not properly planned and integrated across the separate ADO org, it may increase complexity and effort for the GST portion of the MVP. This could cause delays or force scope adjustments for GST in the Q2 delivery window.
risks.mitigation: Meet with GST teams to walk through the current setup, document the proposal for integration, and validate expectations with stakeholders. Use that walkthrough to refine the integration approach for the TaxTrade ADO project.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: ServiceNow access and field definition gap
risks.description: Baseline mapping for ServiceNow cannot be completed because the standardized ServiceNow fields and access for analysis are not yet available.
risks.impact_description: If ServiceNow field definitions and access are not provided, the team cannot complete Salesforce‑to‑ServiceNow mappings. This will delay ServiceNow integration work planned for later phases and could postpone post‑MVP expansion of the customer ticket journey to include service management workflows.
risks.mitigation: Provide Mike Polk with a list of standardized ServiceNow fields and ensure access via the ServiceNow delivery team. Leverage existing ServiceNow request RITM0097299 to cover the work and support baseline mapping.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Potential gap in ticket synchronization capabilities between Salesforce, ServiceNow, and ADO
risks.description: Exalate subscription may expire prior to the go-live of the replacement solution (including the Boomi integration layer), resulting in a potential gap in ticket synchronization capabilities between Salesforce, ServiceNow, and ADO
risks.impact_description: This could lead to disruption in end-to-end ticket traceability, delays in issue handling, and increased manual effort for teams, impacting overall workflow efficiency and alignment to the Customer Ticket Journey objectives.
risks.mitigation: Confirm alignment between the Exalate subscription end date and the Boomi integration go-live timeline, and initiate an extension or interim coverage if a gap is identified. In parallel, establish and communicate a fallback process and execute a defined cutover plan to ensure uninterrupted ticket synchronization.

risks.title: ServiceNow readiness for Q3 may lag behind Salesforce–ADO MVP
risks.description: The June 30 MVP focuses on Salesforce–ADO integration, but overall program health depends on ServiceNow readiness for a later phase (targeted around Q3). ServiceNow field definitions, design, and implementation are still pending.
risks.impact_description: If ServiceNow is not ready in Q3, the program will continue to lack full coverage of the customer ticket journey across Service Management workflows. This delays benefits such as unified incident handling and full end‑to‑end traceability and may require additional planning cycles and stakeholder re‑engagement.
risks.mitigation: Plan and track ServiceNow readiness as a follow‑on phase after the Salesforce–ADO MVP. Continue work on ServiceNow field definitions, access, and integration design so that Q3 delivery can proceed without reintroducing earlier blockers.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Scope creep from over‑synchronization
risks.description: There is a risk that teams will attempt to synchronize too much data between Salesforce, ServiceNow, and ADO rather than focusing on controlled, intentional integrations.
risks.impact_description: If over‑synchronization occurs, integration complexity and operational load will increase, jeopardizing the Q2 MVP timeline. It may also create unnecessary data replication, increase security and compliance exposure, and make support of the integration more difficult.
risks.mitigation: Do not push every update across systems. Agree on controlled, intentional data exchanges and use external links to source systems for detailed record views instead of full data synchronization.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: No agreed High‑Level Design (HLD) and phase‑1 scope
risks.description: A formal High‑Level Design and clearly defined phase‑1 (Q2 MVP) scope are not yet fully agreed across Salesforce, Boomi, ADO, and ServiceNow architects.
risks.impact_description: Without an agreed HLD and phase‑1 scope, teams may implement inconsistent integration patterns, over‑synchronize data, or work to different assumptions about systems, instances, and use cases. This threatens the ability to deliver a coherent, supportable Q2 MVP and may cause rework, scope creep, or missed June 30 timelines.
risks.mitigation: Develop a High‑Level Design that shows Boomi orchestration, defines phased delivery with clear phase‑1 scope, aligns Salesforce, Boomi, ADO, and ServiceNow architects, and provides explicit guidance to limit data exchanges to agreed key events while using links instead of full synchronization for detailed records.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Customer Support developer resource capacity
risks.description: Concerns were raised that Customer Support developer capacity might be insufficient to drive key Salesforce integration priorities in parallel for the Q2 MVP.
risks.impact_description: If Customer Support developers are not available, Salesforce changes needed for intake fields, case linking, and integration triggers could be delayed, putting the Q2 MVP schedule at risk.
risks.mitigation: Validate developer resource capacity and secure commitment to support the Salesforce integration work for the Q2 MVP.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Initial misunderstanding of total integration count
risks.description: Early in planning, the team believed there were approximately 11+ integrations required, which overestimated effort and created timeline concerns.
risks.impact_description: If the integration count remained overestimated, it would have led to unrealistic expectations, inflated scope, and perceived infeasibility of delivering a Q2 MVP.
risks.mitigation: Clarify MVP scope to focus on Salesforce ↔ ADO bidirectional integration only and reduce the perceived number of integrations. Align on ~3 core interfaces for the MVP.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Dependency on availability of ADO architects and business analysts
risks.description: Requirements finalization and mapping reviews depend on the timely participation of ADO architects and BAs, whose availability is uncertain.
risks.impact_description: If ADO architects and BAs are not available for mapping review sessions, ADO constraints and work item requirements may not be fully understood, causing design gaps, integration rework, and potential delays to Sprint 9/10 and the Q2 MVP.
risks.mitigation: Identify named ADO architects and BAs and ensure their attendance at mapping review sessions to finalize requirements and constraints.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Business process readiness and handoffs not defined alongside technical MVP
risks.description: Successful June 30 MVP delivery depends not only on technical Salesforce–ADO integration but also on clear end‑to‑end business processes, including handoffs, SLAs, ownership, and customer communication across Support and Engineering. These processes are not yet fully defined and owned.
risks.impact_description: If business processes, roles, and SLAs are not defined and operationalized by the time the technical MVP goes live, teams may struggle with ownership, escalation paths, and customer communication, resulting in inconsistent execution, degraded customer experience, and limited realized value from the integration.
risks.mitigation: Align MVP definition to include process outcomes, not just integration. Use Action A28 to ensure end‑to‑end business processes, handoffs, SLAs, and ownership are clearly defined, aligned, and approved to operate alongside the June 30 technical MVP.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Boomi capacity constraints for Q2 MVP
risks.description: Boomi integration teams are fully committed to the Pagero integration for Sprints 9–10 and have limited capacity to take on additional scope for other products during the same period.
risks.impact_description: If Boomi capacity is exceeded or additional scope is added, the team may not complete the Salesforce–ADO integrations for Pagero, HighQ, Indirect Tax, and GST by June 30. This would delay the MVP, potentially incur licensing extension costs (e.g., Pagero Exalate renewal), and reduce leadership confidence in delivery.
risks.mitigation: Maintain a tightly controlled MVP scope limited to Salesforce ↔ ADO via Boomi. Secure leadership support to enforce scope discipline and acknowledge Boomi capacity limits. Reallocate resources and improve productivity within the Boomi team to cover all four MVP products without adding scope.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Cardinality complexity for one‑to‑many and many‑to‑many relationships
risks.description: The integrations must support real‑world one‑to‑many and many‑to‑many relationships between Salesforce cases, ServiceNow incidents/problems, and Azure DevOps work items. Incorrect handling of cardinality would break traceability and reporting for the unified customer ticket journey.
risks.impact_description: If cardinality is not handled correctly, multiple Salesforce cases may not be properly linked to shared ServiceNow incidents or ADO work items. This would lead to broken traceability, inaccurate impact roll‑ups, inconsistent reporting, and confusion over ownership during escalations, undermining the Q2 MVP value.
risks.mitigation: Explicitly account for cardinality rules in the BRD requirements, backlog items, and integration design. Use the BRD as the baseline artifact to ensure all implementation work considers one‑to‑many and many‑to‑many scenarios and avoid assuming one‑to‑one relationships during integration design.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Failure to complete Salesforce–ADO mapping reviews and MVP validation by April 17
risks.description: The Q2 MVP depends on completing all Salesforce–ADO mapping reviews and final MVP validation by April 17 to enable Boomi intake for Sprint 9. Any delay in this validation threatens the June go‑live.
risks.impact_description: If mapping reviews and MVP validation slip past April 17, Boomi cannot start Sprint 9 on time, compressing schedules and increasing the likelihood that the June 30 MVP cannot be met. This could affect delivery for Pagero, HighQ, IDT, and GST and may lead to contract extension costs.
risks.mitigation: Treat April 17 as a hard deadline, schedule and complete mapping review sessions, and obtain explicit MVP validation. Use the Unified CX tracker to ensure all MVP requirements and mappings are captured and assigned owners.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Unclear ADO dev/test environment strategy may block Boomi development
risks.description: The Boomi team requires a clear, unblockable ADO environment strategy (e.g., using a TR Sandbox org vs. a single dev project). Lack of clarity on dev/test environment usage could impede integration development and testing.
risks.impact_description: If the ADO dev/test environment strategy remains unclear, Boomi development and testing may be delayed or blocked, slowing progress toward the June 30 MVP and risking defects slipping into production due to inadequate testing.
risks.mitigation: Define and confirm the dev/test environment strategy, including creation of a new ADO project in the TR Sandbox org, configuration of required work item types, and assignment of service principals. Communicate this plan to the Boomi team so they can proceed with development and testing.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Mappings not reviewed and validated by April 17
risks.description: Salesforce–ADO mappings for Pagero, HighQ, Indirect Tax, and GST must be reviewed and validated by mid‑April to enable Boomi Sprint 9 intake and Q2 MVP delivery, but this review may not be completed on time.
risks.impact_description: If mappings are not reviewed and validated by April 17, Boomi will be unable to start Sprint 9 work as planned. This would threaten the June 30 Q2 MVP delivery for the four in‑scope products and could push integration completion into later sprints.
risks.mitigation: Schedule and execute dedicated working sessions with Salesforce, Boomi, and ADO teams to review mappings. Use existing Pagero mappings as a baseline and confirm readiness for Sprint 9 start.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx

risks.title: Change‑management‑driven validation and business go‑live may significantly lag technical MVP
risks.description: Technical MVP for Salesforce–ADO (and later ServiceNow) is on track, but validation testing and business go‑live are being planned as part of a separate CSS change‑management process led by Darren Thurin’s team. Current indications are that this process could add roughly two months between technical readiness and agent rollout, with unclear ownership of validation and limited early exposure of flows to stakeholders.
risks.impact_description: If validation and business go‑live remain owned exclusively by the CSS change‑management team with a long lead time, the tool may be technically ready by June 30 but not in use by agents until much later. This would delay realization of MVP value, compress the window before critical business periods (e.g., tax peak season for GSTOIT), and increase the chance of late discovery of usability or process issues because sponsors and agents would see end‑to‑end flows only at the end of the change‑management cycle.
risks.mitigation: Work with CSS change‑management (Darren Thurin) and Salesforce leadership (including Mike Polk) to clarify ownership of validation testing and right‑size the change‑management approach. Introduce early demo days and simple end‑to‑end flows (e.g., a basic Salesforce‑to‑engineering escalation) so sponsors and agent representatives can review UX and process well before formal go‑live. Align on a concrete business go‑live date per product that keeps rollout comfortably ahead of critical periods such as GSTOIT tax peak season, and adjust the plan if the change‑management duration cannot be shortened.
risks.source_file_name: Weekly Sponsor Touch Base - Customer Ticket Journey.docx

risks.title: Data quality gaps in manual cross‑referencing
risks.description: Current manual cross‑referencing between Salesforce, ServiceNow, Azure DevOps and other systems lacks reliable identifiers and source data (such as source system IDs and URLs). Without a consistent common data model and clean cross‑reference data, tickets cannot be reliably linked across systems for the Q2 MVP integrations.
risks.impact_description: If data quality gaps persist, Boomi integrations will not be able to reliably connect Salesforce cases with downstream ServiceNow and ADO tickets, breaking the unified ticket journey. This would compromise traceability, reporting accuracy, and customer communications for the Q2 MVP and could require rework of integration logic after go‑live.
risks.mitigation: Establish a common data model and consistent payload definition so tickets can be reliably connected across systems. Capture both ticket identifiers and source/origin information (system plus URL) going forward. Use the Power BI dashboard to expose current data quality gaps and inform design decisions.
risks.source_file_name: Business Requirements Document (BRD) - Unified Customer Experience - Case Management Integration.docx
