## Executive Summary

Service Health Remediation (SHA) is delivering remediation of SHA recommendations across 24 in-scope products to improve performance, stability, scalability, observability, security posture, and service management alignment. This matters because it reduces service health risks that could impact business outcomes, customer experience, and regulatory or policy compliance.

Remediation efforts are underway for 14 funded products. Out of the 187 recommendations planned for 2026, 31 have been completed. It is tracking to the planned completion date of 31 Dec 2026 with zero schedule variance reported to date.

Overall status is Green, driven by the 2026 remediation milestone tracking to its 31 Dec 2026 target with no reported schedule slippage.

2026 Funding Allocation – In April, OS Income Tax and Pagero submitted funding requests to speed up remediation of critical and high-priority recommendations scheduled for 2026. Finance and leadership teams are currently reviewing these requests for approval. 

## Path to Green

The top risk is Product Engineering capacity, and mitigation focuses on active capacity management, realistic sequencing of remediation work, and escalation of material constraints through SHA governance to protect delivery of the 2026 commitments.

## Milestones

-   Programme start for the 2026 SHA remediation year was on 01 Jan 2026.
    
-   Start of the 2026 Service health remediation milestone occurred on 02 Feb 2026.
    
-   Mitigation plan for the Product Engineering capacity risk is targeted for completion by 2026-12-31.
    
-   Complete remediation of 187 high and critical service health recommendations by 31 Dec 2026, aligning with the overall SHA programme end date of 31 Dec 2026.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

SM Diamond Lanes – DevOps Acceleration is delivering a risk based “Diamond Lane” change model so mature applications can ship production changes faster while maintaining stability, governance, and compliance. It does this by wiring approvals and controls into CI/CD automation, ServiceNow, and rollback patterns instead of relying on manual reviews.

Out of 13 defined milestones, 3 are completed (including the initial CoCounsel and Materia pilot and product prioritization), 7 are in progress, and 3 are not yet started, with all major delivery work currently planned to complete by 31 Dec 2026. Near term milestones to complete pipeline driven automation by 31 May 2026 and finalize CI criteria, contracts, rollback patterns, and ServiceNow policy design by 30 Jun 2026 remain active and carry elevated risk due to dependencies on Product Engineering, SRE, and the ServiceNow core team.

Overall status is AMBER, driven by pilot automation and rollback milestones that are still in progress against 30 Jun 2026 targets and depend on constrained Product Engineering and SRE engagement to close readiness gaps.

## Path to Green

The path to Green focuses on locking in Product Engineering and SRE commitments through 30 Jun 2026 to complete CI criteria, pilot contracts and scorecards, pipeline driven routing, and crawl and walk/run rollback patterns while time boxing scope to CoCounsel and Materia. In parallel, we will align with the ServiceNow core team to finalize and approve templates, complete CoCounsel ServiceNow integration by 30 Jun 2026, and defer broader product onboarding until KPI validation and templates are stable.

## Milestones

- Complete the Project Roadmap Creation for 2026 DevOps Acceleration and value capture by 30 May 2026.
- Complete the Pipeline Driven Change Automation pilot for Diamond Lane routing in non production contexts by 31 May 2026.
- By 30 Jun 2026, finalize Diamond Lane CI criteria, publish and exercise pilot contracts and change scorecards v1, and establish validated crawl and walk/run automated rollback patterns for pilot products.
- By 30 Jun 2026, resolve ServiceNow Diamond Lane policy and CoCounsel ServiceNow integration risks by approving templates and enabling automated change ticket creation in deployment pipelines.
- By 31 Dec 2026, complete the phased KPI framework, broader expansion and enablement assets, crawl stage application onboarding to Diamond Lane, and formally close the DevOps Acceleration program.

risks.title: ServiceNow integration — automation ownership and readiness for CoCounsel
risks.description: CoCounsel is awaiting ServiceNow CHG ticket creation within deployment pipelines. Cumulus automation hooks are in place; however, ServiceNow templates must be finalized and approved by the ServiceNow core team to complete onboarding.
risks.impact_description: Delays in ServiceNow integration may block standardized change management workflows and delay delivery timelines for CoCounsel within the Diamond Lane pilot.
risks.mitigation: Align with the ServiceNow core team on required templates and approvals; assign a clear owner and due date for CoCounsel completion.

risks.title: Rollback scenarios and eligibility rules lagging automation and integration
risks.description: Rollback scenarios and eligibility criteria may lag pipeline automation and ServiceNow integration. Without validated, enforceable criteria for supported automated rollback, deployments may be incorrectly classified as Diamond Lane eligible or ineligible.
risks.impact_description: Incorrect eligibility classification increases incident risk and slows delivery due to review rework and exceptions during the Diamond Lane pilot.
risks.mitigation: Standardize and automate eligibility gates (e.g., testing, dependency checks, observability requirements) supported by a versioned criteria specification and a clearly defined exception path.

risks.title: CoCounsel Legal onboarding dependency and constrained Product Engineering and SRE engagement
risks.description: CoCounsel Legal requires additional deployment controls, eligibility data plumbing, and rollback automation; limited Product Engineering/SRE bandwidth and unclear engagement model are slowing prerequisite completion.
risks.impact_description: Slower onboarding timeline and limited ability to standardize deployment/eligibility patterns and implement automation could delay demonstrating pilot success across a second app.
risks.mitigation: Establish a clear engagement model with product engineering, escalate to Product engineering leadership, define minimum integration requirements, and time-box blockers, identify an alternate “next candidate” app if CoCounsel Legal cannot meet pilot milestones.

risks.title: DORA metric accuracy and trustworthiness (multi-repo lead time mapping)
risks.description: Lead-time metrics are correct for single repos but multi-repository services still have incomplete commit-to-deploy correlation (e.g., missing/ambiguous commit SHA mapping), which can skew DORA reporting in Port/IDP.
risks.impact_description: Misleading readiness signals could drive incorrect gate decisions or erode stakeholder confidence, slowing adoption and scaling.
risks.mitigation: Run parallel validation against known deployments, document assumptions, and implement multi-source aggregation/custom hooks where needed; delay enforcement decisions until metrics pass validation criteria.

risks.title: Roadmap pressure to onboard additional products before pilot maturity
risks.description: Stakeholders are requesting additional app onboarding before the pilot has stabilized templates, validation criteria, and automation, creating pull to scale ahead of demonstrated repeatability.
risks.impact_description: Context switching and overcommitment could dilute focus, increase defects, and slow time-to-green for the core platform.
risks.mitigation: Communicate entry criteria for new apps, share a phased scaling plan (pilot → validate → template → expand), and provide periodic executive checkpoints on readiness metrics

risks.title: Pilot readiness gaps (test coverage, data availability, automation prerequisites)
risks.description: Several pilot prerequisites are only partially met (automated tests, reliable signals/metrics, eligibility data capture, and pipeline automation), leaving readiness checks incomplete and increasing manual effort.
risks.impact_description: Eligibility checks may be incomplete or noisy, preventing automation of approval gates and extending reliance on manual promotion/approvals.
risks.mitigation: Lock in commitment and timing from Product Engineering with support from leadership for near and midterm deployment enhancements

milestones.name: Milestones 3–4: Diamond Lane Contracts & Change Scorecard (v1)
milestones.description: Formalize Diamond Lane participation as an explicit, auditable contract between Product Engineering and Service Management, and establish an initial scorecard to transparently evaluate readiness against that contract.
milestones.metrics: Product‑specific contracts and scorecards drafted and approved for pilot products; scorecards exercised in pilot reviews with traceable outcomes.
milestones.variance_statement: RAG Amber; progress is dependent on alignment and validation with Product Engineering and SRE and remains pilot‑oriented.

milestones.name: Milestone 11: Application Onboarding to Diamond Lane (Crawl‑Stage Adoption)
milestones.description: Enable controlled, crawl‑stage onboarding of applications to Diamond Lane using validated patterns, signals, and readiness criteria, including both in‑flight and newly onboarded applications.
milestones.metrics: Number of applications onboarded to Diamond Lane using crawl‑stage patterns; successful completion of onboarding checklists; pilot learnings captured and fed back into criteria and tooling.

milestones.name: Milestone 12: Project Roadmap Creation
milestones.description: Create a 2026 roadmap for DevOps Acceleration & VC realization beyond CoCounsel and Materia

milestones.name: Milestone 5: ServiceNow Diamond Lane Policy & Standard Change Integration (Deferred)
milestones.description: Translate Diamond Lane outcomes into controlled, auditable ServiceNow change behavior, enabling consistent change classification (Standard vs Normal vs "would block") without forcing teams to change delivery tooling prematurely.
milestones.metrics: Future state: ServiceNow policies and templates defined and piloted; for now, success is measured by capturing pilot learnings to inform later policy/template design.
milestones.variance_statement: RAG Red; milestone intentionally deferred with pilot initially leveraging existing ServiceNow templates and automation.

milestones.name: Milestone 1: Initial Pilot - Selected Repos: CoCounsel & Materia
milestones.description: Define and implement the minimum automated engineering and operational standards required for CoCounsel and Materia to participate in the Diamond Lane pilot, focusing on CI/CD rigor and pipeline‑embedded controls.
milestones.metrics: Branch protections enforced; PR‑only merges with required approvals; mandatory CI status checks; automated unit tests and code quality checks running on all PRs for CoCounsel and Materia.

milestones.name: Milestone 8: KPI Framework, Feedback Loops, and Maturity Progression
milestones.description: Establish a phased KPI framework (v1/v2/v3) for the Diamond Lane pilot to provide visibility into delivery performance, adoption, and readiness, emphasizing learning‑oriented feedback loops over enforcement.
milestones.metrics: Initial DORA and related pilot KPIs defined and instrumented; v1 KPI set in use; documented feedback loops with teams leveraging KPI insights for continuous improvement.

milestones.name: Milestone 9: Expansion & Enablement (Participation Readiness & Adoption Support)
milestones.description: Prepare and support broader Diamond Lane adoption by defining clear participation criteria, shared language, and enablement assets so teams can understand and opt in with confidence during crawl‑stage participation.
milestones.metrics: Enablement materials, participation guides, and communication assets created; additional teams onboarded using repeatable patterns; adoption tracked against target participation goals.

milestones.name: Milestone 7: Automated Rollback & Resilience (Crawl)
milestones.description: Define and validate a crawl‑stage automated rollback and resilience approach that supports Diamond Lane acceleration while maintaining production safety, focusing on rollback‑safe change types and pre‑production validation.
milestones.metrics: Rollback‑safe change classes identified; crawl‑stage rollback patterns tested in pre‑production; alignment achieved with Product Engineering and SRE on readiness criteria.

milestones.name: Milestone 6: Pipeline‑Driven Change Automation
milestones.description: Enable deployment pipelines to automatically participate in the Diamond Lane decision flow, using scorecard outcomes to route changes either through a fast Diamond Lane path or the standard approval path without altering developer workflows prematurely.
milestones.metrics: Pilot pipelines exercising automated eligibility evaluation and post‑deployment checks; reference patterns documented; eligibility‑driven routing validated in non‑production contexts.
milestones.variance_statement: RAG Amber; automation is in active pilot execution and requires additional work to standardize across pipeline models and products.

milestones.name: Milestone 2: Engineering Signal Integrity & Controlled Enforcement Enablement
milestones.description: Transition Diamond Lane from raw signal visibility to enforcement‑ready readiness by stabilizing metrics, standardizing enforcement mechanisms, and preparing teams for incremental enforcement.
milestones.metrics: Signal integrity validated across pipelines; enforcement‑ready metrics and evaluators in place without activating policy; pilot products able to rely on consistent signals.

milestones.name: Product Prioritization
milestones.description: Confirm product prioritization should be based on both technical feasibility and size of VC opportunity, equally

milestones.name: Milestone 10: Automated Rollback & Resilience (Walk / Run)
milestones.description: Extend rollback automation maturity beyond crawl into walk/run stages, informed by observed outcomes, product readiness, and operational confidence, without default enforcement.
milestones.metrics: Walk/run rollback patterns defined and exercised with selected products; evidence of safe, reliable automated rollback and resilience behaviors in higher‑maturity contexts.

milestones.name: Diamond Lane CI Criteria Definition & Formalization
milestones.description: Establish formal, documented eligibility criteria for Diamond Lane, defining the signals and standards applications must meet to participate.
milestones.metrics: Formal criteria set published; used by pilot teams as the basis for eligibility assessment; criteria adopted as the single source of truth for Diamond Lane participation.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

FedRAMP - Akkadia is delivering a new Akkadia-based content platform and Tabular Analysis capability in AWS GovCloud so regulated customers can access advanced CoCounsel Legal Research within the existing FedRAMP Moderate boundary. This replaces S3-based storage with a purpose-built, GovCloud-hosted platform that aligns FedRAMP and commercial architectures while preserving authorization.

Architecture and scope alignment is complete as of 13 May 2026, and GovCloud Dev/QA builds in US Gov East and West are 37% complete toward 100% readiness by 01 Jul 2026 with no reported schedule variance. UAT/Production tracks for both regions and the overall project completion milestone are planned to reach readiness by 01 Sep 2026 while maintaining the current FedRAMP authorization baseline.

Overall status is Green, driven by Akkadia architecture decisions being closed and all GovCloud environment milestones tracking to their July and September 2026 dates.

## Milestones

-   Complete GovCloud Dev/QA readiness for US Gov East and US Gov West by 01 Jul 2026.
    
-   Promote Akkadia to UAT/Production in US Gov East by 01 Sep 2026.
    
-   Promote Akkadia to UAT/Production in US Gov West by 01 Sep 2026.
    
-   Achieve overall project completion, including SCR approval and 3PAO audit closure, by 01 Sep 2026.
    
-   Transition to long-term steady-state operations for FedRAMP Akkadia and CoCounsel Legal Research by 31 Mar 2027.

risks.title: GovCloud feature gaps may require Akkadia design adjustments
risks.description: Differences in AWS GovCloud feature availability versus commercial regions may require Akkadia design adjustments. If identified late or complex to resolve, these gaps could impact architecture timelines, delay environment readiness milestones, or limit parity with commercial CoCounsel.
risks.impact_description:
If critical Akkadia or supporting service features available in commercial AWS are limited or unavailable in GovCloud and require significant redesign:

Architecture validation may extend beyond plan, delaying Dev/QA readiness (1-Jul-2026).
Rework and retesting could push UAT/Prod readiness beyond September 2026.
Late SCR updates may drive documentation churn and review delays.
Full architectural parity with commercial CoCounsel may not be achieved, increasing long-term technical debt and operational complexity.

raised_by.name: FedRAMP - Akkadia Status report dated 2026-04-27 (Executive Summary)

risks.mitigation: Explicitly assess GovCloud feature differences during architecture validation by comparing commercial Akkadia patterns to GovCloud capabilities early, identifying required design changes, and incorporating them into technical designs before build-out advances. Use early security documentation and review cycles to ensure continued FedRAMP alignment.

risks.title: Akkadia as largest new FedRAMP risk surface in Packet #2
risks.description: As Akkadia is new to the FedRAMP boundary, late identification of FedRAMP security or architectural gaps for Akkadia could delay GovCloud milestones, slow SCR approval, increase 3PAO remediation cost, and risk continuity of the existing Moderate authorization.
risks.impact_description: Late findings could delay GovCloud Dev/QA and UAT/Prod milestones, slow or complicate FedRAMP Significant Change Request (SCR) approval, increase 3PAO findings and remediation scope, drive additional cost and resource demand, and put continuity of the existing FedRAMP Moderate authorization at risk.

raised_by.name: FedRAMP - Akkadia Status report dated 2026-04-27 (Executive Summary)

risks.mitigation: Apply early discovery and disciplined governance to Akkadia onboarding in GovCloud, validating security, architecture, and FedRAMP boundary alignment upfront. Reuse proven commercial Akkadia patterns—adapted for GovCloud as needed—and embed these checks into early architecture and security documentation to identify and resolve high‑impact gaps ahead of Dev/QA and UAT/Prod readiness.

assumptions.title: Akkadia can be instantiated in AWS GovCloud and approved via a FedRAMP Significant Change Request while maintaining Moderate authorization
assumptions.description: The project assumes that Akkadia can be established from the ground up in AWS GovCloud and successfully approved as part of the existing FedRAMP system through a Significant Change Request, without requiring a new authorization or disrupting the current Moderate ATO.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The purpose statement explicitly states that Akkadia will be introduced into the FedRAMP boundary via a FedRAMP Significant Change Request to maintain continuity of the existing Moderate authorization.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The FedRAMP framework and the project’s existing Moderate authorization support the concept of managing substantial architecture changes through SCRs. However, the precise acceptability of introducing Akkadia via SCR depends on detailed boundary definitions, risk assessments, and agency acceptance, which have not yet been formally finalized for this change.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If the SCR path is not accepted or proves insufficient, prepare to adjust the authorization strategy (e.g., broader reassessment or incremental authorization), extend timelines, and potentially sequence Akkadia adoption in stages, while keeping a fallback path of continued S3 usage to avoid disruption to authorized services.
assumptions.validation_method: Engage early with Fortreum (3PAO) and the FedRAMP Program Office to confirm the SCR approach, boundary definition, and documentation expectations, and obtain formal acceptance of the SCR path as part of the FedRAMP process.

assumptions.title: All existing FedRAMP Legal Research data can be migrated from S3 to Akkadia with zero data loss
assumptions.description: The project assumes it can migrate all existing FedRAMP Legal Research data from the current Amazon S3 storage to Akkadia without any data loss, ensuring continuity of historical content and research results.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The purpose statement explicitly calls out migrating all existing FedRAMP Legal Research data with zero data loss as an objective of the project, indicating that planning and expectations are set on this outcome.
assumptions.validity_explanation: While zero data loss is technically challenging, careful design of migration procedures, robust backup and validation strategies, and repeated dress rehearsals can make it achievable. However, until real data migrations are successfully completed and validated, this remains an assumption rather than a proven fact.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If minor discrepancies or losses are detected, leverage backups and logs to restore affected data and, if needed, rerun portions of the migration. If significant issues arise, roll back to the S3-based solution temporarily while revising migration tooling and plans before attempting another cutover.
assumptions.validation_method: Execute test migrations and reconciliation in non‑production environments, perform checksums and record‑level comparisons, and validate functional search and retrieval across a representative dataset before production cutover.

assumptions.title: Service continuity for FedRAMP CoCounsel Legal Research will be maintained during Akkadia onboarding and data migration
assumptions.description: The initiative assumes that the introduction of Akkadia, Turbo backend integration, and data migration from S3 can be completed while maintaining service continuity for FedRAMP Legal Research users, with minimal disruption.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The purpose statement notes that the project is intentionally scoped to maintain service continuity while delivering new capabilities and completing the data migration.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The involvement of SRE, service management, and architecture roles in the stakeholder list indicates that operational impacts are being considered. Nonetheless, the exact behavior under production load and integration with Turbo and GovCloud infrastructure is not yet fully validated.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: Plan for maintenance windows and communicate them to stakeholders, prepare a tested rollback path to the prior storage configuration, and ensure incident response playbooks are ready to handle any unexpected service degradation or outages during cutover.
assumptions.validation_method: Conduct non‑production failover and deployment tests, simulate cutover scenarios, and monitor performance and availability metrics during pilot or phased deployments before full production migration.

assumptions.title: The Akkadia-based FedRAMP architecture will provide a scalable foundation for future Legal Research enhancements
assumptions.description: The project assumes that by aligning the FedRAMP architecture with the commercial CoCounsel baseline through Akkadia, it will establish a scalable, extensible platform that supports future FedRAMP Legal Research enhancements beyond this initial scope.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The purpose statement describes the project as creating a scalable foundation for future FedRAMP Legal Research enhancements by aligning architecture with the commercial baseline and leveraging Akkadia’s platform capabilities.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Architectural alignment with a proven commercial baseline increases confidence that the FedRAMP implementation can support future enhancements. However, differences in compliance constraints, infrastructure (GovCloud), and agency requirements may introduce limitations that are not yet fully understood.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If scalability or extensibility limitations are discovered, plan targeted architectural refactoring, introduce supporting services or patterns that better accommodate future features, and adjust roadmap expectations for new FedRAMP Legal Research capabilities.
assumptions.validation_method: Review target architecture against anticipated future use cases, stress-test scalability of Akkadia in GovCloud, and compare patterns with the commercial implementation to confirm reusability and extensibility.

assumptions.title: Cloudflare will not be required for Akkadia because it is a backend-only service and failover will be handled via Route 53 or similar mechanisms
assumptions.description: The planning discussion on 2026-04-29 indicated a working assumption that Cloudflare is not needed for Akkadia, because Akkadia is a backend document storage service with no direct customer-facing front end. Both Ervan Setiawan and Peter France noted that Akkadia and Turbo are backend services, and Kamaluddin Mohammed confirmed that Akkadia currently relies on Route 53 for failover in commercial environments. While a Cloudflare line item is being kept open "for awareness" pending final design, the implicit assumption is that no additional Cloudflare work will be required specifically for Akkadia.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Initial FedRAMP Akkadia planning sessions concluded that Akkadia is not directly exposed to customers and already uses Route 53-based failover in commercial deployments. In the 2026-05-13 planning meeting, Kamaluddin Mohammed stated that the Cloudflare sizing item could be removed entirely, reinforcing the expectation that Cloudflare will not be needed for Akkadia.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Recent planning decisions (2026-05-13 meeting) removed the Cloudflare sizing task for Akkadia, with Kamaluddin Mohammed explicitly stating that the item can go away as not needed. Combined with existing Route 53-based patterns in commercial deployments, this substantially increases confidence that Cloudflare will not be required for Akkadia in FedRAMP.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If Cloudflare is later determined to be required for Akkadia, reintroduce Cloudflare tasks into the project plan, update architecture diagrams, coordinate sizing and configuration with Cloud Networking, and adjust timelines to cover any new work and FedRAMP evidence updates.
assumptions.validation_method: Finalize network and traffic management design for Akkadia, confirming that all relevant endpoints use Route 53 or similar mechanisms without Cloudflare. Obtain agreement from Cloud Networking and CoCounsel architecture that Cloudflare is not in the critical path.

assumptions.title: GovCloud CI/CD GitHub integration for Akkadia will be BAU reuse from previous project
assumptions.description: It is assumed that the GovCloud CI/CD GitHub integration required for Akkadia will be a business-as-usual (BAU) reuse of patterns from a previous project plan, requiring minimal new design or coordination. During the 2026-04-29 meeting, Ervan Setiawan noted that the GovCloud GitHub integration task was copied from a previous project plan and "should be just BAU," with Kyle identified as the contact, and did not anticipate needing a dedicated meeting.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The CI/CD GitHub integration task for GovCloud was explicitly described as a copy from a previous project plan, and Ervan stated that it should be business-as-usual, implying that existing, proven patterns are expected to work without major changes.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Current evidence suggests that this is a straightforward reuse of established GovCloud CI/CD patterns, and specific contacts (Kyle) have already been identified. However, until actual Akkadia pipelines are created and validated in GovCloud, there remains some uncertainty about subtle differences in requirements or configurations.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If reuse of existing GovCloud GitHub CI/CD patterns is not possible, escalate early to establish a dedicated design and implementation workstream for Akkadia CI/CD, allocate additional engineering time, and adjust environment readiness dates accordingly. Ensure any new patterns are reviewed and approved by security/compliance before widespread use.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm with Kyle and Anders that existing GovCloud GitHub CI/CD patterns can be reused for Akkadia without significant changes, and validate that required repositories, pipelines, and permissions are configured and functional in a test deployment.

dependencies.title: Akkadia security control gap assessment depends on completion of SIA questionnaire
dependencies.description: The Akkadia security control gap assessment depends on completion of the Security Impact Analysis (SIA) questionnaire, which provides precursor information that Fortreum and the FedRAMP team will use to structure the assessment.
dependencies.dependent_on: Completion of Akkadia SIA questionnaire by Mohammed, Kamaluddin (TR Technology)
dependencies.consumer: Fortreum-led Akkadia security control gap assessment and subsequent Significant Change Request documentation
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If the SIA questionnaire is not completed promptly, the Akkadia security control gap assessment may be delayed, compressing the time available for June remediation and putting pressure on FedRAMP Significant Change timelines.
dependencies.mitigation: France, Peter will promptly provide the SIA template and examples, and Kamaluddin will prioritize completion ahead of the planned end-of-May gap assessment, escalating if additional guidance or approvals are required.

decisions.title: Use of Terraform vs Cumulus for Akkadia infrastructure automation in GovCloud
decisions.description: Determine whether Akkadia infrastructure automation in FedRAMP GovCloud will be implemented using Terraform only, replicating Cumulus capabilities, or whether Cumulus will remain in scope based on the technical evaluation with Cumulus/platform architecture.
decisions.options_considered:
Option 1: Use Terraform to implement all required infrastructure capabilities currently provided by Cumulus, aligning with existing team skills.
Option 2: Use Cumulus where necessary, based on the pros and guidance provided by Johannes Hartman.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Impacts infrastructure-as-code patterns for Akkadia in GovCloud and interacts with CI/CD GitHub integration and landing zone design.

decisions.title: Selection of container orchestration approach for Akkadia in GovCloud (ECS Fargate vs Plexus)
decisions.description: Decide whether Akkadia in the FedRAMP GovCloud environment will run on ECS Fargate (reusing the commercial pattern with ChainGuard images) or continue with the previously considered Plexus approach, based on suitability for the Akkadia use case and alignment with FedRAMP requirements.
decisions.options_considered:
Option 1: ECS Fargate using ChainGuard images, aligning with the commercial Akkadia deployment that already uses ECS Fargate.
Option 2: Plexus-based deployment if ECS Fargate does not meet the Akkadia FedRAMP use case or constraints.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Impacts Akkadia deployment architecture and could influence GovCloud feature gap risk resolution and CI/CD patterns.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

SM AIOps/Event Management (ServiceNow) is implementing an event‑first, correlation‑driven alert pipeline that ingests Datadog (and other) signals into ServiceNow to cut alert noise, reduce mean time to resolve, and provide a scalable AIOps foundation for Tier 1 services, starting with Legal Tracker. This matters because it replaces the current 1:1 alert‑to‑incident pattern with governed grouping, CI binding, and prioritized incidents that can later support automation.

For the Legal Tracker proof of value, incident volume from monitoring has been reduced by 60% while running 100% in production, against a longer‑term success target of ~90% incident compression from baselines (~1,500 Datadog incidents to ~20 AIOps incidents). MVP early adopter onboarding for three additional apps (including ONESOURCE GTM and CIAM) is in progress for completion by 31 May 2026, while the broader scale‑out to 25 priority apps (covering 60% of alert volume) is planned from 01 Jun 2026 through 04 Dec 2026.

Overall status is AMBER, driven primarily by unresolved CI/CMDB data‑quality and CI–service association gaps that limit reliable CI binding and impacted‑service mapping and therefore constrain full cutover from Datadog‑direct incidents.

## Path to Green

The path to Green focuses on closing the open CI/CMDB risk by standardising on VM object IDs and tags, completing CI‑binding validation and CI–service association fixes (including the ~1,000‑CI‑per‑service constraint) and wiring these checks into the onboarding checklist before switching off Datadog‑direct incident creation for Legal Tracker and new products. In parallel, the team will complete QA‑first onboarding for GTM4 and SIAM, finalise the FedRAMP governance package and configuration by 29 May 2026, and tune or constrain machine‑learning alert grouping so Legal Tracker and GCC can trust grouped alerts and AIOps‑generated incidents as the system of record.

## Milestones

- Complete the Legal Tracker proof of value, with 100% production traffic via the AIOps pipeline and a validated 60% incident‑volume reduction, by 29 May 2026.  
- Finish MVP early adopter onboarding for ONESOURCE GTM and CIAM, with three apps onboarded and a 60% reduction in alert and incident volume, by 31 May 2026.  
- Update GTM4 and SIAM FinOpsDatadogAlerts monitors with standardised tags and route them to the AIOps webhook by 21 May 2026.  
- Complete the FedRAMP AIOps governance and compliance spreadsheet and mirror required AIOps/Event Management configuration into the FedRAMP ServiceNow instance by 29 May 2026.  
- Transition the AIOps program to steady‑state operations and close the project by 30 Nov 2026.

risks.title: Unresolved ServiceNow CI–service association behaviour may block cutover from Datadog incidents
risks.description: During the May 12, 2026 AIOps Product Onboarding regional sync, the team observed that ServiceNow is not associating services with the correct CIs for large applications such as Legal Tracker. Internal analysis suggests that a configurable limit of approximately 1,000 CIs per service causes additional CIs to be handled via dynamic CI groups, which in turn prevents correct service association and grouping. ServiceNow’s consultant (Doug) indicated there are “traverse rules” that might address this but needs to consult CMDB experts. Until a clear recommendation and fix are in place, the Legal Tracker product team considers this a showstopper for disabling Datadog-direct incident creation.
risks.impact_description: If ServiceNow continues to mis-associate or partially associate CIs to services due to the current service–CI association behaviour, AIOps cannot reliably determine which service is impacted by an event or alert for large applications. For Legal Tracker, this would mean that incidents created by AIOps could lack correct service context or rely on dynamic CI groups, undermining routing, impact analysis, and leadership reporting. As a result, Legal Tracker stakeholders will not agree to cut over from Datadog-direct incident creation, delaying the POV completion, delaying onboarding of subsequent products, and prolonging reliance on legacy workflows.
risks.mitigation: ServiceNow’s consultant Doug will escalate the CI/service association issue to their CMDB experts to review the current configuration, including the apparent 1,000-CI-per-service association limit and available traverse rules. Together with the TR CMDB team, they will: (1) determine whether the association limit can be safely tuned without degrading ServiceNow performance; (2) design appropriate traverse rules or alternative modelling (e.g., hierarchical services) to support large applications like Legal Tracker; and (3) validate the chosen approach in a lower environment before promoting changes to production. In parallel, Jot will log this as a formal blocker in status reporting, and Talia will escalate via email and stakeholder channels (including Eric and John) to ensure it receives high priority attention from ServiceNow and the CMDB team. Cutover from Datadog-direct incidents for Legal Tracker will be deferred until a recommended and tested fix is in place.
risks.source_file_name: AIOps Product Onboarding Reg Sync 12 May 26.docx

risks.title: Incorrect priority and severity mapping from Datadog to ServiceNow incidents
risks.description: Priority and severity values from Datadog monitors are not yet consistently or correctly mapped into ServiceNow alert and incident fields. Severity has sometimes been populated from unexpected payload fields, custom test fields exist, and the mapping between Datadog alert_priority/alert_type and ServiceNow severity, impact, urgency, and priority is still being designed. If this is not resolved before enabling automated incident creation, incidents may be mis‑prioritized.
risks.impact_description: Mis‑prioritized incidents (e.g., P1 issues created as P3, or minor warnings created as P1) will distort SLAs, paging, and escalation. Major Incident processes could be flooded with false majors or miss real ones. This will reduce trust in the AIOps solution, force manual reprioritization, and may cause teams to resist adopting event‑driven incident creation.
risks.mitigation: Define and document a definitive mapping: use Datadog monitor priority (P1–P5) as the authoritative input, add custom impact and urgency fields on the alert record, map monitor priority into those fields via event rules, and customize the incident-creation subflow to derive incident priority solely from those values. Validate mapping with test payloads and a parallel run comparing new incidents to historical ones before turning off legacy Datadog incident creation.

risks.title: Lack of monitoring governance and standardized thresholds across products
risks.description: There is no centralized event management practice or monitoring governance. Platform Engineering publishes Datadog policies on SharePoint but does not audit or enforce them. Thresholds and configurations vary by product; 80% of monitors are synthetics with product‑specific thresholds, and 75% of GCC events come from one product (HighQ). Many teams do not understand event threshold concepts (informational/warning/critical).
risks.impact_description: Without standardized thresholds, tagging, and governance, noisy or misconfigured monitors will continue to flood Event Management and produce inconsistent event classification across products. AIOps capabilities (filtering, correlation, prioritization) may be overwhelmed or misused, leading to limited noise reduction, poor comparability between services, and difficulty onboarding new teams into the AIOps model.
risks.mitigation: Define and implement a monitoring governance model: standardize thresholds where feasible (infrastructure monitors), define enterprise guidelines for synthetic thresholds, establish tagging standards (including Asset Insight ID, service tags, and TR_‑prefixed custom tags), and create an auditing mechanism to flag non‑compliant monitors. Use Legal Tracker as a pilot to refine policies before scaling to other Tier 1 products such as HighQ.

risks.title: Departure of key AIOps architect (Chris Rutherford) may impact continuity and governance
risks.description: During the 30-Apr-2026 regular sync, Jot and the team thanked Chris Rutherford and noted that he would not be on the project from the following day. Chris has been the primary architect and leadership liaison for the ServiceNow AIOps/Event Management design, including incident priority behaviour, governance model, onboarding approach, and alignment with the Datadog hygiene programme. His departure creates a risk that architectural context, design rationale, and decision history may be lost or diluted, slowing future rule changes, onboarding of new products, and governance maturation.
risks.impact_description: Without Chris’s ongoing involvement, the team may struggle to maintain a consistent architectural vision and governance approach for AIOps. Questions about incident priority tuning, standard rule sets, and onboarding patterns could take longer to resolve; decisions may be revisited without full context; and onboarding of additional products “aggressively” (as planned) may slow or diverge from the intended cookie-cutter model. This could delay achieving scale benefits, increase rework on rules and standards, and reduce leadership confidence that AIOps is being guided by a clear owner.
risks.mitigation:
1) Ensure a structured handover of architectural and governance responsibilities from Chris to designated internal owners (e.g., Paul as programme lead, Prastuti and Vinay on the platform side, and Jot for project coordination).
2) Treat Doug’s in-progress training videos and configuration documentation as critical artefacts and complete them on the agreed timeline, capturing rule designs, priority behaviour, and onboarding patterns in a single reference.
3) Explicitly assign a new technical architecture lead for AIOps/Event Management within TR and communicate this to all stakeholders and vendors.
4) Review open design decisions and risks that had Chris as owner or key contributor, and confirm updated ownership and next steps so that work does not stall when onboarding new products “aggressively.”

risks.title: High concentration of noise from HighQ overshadowing other Tier 1 services
risks.description: 75% of GCC monthly events come from a single product (HighQ) out of ~50 Tier 1 products. If this concentration of noise is not addressed, it will continue to dominate GCC workload and may mask important events from other services, even after Event Management is enabled.
risks.impact_description: HighQ’s excessive alert volume may consume much of GCC and AIOps analysis capacity, leaving less focus on other services and skewing correlation and reporting. Important issues in other Tier 1 products could be delayed or overlooked, undermining fairness and effectiveness of the event management rollout.
risks.mitigation: Treat HighQ as a specific remediation target in the monitoring governance program: review and rationalize its monitors, apply stricter thresholds and suppression for noisy synthetics, and consider product‑specific filtering and correlation rules. Use HighQ data as a pilot to demonstrate volume reduction and incorporate lessons into broader standards before onboarding all Tier 1 products.

risks.title: Datadog and ServiceNow event volume and storage constraints
risks.description: There are concerns about the volume of events if all Datadog accounts send events into ServiceNow. While Datadog does not charge egress fees, ServiceNow storage is finite (e.g., ~4TB per instance), and high event volume could consume storage and impact performance if retention and filtering strategies are not defined.
risks.impact_description: If too many raw events are ingested without filtering and reasonable retention policies, ServiceNow databases may grow rapidly, potentially degrading performance or forcing unplanned data purges. Budget discussions with ServiceNow may be triggered, and the team might need to rework the architecture (e.g., move some correlation back to Datadog).
risks.mitigation: Engage the ServiceNow account team to confirm event storage limits, recommended retention periods, and cost implications. Implement lifecycle rules to purge older events while retaining alerts and incidents for reporting. Decide on a scoped ingestion strategy (starting with Legal Tracker and a subset of monitors), and only expand the number of sources and products once event filtering and correlation are proven to reduce noise.

risks.title: Teams without Event Management access losing visibility during cutover
risks.description: Not all operational teams (e.g., Major Incident team) currently have access to the Event Management module and dashboards. If the legacy Datadog–driven incident creation is disabled before those teams have alternative visibility, they may not see or manage critical events during and after cutover.
risks.impact_description: Major Incident and other central teams could lose timely visibility into critical alerts and incidents, delaying triage, page-outs, and communications. This would directly increase MTTA/MTTR and could cause missed SLAs for high-priority services like Legal Tracker.
risks.mitigation: Run legacy and new integrations in parallel for at least 24 hours while verifying parity, and only decommission the legacy path once all necessary operational teams have appropriate access to Event Management or alternate views. As part of cutover planning, review and adjust role assignments so Major Incident and other key groups can see grouped alerts, incidents, and AIOps dashboards. Following the 12 May 2026 regular sync, extend this to ensure GCC managers and operators (e.g., Rajendran’s team supporting Legal Tracker) are explicitly granted Event Management access before they are expected to monitor alerts, so that Legal Tracker and GCC can align their support model around the event-first view.

risks.title: CI binding from events/alerts to CMDB CIs may not work reliably
risks.description: Despite existing CIs in the CMDB with matching names, ServiceNow’s out‑of‑the‑box CI identification and binding logic is often failing to associate incoming Datadog events/alerts with the correct CI records.
risks.impact_description: If CI binding continues to fail, alerts and incidents generated by Event Management will not be accurately tied to infrastructure or application CIs. This will reduce the value of correlation, service impact analysis, and reporting, and could cause confusion during incident triage (wrong CI, or no CI attached). It may also block some auto‑remediation flows that depend on CI context and erode stakeholder confidence in the AIOps solution.
risks.mitigation: Doug and the ServiceNow team will analyze why out‑of‑the‑box CI identification is not working despite seemingly matching CI names and host attributes. They will review event payload mappings, identification rules, and any missing attributes (e.g., host vs. FQDN vs. CI name). Legal Tracker and GCC will provide additional event samples (including synthetic tests) to validate host/CI mappings. Where needed, adjust event rules or identification logic, and document any required payload standards back to Datadog (e.g., always sending host rather than FQDN).

risks.title: Legal Tracker monitor priorities and severities may not align with TR standards needed for AIOps
risks.description: Legal Tracker’s Datadog monitors currently have impact, urgency, and priority configured in Terraform, but those settings may not align with the TR incident priority matrix or with what AIOps expects to calculate severity/priority in ServiceNow.
risks.impact_description: If Legal Tracker monitors are not using severity/priority consistently with TR standards, the incidents created by AIOps may have inappropriate impact/urgency, leading to mis‑prioritized work (e.g., too many high‑priority incidents or true P1s classified lower). This could reduce trust in the new solution and require rework after go‑live.
risks.mitigation: Andrea and the Legal Tracker team will review all monitors in Terraform to ensure severity and priority reflect actual business impact and urgency, aligning with TR’s incident priority matrix. They will work with Luis and GCC to confirm how these values map into ServiceNow AIOps, and adjust monitor configurations where needed. This review will be incorporated into the onboarding checklist for Legal Tracker before final incident‑creation cutover.

risks.title: Production go-live before Event Management configuration and plugins are stable
risks.description: Event rules, respond rules, CI binding logic, and some plugins/scheduled jobs in upper environments are still under active revision. Doug has had to rebuild event rules from scratch due to conflicting behaviors, and some plugins in cloned environments require repair. There is pressure to meet the April 1, 2026 go‑live date for AIOps Event Management.
risks.impact_description: If incident creation and event processing are enabled in production before rules, mappings, and plugins are stable, the platform may create duplicate or missing incidents, fail to bind CIs, or mis‑route alerts. This could disrupt operations, undermine confidence in the new solution, and require emergency fixes in production.
risks.mitigation: Delay full go‑live of automated incident creation until: (1) event rules and respond rules are cleaned up and only approved rules are migrated; (2) required plugins and scheduled jobs are repaired in upper environments; (3) Datadog webhook payloads are standardized; and (4) a 24‑hour (or longer) dual‑run period validates behavior. Implement a change freeze so only Doug modifies AIOps event and alert rules until configuration is finalized, and prepare a clear checklist and ownership map for production enablement.

risks.title: Event forwarding between ServiceNow production and lower environments will function for test data
risks.description: The team is planning to use ServiceNow’s event forwarding from the production instance to dev and QA so that lower environments receive representative Datadog event traffic for testing rules and correlation without needing separate Datadog integrations for each environment.
risks.impact_description: If event forwarding between the production and lower environments does not function reliably, dev and QA will not receive representative production event traffic. This will limit the team’s ability to safely test new event rules, correlation logic, and responder rules using real-world data, increasing the risk that problematic configurations are promoted directly to production or that rule tuning is delayed.
risks.mitigation: Enable the event forwarding configuration in production, trigger Datadog events into the SNOW prod instance after webhook cutover, and confirm that corresponding events appear in dev (and subsequently QA) according to the expected schedule. If forwarding proves unreliable, fall back to (1) pointing Datadog test webhooks directly to dev/QA for specific monitors, or (2) manually injecting sample events into lower environments for rule testing. Coordinate with Doug to adjust or repair event management plugins if out-of-box forwarding behaviour is defective.

risks.title: Delayed monitor and tag standardization for GTM4 and SIAM may slip AIOps onboarding timelines
risks.description: GTM4 and SIAM subject-matter experts have expressed concerns that they may not be able to complete required Datadog monitor/tag standardization work (FinOpsDatadogAlerts updates, Asset Insight ID, primary support group, TR API name tags) by the targeted dates (end of this week / May 18). Luis has begun making some standardization changes, but key inputs such as synthetic monitor design and TR API name still depend on product teams. Without those updates, the AIOps webhook cannot be enabled because payloads would lack required fields, preventing correct grouping, routing, and service identification for these products.
risks.impact_description: If GTM4 and SIAM cannot complete the required Datadog monitor and tagging updates on time, the team will be unable to safely point their monitors at the AIOps webhook. This will delay onboarding for these early adopter products, push out the MVP / early adopter milestone, and limit the evidence base beyond Legal Tracker for demonstrating AIOps value. It may also create a staggered, uncoordinated rollout and erode stakeholder confidence if timelines repeatedly slip due to insufficient preparatory work on the product side.
risks.mitigation: Continue working closely with GTM4 and SIAM SMEs over the remaining working sessions (through May 18) to (1) explicitly list the required tag and monitor changes (Asset Insight ID, primary support group, TR API name, environment type) for each FinOpsDatadogAlerts monitor; (2) apply as many standardization changes centrally as possible where Luis can safely do so; (3) obtain product-team decisions on synthetic monitor design and TR API names during the current working sessions rather than deferring; and (4) only enable the webhook for each product once the minimum payload/tagging standard is verified. If a team cannot complete changes by May 18, re-plan their onboarding date explicitly rather than proceeding with incomplete data.

risks.title: Missing Service Associations in AIOps-generated incidents may delay Datadog cutover
risks.description: Legal Tracker incidents created via AIOps in ServiceNow are missing service associations (impacted service mappings) or have them populated incorrectly. As of 12-May, this is called out as an LT blocker and work-in-progress item owned by Doug, with the project explicitly stating that Datadog direct incident creation cannot be cut off until the service association issue is resolved.
risks.impact_description: If impacted services continue to be missing from or incorrectly populated in AIOps-generated incidents, the team will be unable to safely disable Datadog’s direct incident creation for Legal Tracker. This will prolong the dual-run period, maintain duplicate/parallel incidents, and delay full realization of AIOps benefits such as reduced incident volume and improved routing. It may also erode stakeholder confidence if incidents lack correct service context, complicating impact assessment and communications during incidents.
risks.mitigation: Continue treating the missing service association as a critical blocker for Legal Tracker cutover. Doug and Yash to (1) analyze current CI and service-mapping logic used by Event Management and incident creation flows; (2) update mapping rules so that service associations are derived correctly from Datadog payload fields (e.g., Asset Insight ID, service tags) and CI bindings; (3) validate behaviour on recent Legal Tracker incidents to confirm services populate as expected; and (4) only after consistent service association is confirmed, plan and execute the cutover step to disable Datadog-driven incident creation for Legal Tracker. Document the final mapping approach as part of the central configuration standards so it can be reused for future products.

risks.title: FedRAMP governance and plugin enablement may constrain or delay AIOps usage in regulated environments
risks.description: For FedRAMP, the team must complete governance and compliance documentation (a spreadsheet demonstrating controls and processes) and has opted in to all relevant ServiceNow plugins ahead of a platform clone over the weekend. Tim expects no significant change impact, but until the documentation is accepted and post-clone behaviour is validated, there is residual uncertainty about whether FedRAMP requirements or plugin changes could constrain or delay use of AIOps integrations in regulated environments.
risks.impact_description: If FedRAMP reviewers determine that governance and compliance evidence is insufficient, or if the newly enabled plugins introduce unforeseen behaviour after the clone, AIOps integrations might be delayed or restricted in FedRAMP-regulated environments. This could force separate configurations or postpone onboarding of FedRAMP-scoped products, increasing operational overhead and fragmenting the standardized AIOps approach across environments.
risks.mitigation: Complete the required FedRAMP governance spreadsheet by end of day as planned, clearly documenting AIOps governance and compliance controls. Enable and sync all required plugins prior to the scheduled clone so their configuration cascades to lower environments. After the clone, run targeted smoke tests of AIOps connectivity, event ingestion, and dashboards in the FedRAMP context to confirm there are no unexpected constraints. If any FedRAMP or plugin-related issues surface, engage ServiceNow and internal compliance teams promptly to adjust configuration or scope while preserving the standardized AIOps model as much as possible.

risks.title: Lack of standardized Datadog monitor configuration and observability governance may hinder AIOps rollout
risks.description: Datadog monitors across Thomson Reuters are owned by many different teams without a single centralized observability practice. Priority, severity, tags, and other configuration standards are inconsistently applied, and many monitors are configured primarily for escalation convenience (e.g., over‑using P1/P2).
risks.impact_description: Without consistent monitor configuration and centralized ownership, the payloads feeding ServiceNow Event Management will vary widely in quality and semantics. This threatens the accuracy of correlation, severity/priority calculation, and CI binding, and will make it difficult to apply generic rules at scale. It also increases the overhead of onboarding each product and may require significant cleanup or refactoring later.
risks.mitigation: (1) Establish GCC as the central practice owner for event management and observability, working with Platform Engineering and product teams; (2) align the Datadog hygiene programme that Mike Krause is running with the requirements of AIOps, so payload and monitor configuration standards are unified; (3) define and publish TR‑wide standards for monitors (priority/severity usage, tags, asset IDs, service and CI tagging) that support ServiceNow AIOps; (4) consider progressively migrating monitors to "monitoring as code" (Terraform) for centralized management where feasible; and (5) incorporate monitor‑configuration checks into the onboarding checklist for each application before enabling AIOps for them.

risks.title: Single-occurrence Datadog alerts remaining as orphan alerts without incidents
risks.description: ServiceNow AIOps is currently configured so that incidents are only created after grouping multiple alerts. During the 11 May 2026 sync, Luis noted that some alerts are left as 'orphans' because they only occur once and therefore never become part of a multi-alert group that triggers incident creation. Until expectations are clarified with the Legal Tracker team and configuration is adjusted, there is a risk that valid single-occurrence alerts will not generate incidents, reducing visibility into certain issues.
risks.impact_description: If single-occurrence alerts remain as orphan alerts that never create incidents, the Legal Tracker support team and GCC may miss issues that only fire once (for example, short-lived but impactful failures). This will lead to gaps in incident records, incomplete service-impact reporting, and potential delays in triage and remediation when teams rely on incidents as their primary work object. It may also reduce confidence in the AIOps model if stakeholders discover problems that were visible as alerts but never escalated to incidents.
risks.mitigation: Work with the Legal Tracker product team (Elizabeth and Andrea) to review a sample set of orphan alerts and agree on which types must always generate incidents, even if they occur only once. Based on this feedback, adjust Event Management configuration so that certain alert types or severities (for example, critical P1/P2 alerts, or specific monitor scopes) can create incidents on first occurrence, while less critical alerts continue to rely on grouping. Validate the updated behaviour over several days with Legal Tracker and GCC, ensuring no critical alerts remain orphaned and that incident volume remains manageable.

risks.title: Out-of-the-box event and alert rules may not cover all Legal Tracker scenarios
risks.description: The team intends to start with mostly out‑of‑the‑box ServiceNow event rules and a very small number of TR‑specific rules (around three). Some known scenarios, such as monitors triggering on multiple hosts, are not fully addressed yet and cause sub‑optimal grouping.
risks.impact_description: If key Legal Tracker use cases are not adequately covered by the event rules and alert correlation, different issues could be grouped into a single alert (e.g., same monitor on multiple hosts), or too many alerts could be created. This would reduce clarity for GCC and Legal Tracker operations and could either hide problems or generate excess noise.
risks.mitigation: Use out‑of‑the‑box rules as the baseline for MVP but plan iterative refinement. Luis will adjust event rules (e.g., message keys) to avoid grouping alerts from the same monitor across different hosts where that is undesirable, and will test these changes in dev/QA using simulated events. Only once behaviour is acceptable will rules be promoted to production. For edge cases not covered by generic rules, design narrowly scoped TR‑specific rules while avoiding over‑customization.

risks.title: No clear ownership and governance model for Event Management could recreate Datadog ‘mess’
risks.description: There is currently no formally established owner for ServiceNow Event Management and AIOps governance; without this, different teams may create and modify rules, payloads, and processes inconsistently, similar to the fragmented situation in Datadog today.
risks.impact_description: If Event Management governance is not defined, teams may implement their own rules and changes without control, leading to inconsistent correlation, rule conflicts, and a "free-for-all" configuration state. This undermines the platform’s reliability, complicates support, and increases the risk of regressions when new products are onboarded.
risks.mitigation: Propose and agree that GCC will own Event Management practice and governance across TR, in partnership with Platform Engineering and ServiceNow platform owners. Define roles for central rule configuration vs. permitted local customization (e.g., event super-users), establish change governance for event/alert rules (including how to test in lower environments), and agree that non-compliant teams can have their configuration rights reduced. Consult ServiceNow on governance patterns used by other customers. Following the April 21, 2026 lessons-learned session, implement an interim hypercare model where a core team (including Prastuti, Vinay, Chris and GCC representatives like Luis) rapidly addresses configuration issues and rule changes, while Chris, Prastuti and Vinay design a durable role and access model (e.g., event management admin persona and controlled SRE roles) to avoid both over-centralization and ‘Wild West’ configuration as more products onboard.

risks.title: Poor KB/runbook quality limiting AI-driven remediation and playbooks
risks.description: Existing knowledge base articles and runbooks are fragmented, often stored in Azure DevOps wikis, and of uneven quality. The project intends to use ServiceNow AIOps (LEAP, Now Assist) and playbooks for automated or assisted remediation, which depend heavily on reliable KB content and standardized runbooks.
risks.impact_description: If KB and runbook content is not consolidated and improved, AI capabilities and playbooks will have limited material to learn from and recommend. Automated remediation and agent assist features may produce weak or incorrect guidance, reducing trust in the platform and limiting the shift from manual to automated L0 remediation. The project may achieve correlation but fail to realize remediation and MTTR reduction benefits.
risks.mitigation: Identify top recurring incident scenarios (starting with Legal Tracker infrastructure and CPU/disk cleanup workflows), migrate SOPs from Azure DevOps into ServiceNow knowledge bases, and standardize runbook formats. Enable LEAP on incident data, review generated automation opportunities, and create corresponding Flow Designer playbooks integrated with existing GitHub Actions and Azure Runbooks. Treat KB/runbook uplift as a prerequisite workstream for advanced AIOps phases.

risks.title: Datadog → ServiceNow production connectivity may not be working at go‑live
risks.description: OAuth / webhook connectivity from Datadog production to the ServiceNow production event table may fail (401 errors or authorization issues), preventing events from being ingested when the webhook endpoint is cut over to production.
risks.impact_description: If Datadog cannot authenticate to the ServiceNow production instance, no Datadog events will be ingested into Event Management. This will block testing of plugins, grouping, and event forwarding, and could delay or prevent the AIOps go‑live for Legal Tracker. Operations would have to continue relying solely on existing Datadog→SNOW incident integrations and would lose the benefits of correlation and alerting in SNOW.
risks.mitigation: Yash and Luis are jointly troubleshooting the OAuth and webhook configuration for the production instance: (1) verify and correct the OAuth access token URL to use the production SNOW instance, (2) confirm client ID and client secret values and update the Datadog auth method, (3) add any missing OAuth scopes as seen in the working dev configuration, (4) if necessary, create a new auth method in Datadog and re‑bind the webhook, and (5) engage Doug from ServiceNow to review SNOW‑side configuration and SMC logs if 401/authorization errors persist. Use test monitors in Datadog prod to validate end‑to‑end event receipt in SNOW prod before full cutover.

risks.title: Insufficient Legal Tracker event volume for tuning event rules and correlation
risks.description: Current Legal Tracker monitors are only sending a small number of events (e.g., 40–50) into the ServiceNow dev event table, far below the true number of monitors (~900+). This provides too little variety and volume to reliably design and test event rules, alert grouping, and CI binding before go‑live.
risks.impact_description: If the team does not have representative event samples from all key Legal Tracker monitors, they cannot properly analyze data behaviour, define generic vs. application‑specific event rules, or validate CI binding and out‑of‑box correlation. This may lead to poorly tuned rules, missed correlations, incorrect incidents, or delays to the planned end‑of‑March / early‑April go‑live for Legal Tracker in AIOps/Event Management.
risks.mitigation: Have the Legal Tracker team (Elizabeth and Andrea) systematically trigger test alerts for all key monitors and synthetics. Where possible, script bulk simulation by cloning monitors that point only to the dev webhook, so no production incidents are created. Coordinate with Yash so that simulated events are captured and analyzed in SNOW dev to understand different alert types, payload patterns, and CI/host identifiers before finalizing event rules and response rules.

risks.title: Machine-learning-based alert grouping may incorrectly group unrelated alerts and erode trust in AIOps
risks.description: ServiceNow’s machine-learning-based alert grouping is currently grouping unrelated alerts (e.g., a synthetic and an infrastructure monitor) into a single group for Legal Tracker, apparently based on CI relationships. Andrea and Luis observed at least one recent example where the impacted services differed but the alerts were still grouped, and Luis confirmed this grouping did not come from the TR-defined rules but from ServiceNow’s ML logic. If ML continues to group unrelated alerts, Legal Tracker and GCC will not be able to rely on alert groups to understand issues, and teams may push to disable AI features entirely, undermining the value of AIOps.
risks.impact_description: If ML-based alert grouping continues to behave unpredictably and combines unrelated alerts: (1) alert groups and resulting incidents may misrepresent the underlying problems, confusing Legal Tracker SREs and GCC; (2) operators may have to drill into individual alerts and incidents to understand what is actually happening, increasing workload and MTTR; (3) Legal Tracker and GCC will lose trust in AIOps, treating it as "not a reliable product" and resisting full onboarding; (4) stakeholders may insist on disabling ML features to avoid bad groupings, which would remove a core AIOps benefit (AI-driven incident reduction) and reduce the business case for further rollout; and (5) inability to demonstrate safe, beneficial AI usage will make leadership wary of expanding AIOps (including to FedRAMP applications).
risks.mitigation: Luis will collect concrete examples of incorrect ML-based groupings (such as the synthetic + monitor example raised by Andrea) and review them with Doug to confirm whether ServiceNow’s AI/ML grouping is still active and how it is making decisions (e.g., via CI relationships). Together, they will (1) analyse current ML configurations and correlation patterns, (2) determine whether ML grouping should be tuned (e.g., adjusting CI-relationship rules, thresholds, or training data) or temporarily disabled for Legal Tracker until behaviour is acceptable, and (3) design a validation plan using the AIOps dashboards to show how ML grouping reduces incidents without introducing mis-groupings. Only after this tuning and validation will the team encourage Legal Tracker and GCC to rely on ML-based groups for day-to-day operations.

risks.title: Loss of AIOps program lead may impact configuration and governance continuity
risks.description: Chris Rutherford, the ServiceNow / Platform Engineering leader and de facto program lead for the SNOW AIOps implementation, is leaving the project as of the end of April 2026. Chris has been a key architect for event management design, incident priority behaviour, and governance decisions. His departure may slow decision-making on rule changes, governance models, and onboarding patterns for new products, especially while Legal Tracker is still stabilising and additional products are preparing to onboard.
risks.impact_description: If responsibilities held by Chris Rutherford are not effectively transitioned, the project could experience delays in refining event rules, incident priority logic, and governance standards; slower responses to new issues raised by product teams (e.g., Legal Tracker, future early adopters); and reduced clarity on the long-term AIOps operating model. This may delay Legal Tracker stabilisation, slow onboarding of subsequent products, and increase dependency on the external ServiceNow consultant for platform decisions, potentially impacting schedule and cost.
risks.mitigation: Formalize a transition plan for Chris Rutherford’s responsibilities by: (1) identifying successor owners for platform configuration and governance decisions (e.g., Prastuti Khanna and Vinay Kumar for ServiceNow platform, Paul Berry for program governance); (2) ensuring Chris’s design decisions and rationale are captured in written standards and the AIOps configuration reference document that Doug is preparing; (3) confirming that open risks and actions where Chris is owner are reassigned to named TR staff; and (4) using the regular AIOps sync to validate that new issues (e.g., incident priority mismatches, onboarding patterns for new products) have clear internal owners rather than relying on Chris post-departure.

risks.title: ServiceNow CIservice association behaviour may block cutover from Datadog incidents
risks.description: During the May 12, 2026 AIOps Product Onboarding regional sync, the team observed that ServiceNow is not associating services with the correct CIs for large applications such as Legal Tracker. Internal analysis suggests that a configurable limit of approximately 1,000 CIs per service causes additional CIs to be handled via dynamic CI groups, which in turn prevents correct service association and grouping. ServiceNows consultant (Doug) indicated there are traverse rules that might address this but needs to consult CMDB experts. Until a clear recommendation and fix are in place, the Legal Tracker product team considers this a showstopper for disabling Datadog-direct incident creation.
risks.impact_description: If ServiceNow continues to mis-associate or partially associate CIs to services due to the current serviceCI association behaviour, AIOps cannot reliably determine which service is impacted by an event or alert for large applications. For Legal Tracker, this would mean that incidents created by AIOps could lack correct service context or rely on dynamic CI groups, undermining routing, impact analysis, and leadership reporting. As a result, Legal Tracker stakeholders will not agree to cut over from Datadog-direct incident creation, delaying the POV completion, delaying onboarding of subsequent products, and prolonging reliance on legacy workflows.
risks.mitigation: ServiceNows consultant Doug will escalate the CI/service association issue to their CMDB experts to review the current configuration, including the apparent 1,000-CI-per-service association limit and available traverse rules. Together with the TR CMDB team, they will: (1) determine whether the association limit can be safely tuned without degrading ServiceNow performance; (2) design appropriate traverse rules or alternative modelling (e.g., hierarchical services) to support large applications like Legal Tracker; and (3) validate the chosen approach in a lower environment before promoting changes to production. In parallel, Jot will log this as a formal blocker in status reporting, and Talia will escalate via email and stakeholder channels (including Eric and John) to ensure it receives high priority attention from ServiceNow and the CMDB team. Cutover from Datadog-direct incidents for Legal Tracker will be deferred until a recommended and tested fix is in place.

risks.title: Legal Tracker AIOps implementation fails to deliver incident reduction and customer value
risks.description: Despite Legal Tracker being the pilot product, AIOps/Event Management is not yet delivering the expected reduction in incidents or operational value. As of the April 21, 2026 lessons-learned session, Legal Tracker remains on a 1:1 Datadog alert-to-incident model in production, grouping rules have recently been configured in a way that adds little value (e.g., grouping by Asset Insight ID only), critical data prerequisites (Datadog tags, assignment groups, CMDB CI state) are still being remediated, and clear success criteria and ownership for rule maintenance are only now being defined. If this continues, the Legal Tracker team may not adopt Event Management as a new way of working, and the pilot will not demonstrate the promised benefits for broader rollout.
risks.impact_description: If Legal Trackers AIOps implementation does not achieve meaningful incident reduction and better grouping (e.g., grouping by API/service and assignment group), the Legal Tracker team will continue to work from noisy 1:1 incidents, undermining the core business case. This will erode stakeholder confidence (particularly Elizabeths team), make it harder to justify onboarding additional products, and may force the organization to fall back to legacy Datadog-driven workflows. Time and budget already invested in Event Management may be perceived as sunk cost with limited return, and leadership may question further AIOps investment.
risks.mitigation:
1) Explicitly define and document success criteria for Legal Tracker with the product team (Elizabeth), focused on grouping related alerts (e.g., 20 API alerts to one incident) by API/service and assignment group and measurable incident reduction.
2) Update ServiceNow AIOps grouping rules to use API name and TR-standard tags (environment type, AAID, and assignment group) rather than grouping primarily by Asset Insight ID; Doug has already added API name to the grouping rule and will iterate based on Legal Tracker feedback.
3) Complete Legal Tracker Datadog monitor/tag hygiene: Andrea and Luis to finish adding required tags (environment type, primary support group, API name) in Terraform and deploy changes, with status reported back to Elizabeth.
4) Engage the CMDB team (e.g., Ragash, Kavi) to remediate Legal Tracker CIs that are incorrectly marked as retired and perform a focused data readiness dry run so CI binding and impacted services populate correctly.
5) Use a short hypercare period with daily checks (Doug + TR core team) to validate alert grouping and incident creation behaviour and adjust rules quickly until Legal Tracker confirms value.
6) Only after Legal Tracker confirms incident-reduction benefits, use this configuration as a reusable baseline for onboarding the next set of products.

risks.title: Machine learning-based 'group text' alert grouping may incorrectly combine or misclassify alerts
risks.description: ServiceNow AIOps is applying machine learning ('group text' type) to group alerts based on similarities in alert descriptions. For Legal Tracker, many alert descriptions share similar text patterns, which has led to at least one case where unrelated alerts were grouped together unexpectedly. Because the ML model is tuned on existing data and technical teams are only now learning how to adjust its behaviour, there is a risk that machine learning-based groupings will over-group or mis-group alerts before the configuration and operating model are fully established.
risks.impact_description: If machine learning-based 'group text' grouping continues to combine alerts incorrectly, Legal Tracker (and later other products) may see unrelated issues collapsed into a single group or important alerts hidden within large, noisy groups. This will reduce triage clarity for SREs and product teams, risk delayed detection of genuine incidents, and undermine stakeholder confidence in AIOps correlation. As more products are onboarded, incorrect ML groupings could scale across services and make it harder to interpret alert queues and incident linkages.
risks.mitigation: Doug will document and provide detailed instructions to the TR technical team (Luis and colleagues) on how to inspect and tune the machine learning-based 'group text' grouping configuration in ServiceNow AIOps. The technical team will (1) review current ML groupings affecting Legal Tracker; (2) adjust relevant parameters or model settings so that legitimate similarities are used without over-grouping; (3) establish an operating procedure where product teams (e.g., Legal Tracker) flag odd 'group text' groupings to the technical AIOps team; and (4) incorporate ML grouping review into ongoing monitoring and onboarding playbooks so that future products have their grouping behaviour validated and tuned early.

risks.title: Duplicate or inflated incident volumes during AIOps and Datadog parallel run
risks.description: When AIOps/Event Management starts creating incidents from alerts while the existing direct Datadog→ServiceNow incident integration is still active, the same underlying issues may result in multiple incidents or an increased incident count during the transition period.
