Event Management Admin role granted to Luis and team

issues.title: Missing or incorrect service associations in AIOps-generated incidents for Legal Tracker
issues.description: Incidents created through the ServiceNow AIOps/Event Management pipeline for Legal Tracker are missing or incorrectly populated service associations (impacted service fields). As a temporary workaround, incident priority and service are being passed directly from Datadog monitors, but a long-term, platform-native fix for impacted service mapping is still being designed and implemented.
issues.impact_assessment: Because service associations in AIOps-generated incidents are missing or incorrect, incident records do not reliably show the impacted services for Legal Tracker. This prevents accurate servicelevel reporting and impact assessment, complicates triage and routing, and undermines confidence in the AIOps implementation. The project cannot safely disable legacy Datadog incident creation until this is resolved, which blocks full cutover to the eventfirst model and delays realization of incident reduction and routing benefits.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on correct ServiceNow Event Management configuration (event and alert-to-incident mappings), underlying CI/CMDB data quality for Legal Tracker services, and Datadog monitor tagging; directly affects the ability to cut off legacy Datadog incident creation for Legal Tracker.
issues.resolution: Design and implement a permanent fix for impacted service mapping in ServiceNow so that AIOps-generated incidents reliably populate the correct impacted service, removing the need to deterministically pass service from Datadog. This includes analysis and configuration by Doug, with input from Kolluru, Prudhvi Yaswanth, and alignment to CI/CMDB data and tagging standards. Refer to Issue#13

issues.title: Confusing incident reopen behaviour and incident number changes for AIOps-generated incidents
issues.description: For Legal Tracker, incidents created via the ServiceNow AIOps/Event Management pipeline are being reopened when new alert groups arrive and, in some cases, the incident number changes and related alerts are unlinked from prior incidents. This behaviour is confusing Legal Tracker stakeholders and may impact historical tracking and reporting.
issues.impact_assessment: The current AIOps configuration causes closed incidents to be reopened and, in at least one observed case, to receive a new incident number when subsequent alerts are grouped. This undermines the stability of incident identifiers used for tracking and historical analysis, and creates confusion for Legal Tracker operators who are not accustomed to incidents reopening from grouped alerts. While not considered a hard blocker, it risks reducing trust in the AIOps workflow, complicating service reporting, and may require re-education or configuration changes before broader rollout.
issues.dependencies_affecting: ServiceNow Event Management respond rules and grouping configuration; Legal Tracker incident workflows; ServiceNow CMDB and CI-binding configuration for Legal Tracker.
issues.resolution: Event management properties changed to resolve the issue

issues.title: CI binding now working but CI–service association limits remain a concern
issues.description: Following recent discovery and CI-binding fixes by Kolluru, Prudhvi Yaswanth, CI binding for Legal Tracker assets is expected to work as intended (no active VMs in retired state, discovery failures remediated, and custom logic deactivated). However, a ServiceNow limitation on the number of CI associations per application service (around 1,000 CIs) may still prevent correct service association for large applications using tag-based service mappings.
issues.impact_assessment: CI records for Legal Tracker now appear to be discovered and active, and CI binding is expected to function, which should unblock AIOps incident creation from a CI perspective. However, the apparent 1,000-CI-per-service association limit in ServiceNow means that not all CIs may be associated with their application services via tag-based mappings. This can lead to incomplete or incorrect impacted service information on incidents, limiting service-level reporting, routing accuracy, and impact analysis for large applications. While Kolluru, Prudhvi Yaswanth and Doug believe this should not block moving forward with production from a CI-binding standpoint, unresolved service association behaviour remains a material concern for cutover and long-term scalability.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on ServiceNow CI–service association configuration, tag-based service mappings, and potential product-level limits on CI associations; affects Legal Tracker AIOps incidents and broader AIOps rollout for large applications.
issues.resolution: TBD - Need guidance from external SNOW resources

issues.title: Inconsistent alert grouping for Legal Tracker due to AI/ML-based CI relationship grouping
issues.description: ServiceNows machine-learning-based event correlation is grouping unrelated Legal Tracker alerts into a single alert group based on inferred CI relationships, including combining a synthetic monitor alert and an infrastructure monitor alert even when impacted services differ. These ML-created groups are not aligned with the TR-defined correlation rules agreed for Legal Tracker.
issues.impact_assessment: Unexpected AI/ML-driven alert groupings make it difficult for the Legal Tracker team and GCC to understand which alerts belong together and to trust alert-centric operations. Because some alert groups contain different types of alerts with different impacted services, operators cannot use alert group context or impacted service filters reliably. This undermines confidence in Event Management, prevents full onboarding of the Legal Tracker team to alerts, and blocks cutover from Datadog-direct incidents.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on ServiceNow AIOps machine-learning correlation configuration, CI relationship data in CMDB, and the TR-standard rule set implemented by Doug and Rodriguez, Luis Jorge; affects Legal Tracker alert review, GCC adoption of Event Management, and incident cutover readiness.
issues.resolution: Refer to Issue#13

issues.title: Incident reopening and incident number changes for AIOps-generated incidents
issues.description: For Legal Tracker, incidents created via the ServiceNow AIOps/Event Management pipeline are being reopened and, in some cases, assigned new incident numbers when additional alerts are grouped into an existing alert group. Related alerts are being unlinked from previous incidents and attached to new ones, causing confusion for operators and complicating historical tracking and reporting.
issues.impact_assessment: This behaviour is confusing to Legal Tracker stakeholders (Morales, Elizabeth and Santana, Andrea) and GCC because closed incidents can be reopened and renumbered when new alerts arrive for the same group. It complicates incident history, makes it harder to track lifecycle and metrics, and may undermine confidence in AIOps-generated incidents. It also risks disrupting reporting for leaders such as Mike Krause and Dominique Schreier who rely on stable incident identifiers and histories.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on ServiceNow Event Management respond rule configuration, Legal Tracker alert grouping rules, and broader AIOps incident creation behaviour; affects Legal Tracker’s ability to adopt the new alert-centric operating model and may influence cutover timing from Datadog-direct incidents.
issues.resolution: Doug will investigate the incident reopen and incident-number-change behaviour with ServiceNow experts to determine if it is standard configuration or a defect, and identify configuration options (e.g., grouping window adjustments or respond rule changes) to prevent unexpected renumbering while still supporting alert-centric operations.

issues.title: CI binding and CI–service association still failing for Legal Tracker after attempted fixes
issues.description: Despite earlier statements that discovery issues were fixed and CI binding should now work, sample checks during the April 30, 2026 AIOps Product Onboarding regional sync showed that recent Legal Tracker alerts in ServiceNow are still missing CI bindings and/or are associated to incorrect services. A suspected ServiceNow product limitation (approximately 1,000 CIs per service) and incomplete follow-up with ServiceNow and internal platform teams are contributing factors.
issues.impact_assessment: Legal Tracker remains unable to rely on AIOps-generated alerts and incidents for accurate CI and service context. This undermines Elizabeth Morales’ willingness to adopt Event Management as the primary workflow, delays safe cutover away from legacy Datadog-direct incident creation, and risks leadership perception that the platform was moved to production before being ready. Continued CI binding and service association failures also consume troubleshooting cycles across TR Technology and ServiceNow and create escalation overhead up to AD and senior leadership.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on ServiceNow discovery configuration, CMDB data quality and modelling for Legal Tracker (including any CI-per-service limits), and timely support from the ServiceNow consultant and platform team. Directly affects AIOps cutover readiness for Legal Tracker and the ability to demonstrate value to stakeholders such as Elizabeth Morales and Will LeBlanc.
issues.resolution: Investigate current CI binding and CI–service association behaviour for Legal Tracker alerts in ServiceNow, including discovery configuration, CMDB records, and any product limits on CIs per service. Work jointly between Kolluru, Prudhvi Yaswanth and Doug (ServiceNow consultant) to (1) confirm whether discovery has fully corrected CI data, (2) quantify how many alerts still lack correct CI/service mappings using a standard CI-binding report, (3) engage ServiceNow support on any product limitation and traverse rule configuration needed, and (4) implement and test corrected binding/association behaviour so that new Legal Tracker alerts consistently attach to the correct CI and service. Only after this is validated with Elizabeth Morales should the team proceed to disable Datadog-direct incident creation. Refer to Issue#13
issues.source_file_name: AIOps Product Onboarding Reg Sync 30 Apr.docx

issues.title: GCC team lacks access to ServiceNow Event Management for Legal Tracker alerts
issues.description: The GCC manager for Legal Tracker (Rajendran Van) and GCC operators do not currently have access to the ServiceNow Event Management workspace, so they cannot see or work Legal Tracker alerts created by AIOps. Luis has explained the application behaviour to GCC, but access has not yet been provisioned.
issues.impact_assessment: Without access to Event Management, GCC cannot participate in alert-centric operations for Legal Tracker, cannot validate alert grouping behaviour, and cannot support Legal Tracker during the transition to AIOps. This creates a misalignment between product support and central operations, reduces coverage on AIOps alerts, and further delays the ability to rely on Event Management and to cut over from Datadog-direct incidents.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on ServiceNow role and access configuration managed by the ServiceNow platform team (e.g., Khanna, Prastuti) and on GCC onboarding processes; affects the Legal Tracker AIOps pilot, GCC readiness for future products, and the previously identified risk about teams losing visibility during cutover.

issues.title: AIOps-generated incident priorities are higher than corresponding alert priorities
issues.description: Incidents created by ServiceNow AIOps from group alerts are being assigned higher priorities (often P1) than expected based on the underlying alert severity and priority. Analysis of the 'create incident TR presets' subflow and related flow actions shows that incident impact and urgency are set to their highest values whenever the alert priority group or severity is 1 or 2, which forces the incident priority matrix to produce P1 incidents. In addition, the alert 'priority group' field is driven by an out-of-the-box priority score that may not align with Thomson Reuters expectations, and current event rules map Datadog monitor priority into alert severity but do not explicitly map priority into the alert priority group. As a result, Legal Tracker alerts with moderate priorities (e.g., P3) can still generate P1 incidents, causing misaligned incident priorities compared to direct Datadog-created incidents.
issues.impact_assessment: The mismatch between alert priority and AIOps-generated incident priority causes Legal Tracker incidents to be raised as P1 when the underlying monitor/alert priority is lower (e.g., P2 or P3). This over-escalation inflates the number of P1 incidents, drives unnecessary major incident engagement, and creates inconsistency between incidents created directly from Datadog and those created via AIOps. It undermines trust in the AIOps implementation, complicates incident reporting and metrics, and makes Legal Tracker and GCC reluctant to rely on AIOps-driven incidents until priority behavior is corrected.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on ServiceNow vendor configuration of the 'create incident TR presets' subflow and priority score thresholds; relies on correct Datadog monitor priority values and current event rules that map Datadog priority into alert severity; interacts with the ServiceNow incident priority matrix and incident management practice settings.
issues.resolution:
Review and adjust the incident creation flow and priority mapping so that incident impact and urgency are derived appropriately from alert severity and priority group without systematically elevating incidents to P1. This includes: (1) analysing the 'create incident TR presets' subflow and its scripted flow actions to change logic that currently sets incident impact/urgency to 1 when alert priority group or severity is 1 or 2; (2) confirming how the alert 'priority group' field is populated from the out-of-the-box priority score and whether threshold properties should be tuned instead of custom code changes; and (3) ensuring event rules that map Datadog monitor priority to alert severity and priority group produce incident priorities aligned with TR's incident priority matrix. Proposed changes will be validated on sample Legal Tracker alerts and incidents before wider rollout.  
*Datadog priority and service directly being transferred to the incident

issues.title: Datadog P3 alerts mapped as critical severity in ServiceNow alerts for Legal Tracker
issues.description: In the ServiceNow production instance, Legal Tracker alerts coming from Datadog with monitor priority P3 are being mapped to critical severity on the ServiceNow alert records. As a result, incidents created from these alerts appear as P1, even though the underlying Datadog monitors are configured as P3. The problem appears to originate in the custom ServiceNow event field mapping rule "Datadog map alert priority to severity" not behaving as it did in dev, potentially due to rule ordering or execution context.
issues.impact_assessment: Because P3 Datadog alerts for Legal Tracker are being mapped to critical severity in ServiceNow, any incidents generated from these alerts are incorrectly created as P1. This mis-prioritization would cause an excessive number of P1 incidents, distort SLAs and reporting, and could trigger unnecessary major incident workflows and on-call paging. The team has therefore disabled automatic incident creation and set the incident-creation subflow to manual to avoid flooding operations with false P1s, which in turn delays full end-to-end testing and cutover to the AIOps event-first model.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on the correct configuration and execution order of the ServiceNow event field mapping rule "Datadog map alert priority to severity" and on availability of representative Legal Tracker alerts from Datadog (including synthetics) for testing. Affects the ability to safely enable AIOps-driven incident creation for Legal Tracker without generating spurious P1 incidents.
issues.resolution:
Investigate and correct the ServiceNow event field mapping rule that converts Datadog alert_priority values (P1–P5) into ServiceNow alert severity. Specifically: (1) review the "Datadog map alert priority to severity" event field mapping script in production; (2) adjust the rule order so that it executes before other mapping rules (e.g., synthetic-related mappings at order 20/25); (3) rerun tests with known P3 Legal Tracker alerts (including synthetics) to confirm that alert severity is set correctly; and (4) only after the mapping is verified, re-enable automatic incident creation for Legal Tracker alerts, starting with manual creation from alerts and then switching back to automatic once behaviour is stable.
Refer to Issue#15

issues.title: Datadog to ServiceNow production OAuth authentication failures (401 errors)

dependencies.title: Datadog hygiene programme alignment with AIOps
dependencies.description: Successful scale‑out of AIOps requires alignment between the Datadog hygiene programme (standard monitor configuration, tagging) and AIOps‑specific needs (payload, severity/priority usage).
dependencies.dependent_on: GCC observability practice (Heymann, Damian) and platform engineering

dependencies.title: Datadog webhook configuration for Legal Tracker

dependencies.title: FedRAMP governance approval and AIOps plugin enablement before ServiceNow clone

dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If AIOps/Event Management is not enabled in the FedRAMP ServiceNow instance in a timely manner, FedRAMP applications will continue to generate unmanaged alert noise, delaying noise reduction and correlation benefits and creating divergence between enterprise and FedRAMP operational models.

dependencies.title: Resolution of CI/service association behaviour by CMDB resource and ServiceNow consultant
dependencies.description: Legal Tracker AIOps alert management and incident routing depend on a CMDB resource (identified by John) and ServiceNow consultant Doug completing analysis and configuration changes to fix CI–service association behaviour so that impacted services populate correctly in AIOps-generated incidents.
dependencies.dependent_on: ServiceNow CMDB expert resource identified by John and Doug’s configuration changes to CI/service association logic

dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If CI/service association behaviour is not corrected in a timely manner, impacted services will remain missing from AIOps-generated incidents, making alert categorization and routing difficult and preventing cutover from legacy Datadog-direct incident creation. dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If vendor rule and mapping work is delayed, the team cannot fully validate CI binding, incident creation behaviour, or implement advanced correlation and responder rules, potentially delaying go-live.

dependencies.title: Establish monitoring governance practice and ownership for Legal Tracker event management
dependencies.description: Formal monitoring governance must be in place so Datadog and Azure Alerts remain the detection layer under a controlled, standardized configuration model. This includes standardized thresholds for infrastructure monitors (~20%), auditing and enforcement of classification standards, and clearly defined ownership of monitor configuration governance for Legal Tracker (and later other products) before and during AIOps rollout.

owner.name: Service Management / GCC monitoring governance lead (e.g., Heymann, Damian)

dependencies.dependent_on: Monitoring governance practice and owner (GCC / Platform Engineering) being defined and operational
dependencies.consumer: ServiceNow Event Management implementation for Legal Tracker
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without a formal monitoring governance practice and owner, Legal Tracker monitors may continue to use inconsistent thresholds and classifications, leading to noisy or misclassified events entering ServiceNow. This will reduce the effectiveness of filtering, prioritization, and correlation, and could undermine confidence in the AIOps solution.
dependencies.mitigation: Proceed with Legal Tracker using interim governance based on existing Datadog hygiene standards while accelerating definition of a formal governance model. Use Legal Tracker as the pilot to refine governance artifacts (policies, review process, exception handling) and then institutionalize them via GCC and Platform Engineering.

dependencies.title: Select and implement integration mechanism for consolidating monitoring sources into ServiceNow
dependencies.description: To redirect events from Datadog and Azure Alerts into the ServiceNow event table, an integration mechanism must be selected and implemented (e.g., Lambda-based integration vs Service Graph Connector). Monitor inventory and integration design must support consolidation of Datadog, Azure Alerts, and cloud-native monitors into a single event ingestion path for Legal Tracker.
dependencies.dependent_on: Chosen integration mechanism (e.g., AWS Lambda integration, Service Graph Connector) and completed monitor inventory for Legal Tracker
dependencies.consumer: ServiceNow Event Management ingestion for Legal Tracker
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If an integration mechanism is not selected and implemented in time, Legal Tracker events from Datadog, Azure Alerts, and other cloud-native monitors cannot be redirected into the ServiceNow event table. This will block the architectural shift from direct-to-incident to event-first processing and delay all downstream capabilities (filtering, correlation, prioritization).
dependencies.mitigation: Use the simplest viable integration (e.g., existing Datadog webhook plus incremental Azure integration) as an MVP while evaluating Service Graph Connector or Lambda for longer-term standardization. Maintain the legacy Datadog→incident path as fallback until consolidated ingestion is proven.

dependencies.title: Define event taxonomy for informational, warning, and exception events
dependencies.description: An event taxonomy must be defined for Legal Tracker monitors to distinguish informational, warning, and exception events. This taxonomy is the basis for filtering, classification rules, and event prioritization in ServiceNow Event Management and will guide which events generate incidents versus being suppressed or treated as informational.

owner.name: Incident Management and AIOps design leads (e.g., Heymann, Damian; Rutherford, Chris)

dependencies.dependent_on: Agreement on Legal Tracker event taxonomy (informational vs warning vs exception) and documentation of how it maps to ServiceNow severity and incident policies
dependencies.consumer: Event filtering and prioritization configuration for Legal Tracker in ServiceNow
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without a defined event taxonomy, filtering and prioritization rules cannot be consistently implemented. This will result in inconsistent suppression of informational events, potential creation of non-actionable incidents, and difficulty standardizing behaviour across monitors and products.
dependencies.mitigation: Draft an initial, directional taxonomy for Legal Tracker based on current incident practices and iterate during early AIOps usage. Use lessons learned to refine and formalize the taxonomy before broader rollout.

dependencies.title: Define incident creation policy for AIOps events
dependencies.description: An explicit incident creation policy must be defined for Legal Tracker to decide when correlated events should generate incidents versus remaining as events or being handled through auto-remediation. This governs whether every actionable event creates an incident or whether some remediation can occur under event records only.

owner.name: AD Al-Ghourabi (TR Technology) with input from Service Management leadership

dependencies.dependent_on: Agreement on incident creation criteria (e.g., only exceptions create incidents; some remediations handled at event level) and configuration of corresponding rules in ServiceNow
dependencies.consumer: ServiceNow Incident Management behaviour for AIOps-generated events in Legal Tracker
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If incident creation policy remains undefined, AIOps may either create too many incidents (replicating the 1:1 pattern) or too few (risking missed incidents). This uncertainty will delay tuning of incident rules and hinder safe cutover from the legacy Datadog incident path.
dependencies.mitigation: Define a provisional incident creation policy for Legal Tracker (e.g., incidents only for exception-level events and primary correlated groups) and validate during a controlled observation period, adjusting policy before applying it as a standard for other products.

dependencies.title: Define notification tiers for after-hours paging vs next-business-day alerts
dependencies.description: Notification tiering rules must be defined to determine what event or incident severities trigger after-hours pages versus next-business-day notifications for Legal Tracker. This is needed to reduce notification noise and align on-call behaviour with the new alert-centric AIOps model.

owner.name: Service Management / Incident Management leadership (e.g., Heymann, Damian)

dependencies.dependent_on: Agreed set of notification tiers mapping event/incident severity to after-hours paging vs next-business-day notification, and corresponding configuration in ServiceNow on-call and notification modules
dependencies.consumer: On-call paging and notification behaviour for Legal Tracker and future AIOps-onboarded products
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Without defined notification tiers, teams may continue to receive excessive after-hours pages for non-critical events or insufficient notifications for true exceptions. This undermines one of the key benefits of AIOps (notification reduction) and may cause resistance from on-call engineers.
dependencies.mitigation: Adopt an interim rule (e.g., only P1/P2 incidents from primary correlated alerts generate after-hours pages) based on current practice, then refine notification tiers once incident creation and prioritization behaviour is stable.

dependencies.title: Improve KB and runbook quality to enable phased automation and AI-assisted resolutions
dependencies.description: KB articles and runbooks must be improved for Legal Tracker so that incidents arriving with enriched context from correlated events can leverage reliable remediation content. This is a prerequisite for introducing automated remediation and AI-recommended resolutions in later phases of Event Management.

owner.name: Knowledge management and AIOps remediation lead (e.g., Doug – ServiceNow consultant – in partnership with GCC)

dependencies.dependent_on: Consolidated, high-quality KB articles and runbooks for top Legal Tracker incident scenarios, integrated with ServiceNow knowledge and Flow Designer
dependencies.consumer: Later-phase AIOps capabilities (automated remediation, Now Assist / LEAP suggestions) for Legal Tracker and other products
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If KB and runbook quality is not improved, later-phase AIOps capabilities such as AI-suggested resolutions and automated remediation workflows will be ineffective or inaccurate. This will limit MTTR improvements and delay realization of higher-stage value from the AIOps program.
dependencies.mitigation: Delay automation-focused capabilities for Legal Tracker until core ingestion, correlation, and incident behaviour are stable, while running a parallel workstream to uplift KB/runbook content for the most frequent incident types.

decisions.title: Use out-of-the-box ServiceNow AIOps incident priority calculation instead of custom impact/urgency event fields
decisions.description: The team will not persist custom impact and urgency fields on ServiceNow event records to mirror Datadog values. Instead, Datadog monitors will be configured with appropriate severity and priority, and ServiceNow will use its out‑of‑the‑box logic (including severity and alert type) to calculate incident impact and urgency.
decisions.rationale: Custom impact/urgency fields add complexity and diverge from the out‑of‑the‑box product design. Using ServiceNow’s standard AIOps logic simplifies maintenance and ensures consistency as the solution scales across products, even though it requires additional work to train teams on correct use of severity and priority in Datadog.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Introduce custom impact/urgency fields on events populated directly from Datadog and map them to incidents.
2) Stay out-of-the-box by configuring severity/priority in Datadog and relying on ServiceNow’s AIOps engine to derive impact/urgency for incidents.
3) Hybrid approach using both custom fields and AIOps calculations.
decisions.dependencies_linked: ServiceNow CI binding and incident creation behaviour; Datadog monitor configuration standards; removal of custom event fields added by Yash.

decisions.title: Legal Tracker AIOps to proceed using minimal rule set (out-of-the-box plus three TR rules)
decisions.description: For Legal Tracker go‑live, the team will rely primarily on out‑of‑the‑box ServiceNow event rules with a small set of three Thomson Reuters–specific rules, rather than waiting to design a comprehensive custom rule library.
decisions.rationale: Using a minimal rule set allows the team to start realizing AIOps value sooner and avoids over‑engineering for the first product. Additional rules can be added iteratively once real event data and behaviours are better understood.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Design extensive custom event and correlation rules for Legal Tracker before go‑live.
2) Use out-of-the-box rules only.
3) Use out-of-the-box rules plus a small number of TR-specific rules for initial go-live.
decisions.dependencies_linked: ServiceNow vendor rule configuration; Datadog payload contents; cutover planning for incidents.

decisions.title: Event forwarding from ServiceNow production to dev/QA is not a go-live blocker
decisions.description: The team agreed that ServiceNow event forwarding from production to lower environments (dev and QA) is helpful for testing but is not required for the initial Legal Tracker go‑live.
decisions.rationale: Forwarding allows consistent test data across environments, but its absence does not prevent AIOps from functioning in production. Delaying go‑live until forwarding is perfect would unnecessarily slow delivery.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Make event forwarding a prerequisite for go-live.
2) Treat forwarding as a post-go-live improvement while focusing on production connectivity and incident behaviour.
decisions.dependencies_linked: ServiceNow event forwarding configuration managed by Yash; Datadog webhook pointing to production.

decisions.title: Pilot parallel incident run in QA before enabling AIOps incidents in production
decisions.description: Before AIOps begins creating incidents in production for Legal Tracker, the team plans a time‑boxed parallel run in a QA environment where AIOps incidents can be compared to existing Datadog‑driven incidents, to assess completeness and volume reduction.
decisions.rationale: A QA parallel run allows the team to validate that AIOps does not miss important incidents and provides incident volume reduction, without risking production operations or confusing support teams with duplicates.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Immediately enable AIOps incident creation in production and disable Datadog incidents.
2) Run AIOps alerts only in production and compare manually.
3) Run AIOps incidents in QA for a short period while keeping production unchanged, then decide on production enablement.
decisions.dependencies_linked: QA environment setup; ability to mirror event data into QA; cutover plan for disabling Datadog incidents per product.

decisions.title: Define notification tiers for after-hours vs next-business-day alerts
decisions.description: The team must decide what severity levels and event types trigger after-hours paging versus next-business-day notification for Legal Tracker, based on correlated incidents and event severity.

decision_owner.name: Service Management / Incident Management leadership (e.g., Heymann, Damian)

decisions.rationale: Tiered notifications reduce alert fatigue by ensuring that teams are only paged for true service-impacting exceptions while less severe events are handled during business hours.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Only P1 (and possibly P2) incidents generated from primary correlated alerts trigger after-hours pages; others become next-business-day notifications.
2) Include some high-severity warnings in after-hours paging for specific services.
3) Maintain current incident-based paging behaviour initially and gradually introduce alert-driven paging tiers.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Incident creation policy, on-call configuration on the ServiceNow alert/incident tables, and Legal Tracker on-call agreements.

decisions.title: Timebox QA observation period for new AIOps product onboardings
decisions.description: For new products being onboarded to AIOps/Event Management (such as ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM), the QA observation period for running their monitors and alerts through ServiceNow will be timeboxed to no more than three to four weeks, with a target of one to two weeks, to avoid prolonged onboarding and encourage iterative movement towards production.
decisions.rationale: AD emphasized the need to avoid letting QA observation drag on, preferring short, iterative cycles so that teams can move to production quickly while still gaining sufficient insight into alert grouping and rule behaviour.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Run QA observation for an open-ended period until all issues are resolved.
2) Timebox QA observation to a maximum of three to four weeks with a target of one to two weeks before deciding on production onboarding.
3) Skip QA observation and onboard directly to production using enterprise rules.
decisions.dependencies_linked: AIOps onboarding plans for ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM; Legal Tracker lessons learned; QA data ingestion for GTM4 and SIAM.

decisions.title: Proceed with onboarding ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM in parallel with caution
decisions.description: The team will initiate AIOps/Event Management onboarding for both ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM in parallel, while closely monitoring the workload and alert volumes from GTM4 and leveraging QA observation to understand and manage the expected high volume of findings.
decisions.rationale: Both GTM4 and SIAM generate significant alert volume and their teams are ready to engage. Despite concerns about the effort required for GTM4, the group agreed that starting with both, with a cautious and timeboxed QA approach, provides maximum learning and impact.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Onboard only ONESOURCE GTM4 first, then onboard SIAM later.
2) Onboard only SIAM first.
3) Onboard both ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM in parallel, with a timeboxed QA observation period and readiness assessments.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Readiness assessments for GTM4 and SIAM monitors; Datadog webhooks and QA event flow; Legal Tracker feedback influencing configuration adjustments.

decisions.title: Prioritize AIOps capabilities in sequence: ingestion → correlation & prioritization → notification → root cause & resolutions
decisions.description: For Legal Tracker, capability rollout will follow a defined order: (1) Alert ingestion (event-first processing) as the foundation; (2) Intelligent correlation as the highest-value capability; (3) Event prioritization and notification reduction; and (4) later-phase root cause identification and AI-suggested resolutions once correlation and data volume are sufficient.
decisions.rationale: Sequencing capabilities ensures a stable foundation before introducing advanced features. Ingestion and correlation deliver the highest immediate value by breaking the 1:1 event-to-incident pattern, while notification reduction and advanced root cause/AI resolutions depend on stable correlation, prioritization, and sufficient historical data.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Implement all capabilities at once (ingestion, correlation, prioritization, notification, root cause, AI resolutions).
2) Focus only on ingestion and correlation for MVP and defer all other capabilities.
3) Implement capabilities in the chosen sequence: ingestion → correlation & prioritization → notification → root cause & resolutions.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Ingestion readiness (integration mechanism), correlation tuning, event taxonomy definition, KB/runbook quality, and sufficient historical incident data.

decisions.title: Adopt deterministic Datadog monitor priority as MVP incident priority for Legal Tracker
decisions.description: For the Legal Tracker MVP, ServiceNow’s out-of-the-box incident priority calculation has been disabled and Datadog monitor priority is passed deterministically through to the incident priority. This patch aligns incident priority with existing Legal Tracker practices while the team gains experience with AIOps and prepares to tune non-deterministic priority behaviour in lower environments.
decisions.rationale: Legal Tracker and GCC are accustomed to deterministic incident priority based directly on Datadog monitors. Early trials of AIOps-native, non-deterministic priority were perceived as too aggressive (e.g., raising priority after only two alerts). To avoid blocking the production MVP and to meet previously communicated timelines, the team agreed to a temporary deterministic configuration as an MVP, while planning a ‘laboratory’ effort in dev/QA to tune native AIOps scoring before reintroducing it.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Keep ServiceNow out-of-the-box non-deterministic incident priority (based on CI importance, blast radius, and alert state).
2) Temporarily disable AIOps-native priority and deterministically map Datadog monitor priority directly to incident priority for Legal Tracker.
3) Delay Legal Tracker MVP until non-deterministic behaviour is fully tuned and accepted by the product team.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to risk 'Reliance on temporary customizations for incident priority and CI binding instead of AIOps-native behaviour' and dependency 'ServiceNow vendor configuration of event rules, responder rules, and mappings'; also interacts with future tuning sessions in dev/QA for non-deterministic priority.

decisions.title: Use incident data from new ServiceNow instance (January 2026 onward) without backfilling legacy instance data for initial AIOps onboarding prioritization
decisions.description: For the first round of AIOps onboarding prioritization, the team will rely on incident data extracted from the new ServiceNow instance (approximately January 2026 onward) combined with existing alert data, and will not pursue extracting or merging historical incident data from the legacy ServiceNow instance at this stage.
decisions.rationale: Paul Berry judged that five months of incident data from the new ServiceNow instance is sufficient to reveal patterns and identify candidate applications for the top 40 AIOps migration list. Fetching and merging legacy incident data would consume additional effort without materially improving the directional signals needed for round-one prioritization. Any anomalies (e.g., applications with high recent incidents but lower historical alert ranking) will themselves be useful signals to investigate rather than reasons to delay decisions.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Extract and merge legacy ServiceNow incident data with new-instance data to create a full-year, like-for-like incident view.
2) Limit analysis to incident data from the new ServiceNow instance (January 2026 onward) and compare with existing alert data for prioritization.
3) Restrict both alert and incident datasets to a common time window starting January 2026, requiring additional re-extraction but still avoiding legacy system queries.
decisions.dependencies_linked: AIOps product prioritization spreadsheet; action for Rodriguez, Luis Jorge to add incident data column from new ServiceNow instance.
decisions.source_file_name: AIOps Product Onboarding Reg Sync 30 Apr.docx

decisions.title: Define ingestion scope for Legal Tracker monitors entering ServiceNow
decisions.description: The team needs to decide whether all Legal Tracker monitors will send events into the ServiceNow event table from the outset, or whether AIOps will start with a defined subset of monitors and expand in later phases.

decision_owner.name: TR AIOps leadership (e.g., Rutherford, Chris; AD Al-Ghourabi)

decisions.rationale: Ingestion scope affects both risk and value. Including all monitors maximizes observability and correlation opportunities but may introduce noise and configuration risk; starting with a subset reduces initial complexity but may limit early value and require additional rollout planning.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Route all Legal Tracker monitors into ServiceNow from day one.
2) Start with a defined subset of monitors (e.g., infrastructure and critical synthetics) and expand in Phase 2.
3) Pilot with only specific regions or monitor types before full ingestion.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Event ingestion dependencies (integration mechanism, monitor inventory) and filtering/correlation configuration for Legal Tracker.

decisions.title: Define Legal Tracker event taxonomy for informational, warning, and exception events
decisions.description: The project must agree on what constitutes informational, warning, and exception events for Legal Tracker monitors. This taxonomy will drive filtering, suppression, and classification rules in ServiceNow Event Management.

decision_owner.name: Incident Management and AIOps design leads (e.g., Heymann, Damian; Rutherford, Chris)

decisions.rationale: A clear event taxonomy is necessary to consistently suppress non-actionable events, classify exceptions that should create incidents, and align monitor configurations with business impact expectations.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Adopt a simple three-level taxonomy (informational, warning, exception) aligned with current incident severity definitions.
2) Use a more granular taxonomy (e.g., multiple warning levels) for synthetics versus infrastructure.
3) Defer to existing Datadog priority levels and map them directly to ServiceNow severities with minimal new taxonomy definition.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Event prioritization configuration, monitor classification standards, and Datadog hygiene programme alignment.

decisions.title: Set incident creation policy for AIOps-correlated events
decisions.description: A decision is required on whether every actionable event should create an incident or whether some remediation can occur at the event level without incident records, based on correlation and classification outcomes.

decision_owner.name: AD Al-Ghourabi (TR Technology) with Service Management leadership

decisions.rationale: Incident creation policy determines the balance between visibility and noise. Creating incidents for all actionable events maintains legacy visibility but risks retaining the 1:1 event-to-incident pattern; restricting incidents to true exceptions reduces noise but requires strong confidence in correlation and remediation processes.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Every actionable event creates an incident.
2) Only exception-level events (as defined by the event taxonomy) create incidents; informational and warning events remain as events.
3) Some remediations are executed and recorded at the event level only, with incidents created only if remediation fails or service impact is detected.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Correlation rule tuning, event taxonomy definition, and incident management SLAs for Legal Tracker.

latest_report.content:
## **Executive Summary**

**Scope:** Cobalt Modernization is migrating Cobalt and Novus Cloud components to AWS with Elastic Search to OpenSearch migration, S3-based document caching, and multi-phase .NET modernization for Westlaw Cobalt Cloud Services. The initiative targets $2.55M in 2026 cost savings through modernization and cloud optimization under the EPC-funded workstream.

**Current Status - AMBER** because Website modernization re-planned from 30 Jul to 30 Sep 2026 creating $274k savings variance. .NET Phase 0 delivered 27 Apr 2026 achieving $143k savings (6% of goal), with Phase 1 targeting 27 May 2026 and remaining milestones tracking to revised dates.

**Key outcomes delivered:**  
• .NET Phase 0 completed - Delivered 27 Apr 2026 with 41-day delay; $143k savings realized; approximately 6% of $2.55M goal achieved.  
• Phase 1 (Doc) progressing - Development underway; $1.46M savings targeted representing 57% of goal; tracking to 27 May 2026 delivery.  
• Website phase re-planned - Shifted from 30 Jul to 30 Sep 2026; $274k 2026 savings impact identified; feasibility assessment ongoing.  
• Elastic Search migration initiated - Five instances mapped; OpenSearch architecture defined; maintaining 01 Oct 2026 target deadline.  
• S3 Document Store advancing - Solution architecture validated; phased approach under evaluation; 01 Jul 2026 target date retained.

**Active RAID items:**  
• I1 — Issue: Website modernization delayed to 30 Sep 2026 creating largest savings gap. Mitigation: Lock feasible delivery profile; validate revised savings timeline; align stakeholder expectations; communicate impact assessment.  
• R1 — Risk: Development resources added from Platform Eng team for Elastic Search migration impacting October deadline. Mitigation: Assessment to see if timeline can be confirmed up in mid-June due to the adding of resources.

## **Path to Green**

Status returns to GREEN by locking feasible Website and S3 Document Store delivery profiles, securing overdue development commitments for Elastic Search migration, and finalizing detailed migration plans ensuring all EPC savings-bearing milestones achieve by 01 Oct 2026.

## **Next Steps**

• Finalize Website delivery profile - Lock feasible timeline; confirm savings realization approach; align stakeholder expectations — by 12 June.  
• Secure Elastic Search resources - Obtain formal development commitments; detail migration plan; confirm instance priorities — by 12 June.  
• Complete Phase 1 (Doc) - Finalize development work; execute integration testing; deploy to production environment — by 27 May.  
• Validate S3 Document Store approach - Confirm phased delivery model; revise savings profile; lock implementation timeline — by 12 June.  
• Progress Website modernization - Initiate development sprint; establish quality checkpoints; track against 30 Sep target — from 01 Jun.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

The IFS (ERP) Cloud Migration project is moving the Pagero IFS Cloud ERP from Nordlo’s on-premise datacentre into a Muzulu-managed Azure environment, with primary Oracle in Azure Sweden Central and DR in Azure Ireland, to improve scalability, resilience, and RTO/RPO while aligning to Thomson Reuters’ cloud-first strategy. Core finance, procurement, supply chain, and reporting processes will continue to operate on a lift-and-shift basis, preserving existing functionality and integrations.

As of 31 Mar 2026, the overall delivery plan is reported 47% complete and late, with the Migration Planning phase 55% complete and trending two weeks beyond its original 17 May 2026 end date (latest estimate 31 May 2026). A key dependency has been cleared with SRB approval for the DR design and migration approach obtained on 21 May 2026, and the production go-live latest estimate has been moved from 20 Jun 2026 to 15 Jul 2026 to accommodate integration and DR readiness.

Overall status is Green, driven by closure of the SRB approval dependency on 21 May 2026, which unlocks Test migration and subsequent execution toward the revised 15 Jul 2026 go-live.

## Path to Green

The top RAID focus is mitigating the risk that a mid-July cutover collides with the European vacation period by completing a structured resource and vacation-planning exercise with all integration and business teams by 30 Jun 2026 and adjusting the final cutover window or coverage roster as needed.

## Milestones

- Complete the Migration Planning Phase and the Migration Execution Phase for the Test environment by 31 May 2026.  
- Achieve UAT signoff for CFG/Test and complete DR testing by 11 Jun 2026.  
- Complete the Migration Execution Phase for the Production environment and secure the Go-No-Go decision by 19 Jun 2026.  
- Deliver Production Go-Live of IFS Cloud ERP on Muzulu Azure Cloud by 15 Jul 2026.  
- Complete post Go-Live hypercare and close the project by 31 Jul 2026.

risks.title: Boomi IP whitelisting and performance testing may not be completed in time for Azure migration
risks.description: Boomi currently exposes services connecting to Conga GSI and ECX/ECM (MDM) that integrate with IFS. Manjunatha reported that the Boomi team expects no application-level service changes as long as endpoints remain the same, but they stated that they will need to whitelist new IP addresses once IFS servers/VMs are created in Azure and will also perform connectivity and load/performance testing. If Boomi-side IP whitelisting and planned tests are not executed in a timely and coordinated way, Boomi integrations may fail or underperform after migration, potentially impacting cutover.
risks.impact_description:
If Boomi does not whitelist the new Azure IP addresses and complete connectivity and load testing:
- Boomi services for Conga GSI and ECX/ECM (MDM) may be unable to connect to the migrated IFS environment, causing integration failures.
- Even if connectivity is established, untested performance could result in degraded response times or throughput issues after go-live, impacting dependent business functions.
- Failures or performance problems could be detected late (during or after cutover), forcing emergency fixes, delaying the go-live, or causing post-go-live instability and rework.
risks.mitigation:
1) Engage Boomi team early: Ravi and Manjunatha will "get them engaged" now, clarify the exact IPs that will need whitelisting on the Boomi side once Azure VMs are created, and agree how and when Boomi will apply the whitelist changes.
2) Define a testing approach: jointly define with Boomi what connectivity, functional, and load/performance tests will be run. Manjunatha emphasized running scripts in lower environments first and then comparing lower-to-lower, with options to also test on production-like hardware.
3) Schedule testing windows: include Boomi testing activities in the detailed migration plan (test, CFG, and Prod phases), sharing timelines so Boomi can plan resources and scripts accordingly.
4) Track whitelisting and test completion as explicit items in the project plan and integration checklist, ensuring they are completed before each environment cutover.
risks.source_file_name: IFS Cloud Migration - Weekly Planning call-22-Apr.docx

risks.title: Delay or failure in coordinating DNS changes with TR IT may extend test environment outage during Azure migration
risks.description: The team plans to migrate the IFS test environment to Muzulu Azure over the weekend of 8–10 May 2026, including cloning the 1.6 TB Oracle database and then changing DNS entries so that existing URLs point to the new Azure-hosted environment. Ravi noted that from the project’s perspective this looks straightforward (clone DB, bring up system, change DNS), but they still need to understand which Thomson Reuters IT/networking team owns the relevant DNS records and how that change process will work. If DNS ownership, change process, or resourcing is unclear or those teams are unavailable during or immediately after the migration window, DNS updates could be delayed, causing a longer-than-expected outage of the IFS test environment and undermining the goal of minimising disruption for development teams.
risks.impact_description:
If DNS changes are not executed promptly during or after the 8–10 May test migration window:
- The IFS test environment may remain unreachable via the standard URLs, preventing developers from accessing it for ongoing work and delaying bridging UAT/SIT preparation.
- Planned testing of integrations against the Azure-hosted test environment (including Boomi, EDL/FireTran, Pagero Online, SFTP and other HTTPS-based integrations) will be delayed, slowing learning and pushing out timelines for CFG and production migrations.
- Any issues discovered late in DNS cutover may require additional coordination and change windows with TR IT, adding administrative overhead and potentially impacting the broader migration schedule and stakeholder confidence in the plan.
- Extended unplanned downtime of the test environment could force teams to shift activity back to Nordlo-hosted environments or delay work altogether, causing rework and confusion.
risks.mitigation:
1) Identify DNS ownership: Ravi and Manjunatha will confirm which TR IT/networking/infra team owns the DNS records for IFS URLs used by test, CFG and production.
2) Define the change process: agree the exact steps, lead times, and approvals required to update DNS for the test environment migration, including any change tickets or CAB reviews.
3) Schedule DNS changes for the migration window: align DNS change implementation with the planned 8–10 May 2026 test migration window, ensuring appropriate TR IT coverage during and immediately after the change.
4) Document rollback: define a clear rollback plan (e.g., revert DNS to Nordlo endpoints) in case issues are detected after cutover.
5) Communicate to stakeholders: inform development and integration teams of the planned DNS change window and expected test environment downtime so that they can plan work accordingly.
risks.source_file_name: IFS Cloud Migration - Weekly Planning call - 22-Apr.docx

risks.title: Delay in confirming IFS integration connectivity details may impact SRB approval and migration timeline
risks.description: Key technical details for IFS Cloud ERP integrations (Boomi, EDL, Pagero Online, SFTP-based flows) are not yet fully understood or documented at the connectivity/port level. Ravi and Manjunatha agreed they still need to (1) speak with Bhanuka regarding Pagero Online and SFTP usage, (2) speak with the EDL contact to confirm how EDL currently pulls data from IFS (FireTran and AWS Glue), and (3) clarify how each integration actually connects (HTTP(S), SFTP, other). These details are required to update the network/integration diagram that will be used for SRB review and approval of the DR and connectivity architecture. If these integration details are not obtained “pretty quickly,” the SRB review could be delayed, which in turn may delay the planned end-of-June cutover/go-live.
risks.impact_description:
If the team cannot obtain and document detailed connectivity information (endpoints, ports, connection methods) for Boomi, EDL, Pagero Online, and SFTP integrations in time:
- The network/integration diagram for SRB will be incomplete, leading to delayed SRB review and approval of the DR and connectivity design.
- Migration planning for integrations and test execution will be delayed because the team will not know exactly what needs to be configured in Azure and in connected systems.
- The overall migration schedule, including phase-one test migration and the targeted end-of-June production cutover, may slip, potentially impacting dependent business activities and stakeholder confidence.
risks.mitigation:
1) In the next 1–2 weeks while DB cloning is in progress, Manjunatha will contact the EDL owner ("EDL guy") to confirm the exact technology and method used to pull data from IFS (e.g., FireTran, AWS Glue, ports/protocols).
2) Ravi will set up and lead a call with Bhanuka and relevant Pagero Online contacts to clarify how Pagero Online and any SFTP-based processes integrate with IFS and which endpoints/ports are used.
3) Ravi will update the network/integration diagram to show one box per integration (e.g., Boomi, EDL, Pagero Online, SFTP) with explicit connection methods and port numbers, avoiding generic "endpoints" labels.
4) The updated diagram will be used for SRB and architecture discussions so concerns can be addressed and approval obtained by the end of the month, protecting the end-of-June cutover timeline.

risks.title: Muzulu DR backup-and-restore approach not aligned with existing DR solution
risks.description: The proposed disaster recovery (DR) approach from Muzulu uses backup and restore at the backend with a three-node high-availability cluster at the frontend for the IFS ERP system. Although this design is expected to meet the defined RTO and RPO objectives, it differs from the existing DR solution and may be time-consuming if database backups take longer than usual. Misalignment with the current DR model and potentially extended restore times could affect acceptance and operational resilience for the migrated ERP platform.
risks.impact_description: If the Muzulu backup-and-restore DR strategy is adopted and database backups or restores take longer than expected, recovery from a major incident could exceed planned timelines, leading to prolonged ERP downtime. This could disrupt finance, procurement, supply chain, and reporting processes during an outage. Additionally, because the approach is not aligned with the existing DR solution, there may be governance or stakeholder acceptance issues that delay sign-off or require rework of the DR design, potentially impacting the migration schedule and costs.
risks.mitigation: Muzulu is revising the DR design to provide a dedicated DR site in the North Europe Azure region, using Oracle Data Guard replication from the primary site. This approach is intended to address concerns raised by Eric and others about DR capability by providing a more standard, continuously replicated DR environment rather than relying mainly on time-consuming backup-and-restore operations. Gareth will be available to explain the updated DR architecture in detail to the SRB/board and to Eric, while Ravi updates the network/integration diagrams to incorporate accurate integration points and connectivity into this DR design. The team is targeting SRB approval by the end of April so that the updated DR approach is fully accepted before proceeding with the main test migration (phase one).

risks.title: Limited ability to test EDL/Data Factory integrations against Azure-hosted IFS Test environment
risks.description: During the 18 May 2026 integration kickoff call, Pransh (representing the Data Factory/EDL team) highlighted that there is currently no live Data Factory/Glue pipeline connected to the IFS Test Oracle instance; only CFG has an active pipeline (and even there, primarily via FireTran, not Glue). Phase 1 of the migration plan assumes validation of data lake/EDL integrations using the migrated IFS Test environment in Muzulu Azure. If no suitable non-production pipeline or test bed is available for Test, the team may be unable to properly exercise FireTran/AWS Glue and related ingestion paths before CFG and Production migrations.
risks.impact_description:
If EDL/Data Factory cannot test against an Azure-hosted non-production IFS database:
- Data ingestion paths (via FireTran and/or AWS Glue) may not be validated until CFG or even Production cutover, increasing the chance that connectivity, authentication, or performance issues are discovered late.
- Undetected issues could cause failures in loading Pagero/IFS data into EDL/Snowflake after go-live, impacting downstream consumers such as HighRadius and finance reporting.
- Late discovery of defects may trigger emergency fixes, rework of pipelines, or rollbacks, consuming contingency and potentially delaying CFG/Production cutovers.
- Confidence in the migration and in the stability of the data platform may be reduced for business and technology stakeholders.
risks.mitigation:
1) Work with the Data Factory/EDL team (Pransh, Eljo) to define a viable non-production test path: either (a) stand up a limited-scope test pipeline pointing to the migrated IFS Test Oracle instance, or (b) agree that initial validation will occur in CFG with clear scope and rollback criteria.
2) Capture the chosen approach in the migration plan, including which environment (Test vs CFG) will be used for first connectivity and functional tests for FireTran/Glue and what data volumes will be used.
3) Schedule a follow-up working session with Data Factory/EDL to design and configure any required test pipelines and credentials ahead of the Test or CFG migration window.
4) Ensure EDL-related test cases are included in the end-to-end test plan (owned by Bhanuka and the testing lead) so that at least basic ingestion, schema mapping, and performance checks are executed prior to Production cutover.
5) If an adequate test bed cannot be established in time, explicitly update the risk register and adjust the cutover plan to reflect higher risk and additional monitoring/rollback safeguards.

risks.title: Mid-July production cutover may collide with European vacation period, reducing availability of key integration and business resources
risks.description: In the 18 May 2026 integration call, Johan (Pagero Online/finance upload owner) noted that the currently proposed production go-live in mid-July falls in the middle of the European vacation period. He warned that it will be difficult to "get hold of people" during this time. The migration plan currently targets weeks 29–30 (mid-July) for production cutover, but has not yet factored in regional holiday/vacation constraints for integration and finance stakeholders.
risks.impact_description:
If production cutover proceeds during peak European vacation weeks without adequate resourcing:
- Key integration owners (e.g., Pagero Online, Boomi, EDL/Data Factory, finance SFTP owners) and finance/business approvers may be unavailable for final testing, go/no-go decisions, and hypercare.
- Limited on-call and support coverage could slow incident response to any integration or functional issues, increasing outage duration and customer impact.
- The project may be forced to accept higher operational risk or to postpone cutover at short notice if critical roles cannot be filled, impacting the mid-July target and downstream projects.
- Business confidence may be eroded if go-live activities conflict with known vacation patterns, especially for a critical ERP platform handling orders and finance processes.

raised_by.name: Lindblom, Johan M. (TR Technology, Pagero Online/finance upload)

risks.mitigation:
1) Work with Bhanuka, Manjunatha, Johan and other integration owners to map key European vacation periods and identify specific weeks where coverage would be insufficient for a major cutover.
2) Evaluate alternative cutover windows (e.g., late June or early September) and discuss trade-offs with Veena (sponsor) and Pagero finance leadership, documenting any decision in the project decisions log.
3) If mid-July remains the target, define a minimum required roster for go-live and hypercare (integration owners, finance approvers, support engineers) and secure explicit commitments, including backup resources where primary contacts are on leave.
4) Include vacation coverage checks in pre-go-live readiness reviews, ensuring that each critical integration/system has at least one available owner and one backup during the cutover and initial hypercare period.
5) Communicate the agreed cutover window and coverage expectations early to all affected teams so they can plan vacations accordingly.
risks.source_file_name: IFS environment Migration from Nordlo to Muzulu-18-May-2026.docx

risks.title: Insufficient regression and performance testing of Boomi and other integrations before go-live
risks.description: Ram (Boomi team) raised concerns in the 18 May 2026 call about regression testing for all integrations, noting that Pagero/IFS is a critical ERP and order failures could trigger P1 incidents. He emphasized the need to involve their testing lead (Soundar Rajanna) and to run at least one end-to-end business transaction in testing. Manjunatha confirmed that regression and performance testing (including Boomi response time checks, previously discussed with Chaitanya and Karthick) is in the plan, but detailed timelines and onboarding of the Boomi testing lead have not yet been finalised. Given tight schedules, there is a risk that regression/performance testing is compressed or incomplete.
risks.impact_description:
If thorough regression and performance testing of Boomi and other integrations is not completed before go-live:
- Critical business flows (orders, customer data, finance transactions) may fail or behave incorrectly after migration, potentially triggering high-severity (P1) incidents.
- Latent performance issues (e.g., increased response times through Boomi due to Azure routing) may not be identified until production, degrading user experience and downstream processes.
- Boomi and other integration teams may have insufficient evidence to sign off on the migration, causing last-minute objections or delaying the go-live decision.
- Post-go-live firefighting and hotfix work could increase, consuming project and operational resources and potentially impacting other initiatives.
risks.mitigation:
1) Formally onboard the Boomi testing lead (Soundar Rajanna) into the migration project, including him in planning meetings and test design sessions.
2) Define a regression testing scope that covers at least one end-to-end business transaction for each critical integration path (e.g., order flow, customer updates, finance postings) across Test/CFG, prioritising Boomi flows.
3) Agree specific performance test scenarios with the Boomi team (building on prior discussions with Chaitanya and Karthick) to benchmark response times before and after migration, and schedule these within the Test and CFG windows.
4) Capture regression and performance tests as explicit tasks in the test plan owned by Bhanuka and the testing lead, with clear exit criteria for Boomi signoff.
5) Ensure that the go/no-go checklist includes confirmation that Boomi regression and performance testing has been completed and accepted; if not, either defer cutover or explicitly document residual risk and compensating controls.
risks.source_file_name: IFS environment Migration from Nordlo to Muzulu-18-May-2026.docx

risks.title: Continued reliance on Nordlo-hosted SFTP servers for finance uploads after IFS migration increases operational complexity and dependency
risks.description: In the 18 May 2026 meeting, Johan explained that transactional finance data is uploaded once a month to an SFTP server hosted by Nordlo, from which IFS reads the data. He asked whether this SFTP would also be moved to Muzulu Azure. Ravi responded that there is currently no plan to move these SFTP servers; the focus is on lifting and shifting IFS, keeping other endpoints "as is". However, Manjunatha noted that, ideally, such SFTP services should also be moved to avoid maintaining infrastructure with two different vendors (Nordlo and Muzulu). This introduces a risk of prolonged dependence on Nordlo-hosted SFTP infrastructure after IFS is moved.
risks.impact_description:
If Nordlo-hosted SFTP servers for finance uploads remain in place without a clear migration or decommissioning plan:
- The project and operations teams will need to maintain security, whitelisting, and support arrangements with two vendors (Nordlo and Muzulu) for related integrations, increasing coordination overhead and potential points of failure.
- Any future changes in Nordlo's hosting, contracts, or security posture could affect the availability of the finance SFTP, potentially disrupting monthly finance uploads and IFS inbound processing.
- The longer the split infrastructure persists, the harder it may become to schedule and execute a later SFTP migration, as dependencies and stakeholders change over time.
- Audit and governance reviews may question why critical finance-related data flows continue to rely on an older vendor after the core ERP has moved to Azure.

raised_by.name: Lindblom, Johan M. (TR Technology, Pagero Online/finance upload)

risks.mitigation:
1) Document all Nordlo-hosted SFTP endpoints currently used by IFS (including the monthly finance upload) in the integration inventory, with clear ownership and criticality.
2) Engage finance and Pagero Online stakeholders (including Johan and Simon) to determine whether these SFTP services should be migrated to Muzulu/TR-managed infrastructure as part of, or shortly after, the IFS migration.
3) If migration is agreed, define a small follow-on workstream to design, build, and cut over equivalent SFTP services in Azure, including appropriate DNS, certificates, and access controls.
4) In the interim, ensure network connectivity, whitelisting, and monitoring between the Azure-hosted IFS and Nordlo SFTP are robust and documented, and include these flows in integration and regression testing.
5) Set a review date post-go-live to reassess the continued need for Nordlo SFTP and reduce dual-vendor dependencies where possible.
risks.source_file_name: IFS environment Migration from Nordlo to Muzulu-18-May-2026.docx

risks.title: Unidentified or mismanaged SFTP/SMTP integrations may fail after migration
risks.description: During the 13 May 2026 planning call, Ravi and Manjunatha reviewed SFTP and SMTP-based integrations (e.g., Pagero Online SFTP readers, PS Sync/payment collection feeds, and the "SMTP Pro Node" mail sender setup hosted by Nordlo). They noted that some SFTP readers and IP addresses (e.g., PO CSV SFTP reader, PS Sync) are not yet clearly owned or fully understood, and that the current SMTP relay (SMTP Pro Node) may still be using a Nordlo-hosted mail domain. If these SFTP endpoints and the SMTP relay are not fully identified, documented, and reconfigured/relayed correctly during the lift-and-shift to Muzulu Azure, file transfers and email notifications dependent on them may silently fail after migration.
risks.impact_description:
If SFTP and SMTP integrations are not correctly migrated and validated:
- Pagero Online–related SFTP flows (inbound and outbound) could stop working, leading to failed or delayed financial document exchanges and customer/supplier data updates.
- PS Sync/payment collection SFTP feeds could fail, disrupting payment collection processes and requiring manual workarounds.
- Emails currently sent via the Nordlo-hosted SMTP Pro Node might not be delivered if the relay is not correctly re-pointed to a TR-managed SMTP service, impacting notifications, alerts, or operational communications from IFS.
- Failures might only be detected after cutover, causing unplanned troubleshooting, temporary data gaps, delayed cash collection, and erosion of confidence in the migration.
- Recovery could require emergency coordination with Pagero, Nordlo, and TR networking/mail teams, potentially consuming migration contingency buffers and impacting other planned test or cutover activities.
risks.mitigation:
1) Use the upcoming integrations kickoff meeting (scheduled by Bhanuka for the Monday following the 13 May 2026 call) to explicitly identify all active SFTP readers and SMTP-based integrations related to IFS, including Pagero Online SFTP readers, PS Sync/payment collection feeds, and any other SFTP endpoints listed in the Connect framework.
2) Confirm, with Pagero/finance contacts (e.g., Simon Landmark) and relevant TR stakeholders, which SFTP feeds and PS Sync flows are still in active use versus decommissioned, and update the integration/contact list accordingly.
3) Engage Nordlo (NodeLo) separately, as Ravi suggested, to understand the current "SMTP Pro Node" configuration and to determine whether it can be safely replaced with a TR-managed SMTP relay; if it is just a simple relay, configure and test a new TR SMTP endpoint for IFS.
4) Update the integration/architecture diagrams to explicitly show these SFTP and SMTP flows (including PS Sync) so they are visible in SRB and architecture reviews.
5) Include targeted SFTP and email test cases in the IFS Test migration validation plan (e.g., sending/receiving sample files and emails) and ensure relevant application/finance owners perform sanity checks post-migration.
6) If any endpoints cannot be migrated as-is, raise specific design and change items early and adjust migration runbooks before CFG and production cutovers.
